chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basics of Production and IE
chunks.x:
Basics of Production and IE
Learn what Industrial Engineering (IE) is and acquire the common language of improvement: productivity, QCDS, 4M, value added, 3M and the 7 wastes.
Explain the purpose of IE and how it developed historically
Calculate productivity and view the shop floor through the QCDS and 4M frameworks
Distinguish value added from waste and identify the 7 wastes
Explain the relationship among muda, muri and mura (3M) and why mura leads to ZEVA
IE improves the system of work (people, machines, materials, methods) by observing, measuring and analysing
Productivity = output ÷ input — remove waste through the system, not by forcing speed
Evaluate results with QCDS; think about causes with 4M
Among the 7 wastes, overproduction is the worst
Mura (variation) breeds muda and muri; ZEVA focuses on this mura

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basics of Production and IE › What is IE?
chunks.x:
What is IE?
Industrial Engineering (IE) is the discipline of designing, improving and sustaining the “system of work” — the combination of people, machines, materials, methods and information — using scientific and engineering methods. Instead of relying only on intuition and experience, the basic attitude of IE is to observe, measure, think in numbers and change the system.
The essence of IE is to find and remove muda, muri and mura (waste, overburden, unevenness) hidden in work, so that the same resources produce more value, more stably.
History of IE: three pioneers
Taylor: time study
In the late 19th century he measured work with a stopwatch and proposed scientific management — setting a standard amount of work scientifically.
The Gilbreths: motion study
They filmed and analysed motions such as bricklaying, split them into basic units (therbligs) and searched for the “one best way”.
Today: improving the system
Time and motion study evolved into process analysis, line balancing, quality control and lean production, forming the base of modern improvement activity.
Two pillars of IE
Pillar
Question
Main methods
Method study
What is the best way to do it?
Process analysis, motion study, ECRS
Work measurement
How long does it take?
Time study, standard time, work sampling
The basic order is: improve the method first, then measure the time.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basics of Production and IE › Productivity and QCDS
chunks.x:
Productivity and QCDS
Productivity is the ratio of results obtained (output) to resources invested (input).
Productivity = Output ÷ Input
units produced, good units, value added, etc.
man-hours, machine hours, materials, energy, etc.
On the shop floor the most common is labour productivity = units ÷ man-hours (units per man-hour).
Worked example: labour productivity
Line A: 5 people × 8 h = 40 man-hours, producing 200 units
Productivity = 200 ÷ 40 = 5.0 units/man-hour
After improvement: 4 people × 8 h = 32 man-hours, same 200 units
Productivity = 200 ÷ 32 = 6.25 units/man-hour
Productivity rose by 6.25 ÷ 5.0 = 1.25×, i.e. +25%.
“Make people work faster” is not productivity improvement
IE does not aim to overwork people; it aims to remove wasted motion and waiting through the system. Forcing speed increases muri and mura and worsens quality and safety.
QCDS: the evaluation axes of the shop floor
QCDS are the four basic axes for measuring manufacturing results. Environment is sometimes added (QCDSE).
Q: Quality
defect rate, repair, customer complaints
C: Cost
man-hours, material cost, inventory, energy
D: Delivery
lead time, on-time delivery, output
S: Safety
accidents, near misses, workload
Connection to ZEVA

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basics of Production and IE › Productivity and QCDS
chunks.x:

D: Delivery
lead time, on-time delivery, output
S: Safety
accidents, near misses, workload
Connection to ZEVA

ZEVA holds that “variation is the root of all QCDS losses”. Rather than chasing each QCDS metric separately, it controls the variation that causes them, aiming to improve QCDS simultaneously.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basics of Production and IE › 4M: the four elements of production
chunks.x:
4M: the four elements of production
Every production activity is a combination of four elements called 4M. When a problem occurs, asking “which of the 4Ms changed?” is the basic pattern for finding the cause.
Element
Content
Examples of change / variation
Man
skill, proficiency, condition of workers
a newcomer takes twice as long as a veteran
Machine
equipment, jigs & tools, gauges
tool wear makes dimensions drift
Material
raw material, parts, consumables
part hardness differs by lot
Method
procedures, conditions, standards
“tighten firmly” is interpreted differently by each person
From 4M to 7 factors
ZEVA extends the 4M with Measurement, Management and Environment into the “7 variation factors” it controls. You will study them in the ZEVA Foundations track.
“Painting defects increase on humid days.” This hardly fits any of the 4Ms. Which of ZEVA’s 7 factors is it?
Measurement
Environment
Management
Temperature, humidity and lighting are Environment factors, managed within defined ranges.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basics of Production and IE › Value added and waste
chunks.x:
Value added and waste
Value added means giving the product a change the customer is willing to pay for. Machining, assembling, fastening — the moments when shape or properties change for the product’s function are value added.
On the other hand, carrying, searching, waiting, counting and inspecting do not change the product. They are non-value time and should be reduced. On real shop floors it is common that only a small part of work time actually adds value.
Adds value
the moment a bolt reaches specified torque
the time a drill is cutting a hole
the moment paint is applied to the surface
Does not add value
walking to the parts shelf
searching for or switching tools
waiting for parts from the previous process
Toward the three categories of the theoretical value
Theoretical value, the base of ZEVA, strictly splits work into value, semi-value and non-value. It distinguishes work that is minimally necessary with the current method, such as “grasping a part”, as semi-value.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basics of Production and IE › 3M: muda, muri, mura
chunks.x:
3M: muda, muri, mura
The targets of improvement are called “3M” after three Japanese words. The three are linked to each other as causes and effects.
Muda (waste)
Muda (waste): activity that adds no value. Capacity > load. e.g. waiting, transport, overproduction.
Muri (overburden)
Muri (overburden): loading people or machines beyond capacity. Capacity < load. e.g. lifting heavy items in bad posture, overloading machines.
Mura (unevenness)
Mura (unevenness): muda and muri alternate and the state is not constant. e.g. output varies greatly by day, work time differs every cycle.
Example: mura creates muri and muda
A process takes 25 s sometimes and 45 s at other times (mura)
At 45 s, the next process waits for parts (muda)
To catch up, the worker rushes (muri)
Rushing causes defects such as missed tightening (quality loss)
If mura is left alone, muda and muri follow in a chain.
Mura = variation: the starting point of ZEVA
Traditional improvement focused on “removing waste”. But where mura (variation) is large, values change every time you measure, and you cannot correctly judge where the real loss is. ZEVA is a production system that shifts the focus from waste removal to eliminating variation (mura).

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basics of Production and IE › The 7 wastes
chunks.x:
The 7 wastes
To make waste easier to spot, typical wastes are classified into the Seven wastes. Once you can name “which waste is this?”, waste becomes visible on the floor.
Waste
Description
Floor example
① Overproduction
making more or earlier than needed; the worst waste
building ahead for the next order and stacking it
② Waiting
people or machines idle
watching a machine run its automatic cycle
③ Transport
unnecessary moving or re-handling of goods
moving twice via a temporary storage area
④ Over-processing
extra processing that adds no quality
polishing a hidden surface to a mirror finish
⑤ Inventory
stagnant materials, WIP, products
piles of WIP between processes
⑥ Motion
body motion that adds no value
turning or bending every time to pick a part
⑦ Defects
defects, repair, scrap
disassembling and reassembling after a mistake
Why overproduction is the worst
Overproduction creates inventory, transport and storage space, and hides other wastes such as defects and waiting.
Which waste? Classify the floor examples
Overproduction
Waiting
Transport
Over-processing
Inventory
Motion
Defects
The parts box is behind the bench; the worker turns around every time
Unnecessary body motion = motion waste. Placing parts within reach removes it.
The first process kept producing although the downstream was stopped
Making earlier than needed = overproduction.

chunks.x:

Making earlier than needed = overproduction.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basics of Production and IE › Seeing the floor with IE eyes
chunks.x:
Seeing the floor with IE eyes
Before learning individual IE techniques, grasp the basic flow of improvement. Each module in this track is a tool used somewhere in this flow.
① Observe
go and see the real place and things
② Measure
quantify time, counts, distance
③ Analyse
identify muda, muri, mura
④ Improve
change the method with ECRS
⑤ Standardize
make the good method the standard
Module
Tool you gain
compare required pace and actual ability with TT, CT, lead time
measure work time correctly and set standard time
find motion waste with motion study
find waste in the whole flow with process analysis
remove imbalance between processes with line balancing
visualise equipment losses with OEE
handle variation numerically with statistics, control charts, capability
implement and sustain improvement with 5S, standard work, ECRS, QC tools
The three “gen” principle
Go to the real place, look at the real thing, grasp the real facts. Not judging only from data in the meeting room is the first step of IE.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basics of Production and IE › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: A line produces 240 units with 5 people × 8 hours. What is labour productivity?
A: 6.0 units/man-hour
Man-hours = 5 × 8 = 40. 240 ÷ 40 = 6.0 units/man-hour.
Q: What does “D” in QCDS stand for?
A: Delivery
Q = quality, C = cost, D = delivery, S = safety.
Q: Which of the following adds value?
A: Fastening a screw to fix a part
Only fastening changes the product for its function. Carrying, counting and waiting do not.
Q: Which of the 7 wastes is called the worst because it hides other wastes?
A: Overproduction
Overproduction creates inventory and transport and makes problems like defects and waiting invisible.
Q: “Work time changes between 25 s and 45 s each cycle” is which of the 3Ms?
A: Mura
An unstable state = mura (variation), which triggers muda and muri.
Q: Which set does ZEVA add to the 4M to make 7 factors?
A: Measurement, Management, Environment
ZEVA’s 7 variation factors are the 4M plus measurement, management and environment.
Q: What is the basic order of method study and work measurement in IE?
A: Improve the method first, then measure time
Precisely timing a bad method has little value, so first improve the method, then time it and make it the standard.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Basics: TT, CT and Lead Time
chunks.x:
Time Basics: TT, CT and Lead Time
Learn the meaning and calculation of available time, takt time, cycle time, lead time and capacity, and compare the required pace with the actual ability of the floor.
Calculate available time and takt time
Explain the difference and relationship between cycle time and takt time
Break lead time into its components
Calculate capacity and judge surplus or shortage against demand
Available time = shift time − planned stops; do not subtract unplanned stops
TT = available time ÷ demand — the pace set by the customer
CT is the floor’s ability — look at variation, not only the average
Most lead time is stagnation — find where the flow stops
Line capacity is set by the bottleneck CT

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Basics: TT, CT and Lead Time › Available time: how much time can we use?
chunks.x:
Available time: how much time can we use?
Time calculation starts by correctly determining the “time usable for production”. Available time is shift time minus breaks, meetings, planned cleaning and other time planned not to produce.
Available time = Shift time − Planned stops (breaks, meetings, cleaning, etc.)
Do not subtract unexpected breakdowns or waiting. Those are losses to be improved later.
Worked example
Shift: 8:00–17:00 = 540 min
Lunch 60 min, two 10-min breaks, 10-min morning meeting
Planned stops = 60 + 20 + 10 = 90 min
Available time = 540 − 90 = 450 min = 27,000 s
450 minutes per day are available for production.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Basics: TT, CT and Lead Time › Takt time (TT): the pace set by the customer
chunks.x:
Takt time (TT): the pace set by the customer
Takt time (TT) shows how often one unit must be made to exactly meet customer demand. “Takt” is German for the conductor’s beat — it represents the rhythm of production.
TT = Available time ÷ Required quantity
available time per day (or shift), in seconds
required quantity (demand) in the same period
TT is a reference value determined by market demand; the floor cannot change it on its own.
Worked example: TT
Available time 27,000 s, daily demand 450 units
TT = 27,000 ÷ 450 = 60 s
If demand rises to 540, TT = 27,000 ÷ 540 = 50 s
The higher the demand, the shorter the TT and the faster the rhythm required.
Do not misunderstand TT
TT is not “how fast we can make” but “at what pace we should make”. Producing faster than TT becomes overproduction; slower causes late delivery.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Basics: TT, CT and Lead Time › Cycle time (CT): the actual ability of the floor
chunks.x:
Cycle time (CT): the actual ability of the floor
Cycle time (CT) is the actual time one process (or worker) needs to complete one cycle of work. If TT is the demand side’s request, CT is the supply side’s ability.
Relationship
State
What happens
Capacity shortage
overtime, late delivery, overburden (muri)
Balanced
flows with demand (but collapses if variation exists)
Capacity surplus
overproduction, waiting (muda); room to rebalance people/processes
Cautions when measuring CT
Measure several (10+) consecutive cycles, not just once
Decide the start and end points (break points) in advance
Record and separate cycles containing abnormalities such as part shortage or machine stops
Look not only at the average but at the gap between minimum and maximum (variation)
Look at CT as a distribution, not an average
Even if average CT is shorter than TT, large CT variation means some cycles exceed TT and the line stops. ZEVA quantifies CT variation with V.Score (σ/μ) and never evaluates by average alone.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Basics: TT, CT and Lead Time › Lead time: from order to delivery
chunks.x:
Lead time: from order to delivery
Lead time is the total elapsed time from a start point (material input, order receipt) to an end point (completion, shipment, delivery). While CT is “time to process one unit”, lead time includes all waiting, transport and stagnation.
Production lead time = Processing + Inspection + Transport + Stagnation (waiting)
Worked example: inside a lead time
Total processing time of 3 processes: 3 min
Inspection: 2 min, transport between processes: 10 min
Waiting in WIP areas between processes: 2 days total (960 min of working time)
Lead time = 3 + 2 + 10 + 960 = 975 min
Processing share = 3 ÷ 975 ≈ 0.3%
Most of the lead time is stagnation. Removing stagnation is far more effective than speeding up processing.
What should you look at first to shorten lead time?
Increase processing speed
Reduce stagnation and waiting
Add inspections
Stagnation usually makes up most of the lead time, so first find where the flow stops.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Basics: TT, CT and Lead Time › Capacity and pitch
chunks.x:
Capacity and pitch
Capacity is the maximum quantity that can be made in a given time. The capacity of a whole line is determined by its slowest process (the bottleneck).
Capacity (units) = Available time ÷ CT of the bottleneck process
Worked example: the bottleneck decides capacity
CTs of 4 processes: 48 s, 55 s, 62 s, 50 s
Bottleneck CT = 62 s
Capacity = 27,000 ÷ 62 ≈ 435 units
Against demand of 450 (TT 60 s): 15 units short
Bringing the 62-s bottleneck to 60 s or less is the top-priority theme.
Pitch (pitch time)
When parts or products move in containers, “TT × pack quantity” is called pitch, used as the interval for conveyance or production instructions. e.g. TT 60 s and 10 pcs per box → pitch = 600 s (10 min), one box withdrawn every 10 minutes.
Position in ZEVA
“Takt-time production” — matching CT to TT — is only achieved with good line balance and stable variation. In ZEVA, capacity calculated from the average of an unstable CT is not considered reliable.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Basics: TT, CT and Lead Time › Organising the time metrics
chunks.x:
Organising the time metrics
Metric
Who decides?
Meaning
Main use
Available time
company work schedule
time usable for production
TT & capacity calculation
customer (demand)
pace we should produce at
basis for staffing & line design
floor methods & equipment
actual time taken
ability assessment, finding targets
Lead time
the whole flow
total time from start to end
delivery responsiveness, finding stagnation
Capacity
bottleneck process
maximum quantity possible
judging surplus/shortage vs demand
Keep units consistent
Many calculation errors come from mixed units (minutes vs seconds). Make it a habit to calculate TT and CT in seconds.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Basics: TT, CT and Lead Time › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Available time 450 min, demand 360 units. What is TT?
A: 75 s
450 min = 27,000 s. 27,000 ÷ 360 = 75 s.
Q: What should be subtracted when calculating available time?
A: Planned break time
Only planned stops (breaks, etc.) are subtracted. Breakdowns, waiting and repair remain as losses to improve.
Q: What tends to happen when CT > TT?
A: Overtime and late delivery
Ability cannot keep up with the demand pace, causing overtime, delays and overburden.
Q: A line has process CTs of 40, 45, 58, 50, 44 s. Capacity with 27,000 s available?
A: about 465 units
Capacity is set by the bottleneck (58 s). 27,000 ÷ 58 ≈ 465 units.
Q: What usually takes the largest share of production lead time?
A: Stagnation / waiting time
Goods waiting between processes usually dominate, making this the largest improvement opportunity.
Q: Average CT is shorter than TT, yet the line is sometimes late. Most likely reason?
A: CT varies a lot, so some cycles exceed TT
Even with a good average, large variation creates cycles above TT. This is one reason ZEVA emphasises variation.
Q: TT 45 s, conveyed in boxes of 20. What is the pitch?
A: 900 s (15 min)
Pitch = TT × pack quantity = 45 × 20 = 900 s.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Study and Standard Time
chunks.x:
Time Study and Standard Time
Learn the procedure of stopwatch time study, breaking work into elements, number of observations, rating and allowances, setting standard time, and an overview of PTS.
Explain the preparation and procedure of a time study
Break work into elements and summarise observation records
Calculate standard time from normal time, rating and allowance
Read variation in measurements and judge the need for standardization
Time study measures methods, not people — explain the purpose and gain cooperation
Split into elements with recognisable break points and measure 10+ consecutive cycles
Minimum = method ability, mean = planning basis, range = sign of variation
Standard time = observed × rating × (1 + allowance)
Large variation increases needed observations and lowers data reliability

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Study and Standard Time › What is time study?
chunks.x:
What is time study?
Time study is a method of directly observing work and measuring and analysing the time it takes with a stopwatch or video. It has three main purposes.
Set standard time
create a basis for staffing, costing and production planning
Find waste and variation
discover which elements are long or vary every cycle
Measure improvement effect
measure before and after with the same method and compare numerically
Time study is not “watching people”
The target of measurement is the work method, not the person. Explaining the purpose and gaining worker cooperation in advance is a prerequisite for accurate data. If the worker is nervous and works differently, data reliability is lost.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Study and Standard Time › Time study procedure
chunks.x:
Time study procedure
1. Prepare
explain purpose, select work & worker, confirm standard WIP and conditions
2. Observe
watch several cycles, confirm the sequence is the same every time (if not, align it first)
3. Break into elements
define break points and list elements on the observation sheet
4. Measure
measure about 10+ consecutive cycles; note any abnormal cycle
5. Summarise & analyse
compute min, max, mean and variation per element and consider causes
6. Set standard time
apply rating and allowance to set the standard time
Measuring methods: continuous and snap-back
Method
How
Advantage
Disadvantage
Continuous
read the clock at each break point without stopping; subtract later
nothing is missed; abnormal time is also captured
more calculation afterwards
Snap-back
reset to zero at each element and read time directly
element times are known immediately
reset errors accumulate
Using video
Filming the work lets you replay frame by frame, making element break points precise, and lets several people discuss the same footage.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Study and Standard Time › Elements and number of observations
chunks.x:
Elements and number of observations
Work element are purpose-based chunks of one work cycle. Break points should be moments anyone can recognise by sound or motion, such as “the moment the hand touches the part” or “the moment the button is pressed”.
Element
End break point
Pick case and set in jig
sound of case hitting jig
Mount the board
moment the board clicks in
Tighten 4 screws
moment the driver is put down
Place unit on conveyor
moment the hand leaves the unit
Example element breakdown (fictional work for illustration)
How many observations?
On the floor, about 10 consecutive cycles is a practical start. Statistically, the more variation, the more observations are needed. For 95% confidence and ±5% error, the required number can be estimated as follows.
n ≈ ( 1.96 × σ ÷ (0.05 × μ) )² = ( 39.2 × V )²
mean of a pilot measurement
standard deviation of the pilot measurement
coefficient of variation σ/μ (same idea as ZEVA V.Score)
e.g. V = 0.05 → n ≈ 3.8, 4 cycles are enough. V = 0.15 → n ≈ 35 cycles. The larger the variation, the harder it is even to measure correctly.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Study and Standard Time › Minimum or mean: reading the measurements
chunks.x:
Minimum or mean: reading the measurements
Which value to take as the representative of 10 measurements depends on the purpose.
Representative value
Meaning
Main use
Minimum
the cycle with the least extra motion or hesitation = what the method can achieve
improvement target, basis of standard work time (common in lean practice)
Mean
time taken overall
basis for staffing and costing (standard time)
Max − Min (range)
cycle-to-cycle variation
detecting lack of standardization and problems
Worked example: 10 measurements
Values (s): 32, 30, 35, 31, 42, 30, 33, 31, 38, 30
Sum = 332, mean = 33.2 s
Min = 30 s, max = 42 s, range = 12 s
Video of the 42-s cycle shows “a part was dropped and picked up”
The gap to the mean (33.2 − 30 = 3.2 s) indicates the amount of waste and variation. Investigating long cycles is the entrance to improvement.
ZEVA view: first remove sequence variation
Measuring work whose sequence changes each time does not show the method’s ability. In ZEVA you first align the sequence with standard work (foundation = standardization), then measure CT and evaluate variation with V.Score (σ/μ) — because data with large variation is unreliable and cannot ground improvement actions.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Study and Standard Time › Standard time: rating and allowance
chunks.x:
Standard time: rating and allowance
Standard time is the time a qualified, trained worker needs to complete one unit using the specified method and equipment at a normal pace, including necessary allowances.
Standard time = Observed time × Rating factor × (1 + Allowance)
representative measured time (e.g. mean excluding abnormal cycles)
factor that adjusts the worker’s pace to “normal”; above 100% if faster
allowance for personal needs, fatigue and unavoidable delays
Observed time × rating factor is called “normal time” (basic time).
Rating
Rating (performance rating) is judging the observed worker’s pace against the normal pace of a standard worker. If the observed worker is 20% faster than normal, the rating is 120%, and normal time is adjusted upward. Even trained observers vary in judgment, so calibrating observers with reference videos is important.
Allowance
Type
Content
Guide (illustrative)
Personal allowance
drinking water, restroom
Fatigue allowance
recovery from fatigue due to load, posture, environment
Work allowance
unavoidable small delays, preparation
Management allowance
unavoidable management delays such as waiting for instructions
Worked example: standard time
Observed (mean) = 50 s, rating = 110%, allowance = 12%
Normal time = 50 × 1.10 = 55 s
Standard time = 55 × (1 + 0.12) = 61.6 s
Standard output per 27,000 s = 27,000 ÷ 61.6 ≈ 438 units

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Study and Standard Time › Standard time: rating and allowance
chunks.x:
110%, allowance = 12%
Normal time = 50 × 1.10 = 55 s
Standard time = 55 × (1 + 0.12) = 61.6 s
Standard output per 27,000 s = 27,000 ÷ 61.6 ≈ 438 units

Standard time is 61.6 s — the basis for staffing and production planning.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Study and Standard Time › PTS: setting time without a stopwatch
chunks.x:
PTS: setting time without a stopwatch
Predetermined Time Standards (Predetermined Time Standards) break work into basic motions such as reach, grasp and move, and sum predetermined time values for each motion type, distance and condition to obtain standard time. MTM and Work-Factor are well-known systems.
Stopwatch study
requires the actual work
rating includes observer subjectivity
relatively easy to learn
PTS
can estimate time at design stage (before the work exists)
no rating needed, more objective
requires skill in motion analysis
Relationship to theoretical values
Building up “the time a motion truly requires”, as PTS does, is close to the idea of the theoretical value (value work + minimum semi-value work) that is the base of ZEVA. Keep the viewpoint of designing “the time it should take”, not only measuring the present.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Study and Standard Time › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Observed 40 s, rating 90%, allowance 10%. Standard time?
A: 39.6 s
Normal time = 40 × 0.9 = 36 s; standard = 36 × 1.1 = 39.6 s.
Q: The observed worker was faster than normal. What happens to the rating?
A: Above 100%
A fast worker’s observed time is short, so a rating above 100% corrects it to normal-pace time.
Q: Which is the most suitable break point for an element?
A: “The moment the part clicks against the jig”
Break points anyone can recognise by sound or motion reduce measurement variation.
Q: What does a large “max − min” in measurements tell you?
A: Sign that the sequence or conditions are unstable and standardization is lacking
The range shows cycle-to-cycle variation and is a clue to investigate causes (sequence, parts, equipment, etc.).
Q: If the pilot coefficient of variation rises from 0.05 to 0.15, the required number of observations…
A: becomes about 9 times
n is proportional to V², so tripling V multiplies n by 9 (about 4 → about 35).
Q: Which is a correct feature of PTS?
A: Can estimate work time even at the design stage
Because it sums predetermined times per basic motion, time can be estimated before the line exists.
Q: Before a time study you find the sequence differs every time. What should you do first?
A: Align the sequence (standardize)

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Time Study and Standard Time › Quiz
chunks.x:
before the line exists.
Q: Before a time study you find the sequence differs every time. What should you do first?
A: Align the sequence (standardize)

Numbers measured with an inconsistent sequence do not represent the method and are unreliable. Align the sequence first (ZEVA’s “foundation = standardization”).

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy
chunks.x:
Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy
Break work into basic motions (therbligs) to find wasted movement, and design work that is easy, fast and stable using the principles of motion economy and work areas.
Classify therbligs into four groups
Find waste such as idle hands and holding with two-hand analysis
Explain and apply the principles of motion economy (body, workplace, tools)
Place parts and tools considering normal and maximum work areas
Motion study explains “why it takes time” at the motion level
Therbligs fall into 4 groups; improve class 3 (hesitation) and class 4 (holding, waiting) first
Motion economy basics: eliminate, reduce, simultaneous, easier
Place frequently used items in the normal work area and golden zone
Reducing, shortening and constraining motions cut both time and variation (ZEVA motion stability)

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy › What is motion study?
chunks.x:
What is motion study?
Motion study observes and analyses the movements of the hands and body in detail to find a method that removes useless motion and lets necessary motion be done more easily, quickly and reliably. While time study asks “how long?”, motion study asks “why does it take that long, and how should we move?”
Level of analysis
Unit
Example
Process
process / workstation
assembly process
Element
purposeful chunk
tighten 4 screws
Motion (therblig)
smallest motion of hand/foot
reach → grasp → move → position
Motion study works at the finest level: motions.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy › Therbligs
chunks.x:
Therbligs
Therbligs are about 18 basic motion symbols devised by the Gilbreths to classify human motion (the name is “Gilbreth” spelled roughly backwards). Grouping them into the four groups below makes the direction of improvement clear.
Group
Main therbligs
Improvement direction
Class 1: advance the work (directly valuable)
assemble, disassemble, use
support to do reliably and easily
Class 2: supporting motions
reach (transport empty), grasp, move (transport loaded), release, position, pre-position
shorten distance, reduce count
Class 3: slow the work (judgment, hesitation)
search, find, select, inspect, plan
eliminate by 3-tei, colour coding and jigs so no one hesitates
Class 4: no progress (waste)
hold, unavoidable delay, avoidable delay, rest
replace holding with jigs, remove waiting by process design
“Holding” is an easily missed waste
Holding a part with one hand while working with the other is the same as having only one working hand. Letting a jig or clamp hold it frees both hands for valuable motion.
Which group is this motion?
Class 1 Advance work
Class 2 Support
Class 3 Slow down
Class 4 No progress
Insert a connector into the board
Assembling the product = advancing the work.
Reach toward the parts box
Reach is a supporting motion; shorten the distance.
Select the right screw among similar ones

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy › Therbligs
chunks.x:
product = advancing the work.
Reach toward the parts box
Reach is a supporting motion; shorten the distance.
Select the right screw among similar ones

Selecting is hesitation; eliminate it with fixed items or colour coding.
Keep holding the case with one hand
Holding is no-progress waste; replace with a jig.
Tighten a screw with a driver
Using the tool changes the product.
Align a part with the hole
Positioning is supporting; guides make it short and reliable.
Look around for where the tool is

Wait for the product from the previous process
An avoidable delay (waiting); review the process flow.
Visually check orientation after assembly
Inspect is class 3; a shape that cannot be assembled backwards (poka-yoke) removes it.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy › Two-hand (left-right hand) analysis
chunks.x:
Two-hand (left-right hand) analysis
Two-hand analysis records the motions of the left and right hands side by side on the same time axis, making it obvious when one hand is holding or idle.
Time
Left hand (before)
Right hand (before)
idle
reach & grasp case
receive case
hand over case
hold case
pick & tighten screws (×2)
put down product
idle
Fictional example: the left hand is idle or holding for 8 of 10 seconds
Improvement thinking
Putting the case in a jig removes 6 s of left-hand holding
Screw feeders on both sides let both hands pick screws simultaneously
Motions become symmetrical and rhythmical
The same job goes from 10 s to about 6 s, and since motions become constant, time variation also shrinks (illustrative numbers).

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy › Principles of motion economy
chunks.x:
Principles of motion economy
The Principles of motion economy principles systematise rules of thumb for working with less fatigue and no waste. First remember the four basic principles that run through them all.
Eliminate
remove motions such as searching, selecting, re-grasping
Reduce
reduce number of motions, distance and eye movement
Simultaneous
use both hands simultaneously and symmetrically; use feet too
Make easier
short distances, use gravity, smart jigs and tools
Principles in three areas
Area
Main principles
A. Use of the body
start and end both hands together; move them symmetrically in opposite directions; use the lowest body segment possible (fingers → wrist → forearm); avoid sharp direction changes, use smooth curves; work with rhythm
B. Arrangement of the workplace
fixed places for tools and materials; place in order of use within normal work area; use gravity to feed and remove parts (chutes, inclined shelves); appropriate work height, allow sitting or standing; adequate lighting
C. Design of tools and equipment
let jigs do the holding; combine two or more tools; use feet for what feet can operate; tools easy to grip and hung so they return when released; make positioning easy with guides and stoppers
Link to ZEVA “principles of motion stability”

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy › Principles of motion economy
chunks.x:
tools easy to grip and hung so they return when released; make positioning easy with guides and stoppers
Link to ZEVA “principles of motion stability”

Motion economy aims mainly at “fast and easy”, while ZEVA additionally emphasises “stable (no variation)”. Shorter distance → law of distance/displacement; fewer motions → law of sequence accumulation; positioning with jigs/guides → law of constraint and guide. The same improvement shortens time and reduces variation.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy › Work areas and the golden zone
chunks.x:
Work areas and the golden zone
A Work area is the range the hands can reach without moving the body. Where parts and tools are placed greatly changes reach distance, body twisting and fatigue.
Normal work area
Reached by swinging the forearm with elbows at the sides (radius about 35–45 cm). Frequently used parts/tools go here.
Maximum work area
Reached with fully extended arms (radius about 55–65 cm). For occasionally used items; beyond this the body must move.
Golden zone
Vertically, between shoulder and waist (around elbow height) is the easiest, fastest and most precise height.
Values are guides
Work-area dimensions depend on body size. Adjust bench height and layout to the actual workers.
Screws used 4 times per cycle, and spare driver bits changed once a day. Which belongs in the normal work area?
The screws
The spare bits
Both outside the maximum area
The more often an item is used, the closer it should be (normal area). Spare bits can be outside.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy › How to carry out motion improvement
chunks.x:
How to carry out motion improvement
Film
several cycles, hands clearly visible
Break down
write therbligs for each hand
Focus
start with class 3 & 4
Improve
eliminate → reduce → simultaneous → easier
Verify & standardize
re-measure CT & variation; update standard work
First ask “can it be eliminated?” Search, select and hold are highly likely removable
Next distance and count: bring parts close, arrange in order of use
Check whether both hands are doing valuable motion simultaneously
Make positioning “fit without thinking” with guides and stoppers
After improving, check not only time but whether motions are the same every cycle (variation)
Do not force speed
The purpose of motion improvement is not to rush workers. Forced speed creates muri and variation. The right direction is to design layouts and tools where “moving normally is naturally fast and the same every time.”

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Which group does the therblig “hold” belong to, and how is it improved?
A: Class 4; let a jig hold
Holding is class 4 no-progress waste; replace with a jig or clamp to free the hand.
Q: Most effective countermeasure to eliminate “search” and “select”?
A: Fixed position/item/quantity (3-tei) and colour coding
Hesitation comes from undefined “where / which”; remove it with a system.
Q: Which is a correct body-use principle of motion economy?
A: Start and finish both hands at the same time
Simultaneous, symmetrical hand motion is balanced and removes idle hands. Use the lowest (smallest) body segment possible.
Q: Where should frequently used parts be placed?
A: Within the normal work area, in order of use
Placing them in order within the normal area (reachable with elbows at the sides) reduces distance and hesitation.
Q: Which waste is easiest to find with two-hand analysis?
A: One hand idle or holding
Left and right on the same time axis make it obvious when one hand is not working.
Q: A positioning guide was added for a part. Which ZEVA motion-stability law applies?
A: Law of constraint and guide
Limiting degrees of freedom to structurally block variation is the law of constraint and guide.
Q: What is the right mindset for motion improvement?
A: Design layouts and tools so normal movement is naturally fast and repeatable

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Motion Study and Principles of Motion Economy › Quiz
chunks.x:
traint and guide.
Q: What is the right mindset for motion improvement?
A: Design layouts and tools so normal movement is naturally fast and repeatable

Changing motion through the system is the IE/ZEVA basic; forced speed breeds muri and variation.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Process Analysis and Work Sampling
chunks.x:
Process Analysis and Work Sampling
Map the flow of materials and people with process symbols to find stagnation, transport and inspection waste, and estimate work status with instantaneous observations (work sampling).
Use the process symbols (operation, transport, delay/storage, inspection) correctly
Perform product and worker process analysis and extract improvement points
Explain the purposes of flow diagrams and man-machine charts
Understand work sampling and calculate required observations and error
Process analysis visualises the whole flow with symbols — seeing the forest
Only operations (○) add value; transport, stagnation and inspection are targets for reduction
Product analysis follows the item; worker analysis follows the person
Flow diagrams reveal layout issues; man-machine charts reveal waiting between people and machines
Work sampling needs n = 4p(1−p)/e²; judge with awareness of error

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Process Analysis and Work Sampling › What is process analysis?
chunks.x:
What is process analysis?
Process analysis records, in order and with defined symbols, the path from raw material to product (or of a worker completing a job), making the whole flow visible. Motion study looks at hand movements; process analysis looks at where in the whole flow goods stop, are carried or are inspected.
In IE improvement it is important to “see the forest before the trees”. Shortening a hand motion by 1 second has little overall effect if goods sit for 2 days before and after it.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Process Analysis and Work Sampling › Process symbols
chunks.x:
Process symbols
In process analysis every step is classified into one of the following Process chart symbols. Only “operation” adds value.
Basic process symbols (JIS Z 8206 / ASME style)
Symbol
Name
Meaning
Value
Operation
change shape or properties, assemble
Yes
Transport
move to another place
No
Storage
planned storage (warehouse, etc.)
No
Delay
unplanned waiting
No
Quantity inspection
count and check quantity
No
Quality inspection
check quality characteristics
No
The transport symbol (⇨ or small ○) differs by standard; use one convention consistently.
Inspection adds no value
Inspection only “finds” defects; it does not “make” good products. ZEVA does not manipulate the result (Y) by tightening inspection but aims to control variation — the cause (X) — in the process and create conditions that guarantee good products (GPC).

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Process Analysis and Work Sampling › Product and worker process analysis
chunks.x:
Product and worker process analysis
Product process analysis (follow the item)
move along as if you were the material or part
grasp the number, distance and time of delays and transports
effective for layout improvement and lead-time reduction
Worker process analysis (follow the person)
follow the worker and record tasks in order
grasp amount of walking, searching and waiting
effective for recombining tasks and designing multi-process handling
Product process analysis example (illustrative)
▽ Stored in parts warehouse (avg. 2 days)
⇨ Carted to the line (80 m)
D Waiting beside line to be unpacked (3 h)
○ Assembly (90 s)
D Waiting for inspection (1 h)
◇ Visual inspection (30 s)
⇨ Moved to shipping area (120 m)
Of 7 steps only one is an operation (○). Most of the time is stagnation (▽, D) and transport totals 200 m. The right order is to attack stagnation and transport first.
Visualise with a summary table
At the end of process analysis, total the count, distance and time per symbol. Comparing the same summary before and after shows the effect at a glance.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Process Analysis and Work Sampling › Flow diagram, man-machine chart, multi-activity analysis
chunks.x:
Flow diagram, man-machine chart, multi-activity analysis
Flow diagram
Flow diagram: draw process symbols and movement paths on the floor plan. Backflow, crossings and long transports become obvious; used for layout improvement.
Man-machine chart
Man-machine chart: place the working and idle time of person and machine on one time axis. Find person waiting during automatic cycles and consider multi-machine handling.
Multi-activity analysis
Analyse waiting time among several workers (or machines) in coordinated work; used to review hand-over timing and staffing.
Man-machine chart worked example
Machine: load/unload 20 s (with person) + auto cycle 100 s = 120 s per cycle
Person: load/unload 20 s + idle 100 s → person utilisation = 20 ÷ 120 ≈ 17%
Line up 3 machines with 10 s walking each: one round = (20+10)×3 = 90 s ≤ 120 s
One person can handle 3 machines, greatly reducing idle time (illustrative numbers).

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Process Analysis and Work Sampling › Work sampling
chunks.x:
Work sampling
Work sampling observes at many random instants, records “what was happening at that moment”, and statistically estimates the time share of each state. You can grasp the utilisation of many people or machines efficiently without timing them all day.
Decide the purpose and the categories of states (e.g. working / transporting / idle / absent)
Set observation times randomly, e.g. with random numbers (regular timing causes bias)
Observe at each chosen instant and record exactly one state
After enough observations, compute the ratio for each state
Estimated ratio p = count of the state ÷ total observations
Required observations n = 4 × p(1 − p) ÷ e² (about 95% confidence)
expected ratio (from pilot observation)
acceptable absolute error (e.g. ±0.05 = ±5 points)
The factor 4 rounds 1.96² ≈ 3.84. Error can also be computed as e = 2 × √( p(1−p) ÷ n ).
Worked example: required observations
Pilot shows working ratio p ≈ 0.70
Desired error e = ±0.05
n = 4 × 0.70 × 0.30 ÷ 0.05² = 0.84 ÷ 0.0025 = 336
For ±0.03, n = 0.84 ÷ 0.0009 ≈ 933
Required observations grow quickly as error shrinks (halving the error needs about 4× observations). Choose the precision that fits the purpose.
The viewpoint of data reliability

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Process Analysis and Work Sampling › Work sampling
chunks.x:
uickly as error shrinks (halving the error needs about 4× observations). Choose the precision that fits the purpose.
The viewpoint of data reliability

Estimates from few observations are heavily affected by chance. ZEVA’s root logic states that “actions based on data require reliable data”. The habit of judging with awareness of how much error a number contains raises the quality of improvement.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Process Analysis and Work Sampling › Improving from process analysis
chunks.x:
Improving from process analysis
Symbol
Improvement question
Example
▽ D Stagnation
Why does it stop? Are we batching?
one-piece flow, synchronising processes, removing storage areas
⇨ Transport
Can processes be moved closer?
adjacent layout, U-shaped line, direct connection
□ ◇ Inspection
Can good quality be guaranteed without inspection?
poka-yoke, in-process quality assurance, condition control
○ Operation
Is this operation really needed? Can it be combined?
ECRS review, combined processing
A flow diagram shows goods going back and forth along the same aisle (backflow). Best countermeasure?
Add more carts
Rearrange equipment in process order
Add an inspection step
Backflow shows the layout does not follow process order. Reduce transport itself by rearranging (ECRS “R”), instead of adding carriers.
Key viewpoint of this unit
Process analysis is a tool for viewing the flow with the eye that “everything except operations is loss”. This matches the idea at the base of ZEVA: “flow only value work at top speed and cut everything else as loss”.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Process Analysis and Work Sampling › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Which process symbol adds value?
A: ○ Operation
Only operations that change shape or properties add value.
Q: Which analysis records by moving along as if you were the material?
A: Product process analysis
Following the item is product process analysis; following the person is worker process analysis.
Q: Which chart best reveals a worker waiting during automatic machining?
A: Man-machine chart
The man-machine chart puts person and machine work/idle on one time axis.
Q: Work sampling with p = 0.5 and e = ±0.05. Required n? (n = 4p(1−p)/e²)
A: 400
n = 4 × 0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 0.0025 = 1 ÷ 0.0025 = 400.
Q: Why are observation times randomised in work sampling?
A: Regular timing can coincide with periodic work and cause bias
Fixed intervals may always coincide with, e.g., breaks or scheduled transport, giving ratios that differ from reality.
Q: Product analysis shows 6 of 7 steps are stagnation, transport or inspection. What to tackle first?
A: Reduce stagnation and transport
Stagnation and transport dominate total time, so attacking them has far greater overall effect.
Q: From ZEVA’s viewpoint, how is “adding inspection because defects are high” evaluated?
A: It only manipulates the result (Y), not controlling the cause (X)
Inspection adds no value and does not reduce the causes of defects. ZEVA controls the variation (X) in the process.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Line Balancing
chunks.x:
Line Balancing
Visualise how work time is spread across processes, calculate the neck process, line balance efficiency and required workers, and design a smoother flow.
Explain what line balance and the neck process are
Calculate line balance efficiency, line balance loss and required workers
Read a yamazumi chart and explain how to rebalance work
Explain the link between line balance and variation from a ZEVA viewpoint
Line output is set by the neck process with the longest CT
Efficiency (basic IE formula) = ΣCT ÷ (neck CT × processes); guide ≥ 90%. ZEVA measures against takt
Required workers = ΣCT ÷ TT (round up); to cut headcount, remove work itself
Visualise with yamazumi; level with ECRS and redistribution
Look at variation, not just averages; with large variation the balance calculation is unreliable

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Line Balancing › What is line balance?
chunks.x:
What is line balance?
On a flow line, a product moves from process 1 → process 2 → process 3 and so on. If the work time (CT) of every process is about the same, products flow without stopping. We call this a well-balanced line — good Line balancing.
If one process takes much longer, work-in-process piles up in front of it and the following processes wait. The output of the whole line is decided by the slowest process. This slowest process is the Neck (bottleneck) process (bottleneck).
Neck process
The process with the longest CT. It sets the speed of the whole line.
Waiting
Time other processes spend waiting. It adds no value.
WIP pile-up
Stock builds up before the neck, increasing space, handling and quality risk.
Analogy
In a bucket relay of five people, if one person is slow, everyone ends up at that person’s pace. No matter how fast the other four are, the water arrives no faster.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Line Balancing › Calculating efficiency and required workers
chunks.x:
Calculating efficiency and required workers
Balance quality is measured by Line balance efficiency. Divide the sum of all process CTs by (neck CT × number of processes).
Line balance efficiency (%) = ΣCT ÷ (Neck CT × Number of processes) × 100
Sum of CTs of all processes (total work content)
The longest CT
The closer to 100%, the more evenly loaded the processes are (less waiting). A common target is 90% or more — a guide for this basic IE formula. ZEVA measures against the takt time and sets no single target (Line balance efficiency).
Line balance loss (%) = 100 − line balance efficiency
Theoretical required workers = ΣCT ÷ TT (round up)
Assumes one worker per process. TT is the pace the customer requires (ie-02).
Worked example: a 5-process line (TT = 60 s)
Process CTs: 52 s, 58 s, 45 s, 60 s, 41 s
ΣCT = 52 + 58 + 45 + 60 + 41 = 256 s
Neck CT = 60 s (process 4)
Efficiency = 256 ÷ (60 × 5) = 256 ÷ 300 = 85.3%
Line balance loss = 14.7% (total idle = 300 − 256 = 44 s per cycle)
Required workers = 256 ÷ 60 = 4.27 → 5 people
If we remove 16 s of work (256 → 240 s), 240 ÷ 60 = 4.0, so a 4-person line becomes theoretically possible.
Four processes have CTs of 40, 50, 45 and 55 s. What is the line balance efficiency?
About 75%
About 86%
About 95%
ΣCT = 190 s, neck CT = 55 s. 190 ÷ (55 × 4) = 190 ÷ 220 = 86.4%.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Line Balancing › Visualising with a yamazumi chart
chunks.x:
Visualising with a yamazumi chart
A Yamazumi chart chart stacks the element times of each process (or worker) as vertical bars. Draw a horizontal TT line and you instantly see which processes exceed TT and which have spare capacity.
Colour the stacks as value / semi-value / non-value work to see what time should be cut.
Bars above TT → cannot keep customer pace. Move or improve work.
Bars far below TT → waiting occurs. Work may be merged to reduce processes.
Record not only bar height but also cycle-to-cycle spread, to judge whether the apparent balance is real.
Tips for making one
① Break work into elements → ② measure each element several times (ie-03) → ③ stack by process → ④ draw the TT line → ⑤ put elements on sticky notes and move them to test rebalancing.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Line Balancing › How to improve line balance
chunks.x:
How to improve line balance
1. Measure
Measure element CTs repeatedly
2. Visualise
Yamazumi + TT line
3. Fix the neck
Reduce work itself with ECRS
4. Redistribute
Move elements to level bars to TT
5. Standardise
Make the new split standard work
The basic tactic is levelling ("yama-kuzushi"): move work from the neck to a neighbouring process with spare time. But moving work does not change ΣCT. To reduce headcount you must remove work itself using ECRS.
Tactic
Effect
Caution
Move work (levelling)
Neck CT falls, efficiency rises
ΣCT unchanged; review part/tool locations too
Remove work (ECRS)
ΣCT falls; fewer workers possible
Do not remove work needed for quality
Parallel stations
Doubles neck capacity
Adds people/equipment; last resort
Reduce variation
CT becomes stable; line flows as calculated
Needs standard work and 5S/3-tei
Rebalancing example (TT = 60 s)
Before: 52, 58, 45, 60, 41 s (ΣCT 256 s, 5 people, 85.3%)
ECRS removes 16 s of non-value work such as searching and re-gripping → ΣCT 240 s
Redistribute into 4 processes: 60, 60, 60, 60 s
Efficiency = 240 ÷ (60 × 4) = 100%
But if every process sits exactly at TT, any small fluctuation causes delay. In practice, reduce cycle-to-cycle variation before tightening.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Line Balancing › The trap of balancing averages
chunks.x:
The trap of balancing averages
Yamazumi bars are usually drawn with average or minimum times. But real work time varies every cycle. A process averaging 55 s that sometimes takes 70 s exceeds the 60 s TT at that moment and stops the whole line.
High-variation process
Average 55 s, range 40–70 s
Sometimes exceeds TT → downstream waits
Calculated efficiency is unreliable
Low-variation process
Average 55 s, range 53–57 s
Always within TT → flow never stops
Headcount and output match the calculation
ZEVA connection
ZEVA never evaluates a line by averages alone. It quantifies cycle-to-cycle variation with V.Score (σ/μ, see ie-08) and standardises the high-variation processes first. While variation is large, measured CTs and efficiency figures cannot be trusted, so correct improvement actions are impossible (ZEVA root logic).
Common mistake
Telling the neck operator to hurry is not improvement. It pushes the result (CT) directly without changing causes (method, part layout), leading to defects, injuries, and quick relapse.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Line Balancing › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Which process decides the output of a line?
A: The process with the longest CT
The slowest (longest CT) neck process sets the pace of the whole line.
Q: Four processes: 30, 36, 33, 27 s. Line balance efficiency?
A: 87.5%
ΣCT = 126 s, neck 36 s. 126 ÷ (36 × 4) = 126 ÷ 144 = 87.5%.
Q: ΣCT = 330 s and TT = 60 s. Theoretical required workers?
A: 6 people
330 ÷ 60 = 5.5. People cannot be split, so round up to 6.
Q: What does NOT change when you only move work to a neighbouring process?
A: ΣCT (total work content)
Moving work keeps the total the same. To lower ΣCT, remove work with ECRS.
Q: On a yamazumi chart, a bar far below the TT line means…
A: Waiting occurs; work might be consolidated
A process far shorter than TT has spare capacity and waits.
Q: The line is perfectly balanced on average CT but often stops. Most likely cause?
A: Large CT variation within processes
Even with equal averages, cycle-to-cycle spread creates moments above TT. This is why ZEVA focuses on variation.
Q: Which is NOT an appropriate improvement for a neck process?
A: Tell the operator to hurry up
Rushing pushes the result (Y) directly; causes (X) do not change, harming quality and safety.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE)
chunks.x:
Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE)
Understand OEE — how much of an equipment’s full potential actually became good products — by breaking it into availability, performance, yield rate and the six big losses.
Explain the time structure: loading time, operating time, etc.
Calculate availability, performance, yield rate and OEE
Classify the six big losses into the three rates
Explain why OEE is a result (Y) indicator
OEE = Availability × Performance × Yield rate; world-class ≈ 85%+
Check: OEE = good count × ideal CT ÷ loading time
Six big losses: breakdown, setup (availability); minor stops, speed (performance); defects, start-up (quality)
Look at the three rates separately and attack the biggest loss
OEE is a result (Y); raise it by controlling causes (X)

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) › What is OEE?
chunks.x:
What is OEE?
Overall Equipment Effectiveness (Overall Equipment Effectiveness) expresses in one number whether equipment ran when it should, at its designed speed, making only good parts. It spread through TPM (Total Productive Maintenance).
High running time alone is not enough. A machine that never stops but runs slowly or makes defects is still wasting its capability. OEE multiplies three factors, so if any one is poor, the total is poor.
OEE = Availability × Performance × Yield rate
A widely quoted world-class benchmark is 85% or more (e.g. 90% × 95% × 99.9% ≈ 85%).
Availability
Did it run without stopping? (downtime loss)
Performance
Did it run at designed speed? (speed loss)
Yield rate
Did it make only good parts? (quality loss)

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) › Time structure and OEE calculation
chunks.x:
Time structure and OEE calculation
Breakdown from loading time to valuable operating time
Time
Meaning
Loading time
Time the equipment is planned to run (operating hours minus planned stops, breaks)
Operating time
Loading time − downtime (breakdown, setup, adjustment)
Net operating time
Operating time − speed losses and minor stops
Valuable operating time
Net operating time − time spent on defects and repair
Availability = Operating time ÷ Loading time
Availability
Performance = (Ideal cycle time × Total count) ÷ Operating time
Performance: the ideal cycle time is the designed speed of the equipment.
Yield rate = Good ÷ total production (excluding Trial)
Yield rate
Worked example
Loading time 480 min, downtime 45 min → operating time 435 min
Availability = 435 ÷ 480 = 90.6%
Ideal CT 1.0 min, total count 380 → performance = (1.0 × 380) ÷ 435 = 87.4%
Good 370 (total production 380, no Trial) → yield rate = 370 ÷ 380 = 97.4%
OEE = 0.906 × 0.874 × 0.974 ≈ 77.1%
Check: 370 good × 1.0 min ÷ 480 min = 77.1% (share of time that created value)
Loss breakdown: downtime 45 min, speed loss 55 min (435 − 380), quality loss 10 min, valuable time 370 min — total 480 min.
Quick check
OEE also equals good count × ideal CT ÷ loading time. If it matches the product of the three rates, your calculation is right.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) › The six big losses
chunks.x:
The six big losses
TPM organises the causes of low OEE as the Six big losses. Improvement starts by breaking down which loss is largest — not just by looking at the OEE number.
Rate
Loss
Example
Availability
① Breakdown loss
Motor burn-out stops the machine for 2 hours
Availability
② Setup & adjustment loss
Model change: die change and trial shots take 40 min
Performance
③ Minor stop & idling loss
Part jams cause repeated stops of tens of seconds
Performance
④ Reduced speed loss
Running slower than designed speed for fear of defects
Quality
⑤ Defect & repair loss
Scrapping or repairing out-of-size parts
Quality
