Defects right after start-up until temperature stabilises
Which rate does this loss reduce?
Availability
Performance
Quality
Machine broke down for 1 hour
Breakdown loss reduces operating time.
Changeover took 30 minutes
Setup loss counts as downtime.
Frequent short stops due to jams
Minor stops are often unrecorded and lower Performance.
Designed 1.0 min/pc but ran at 1.2 min/pc
Reduced speed loss.
Scratched parts were repaired
Repaired items are not counted as first-time good.
Start-up pieces in the morning were defective
Start-up loss.
Machine waited because material did not arrive
An unplanned stop within loading time lowers availability.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) › Using OEE correctly
chunks.x:
Using OEE correctly
Always look at the three rates separately: two lines with OEE 70% may need completely different actions — one has breakdowns, the other defects.
Record minor stops: short stops rarely appear in daily reports and hide inside a low Performance figure. Direct observation reveals them.
Do not inflate the ideal CT: setting a slow ideal CT makes performance look better. Use the designed / theoretical speed.
Watch the trend and spread of OEE: if daily OEE swings widely, the process is not stable.
OEE and OLE
On lines where people do most of the work, the same idea applied to labour — OLE (Overall Labor Effectiveness) — is sometimes used, multiplying people’s availability, performance and quality.
ZEVA connection: OEE is a result (Y)
In ZEVA XY thinking, OEE, time and quality are all results (Y). When OEE is low, "working overtime to make the numbers" manipulates Y directly and is prohibited. The right way is to control causes (X) such as breakdown causes and equipment parameters. In ZEVA, OEE is a GPC-M (equipment control) metric with a target of 85% or more.
NG: pushing Y directly
Low OEE → overtime to hit numbers
Low OEE → reset the ideal CT slower
OK: control cause X
Remove breakdown causes (X) → OEE (Y) rises
Standardise and shorten setup (X) → downtime falls

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Availability 90%, performance 90%, quality 95%. OEE?
A: About 77%
0.90 × 0.90 × 0.95 = 0.7695 ≈ 77%.
Q: Loading time 400 min, downtime 40 min. Availability?
A: 90%
Operating time = 360 min. 360 ÷ 400 = 90%.
Q: Operating time 360 min, ideal CT 0.5 min, total count 630. Performance?
A: 87.5%
0.5 × 630 = 315 min. 315 ÷ 360 = 87.5%.
Q: Minor stops reduce which rate?
A: Performance
Short stops and idling are classified as performance losses.
Q: Which pair of losses reduces the yield rate?
A: Defect/repair and start-up losses
Defects/repair and start-up are quality losses.
Q: For a line with low OEE, which action fits ZEVA XY thinking?
A: Identify and remove causes of breakdowns and stops
OEE is a result (Y). Controlling causes (X) raises it; the others only manipulate Y or the baseline.
Q: In ZEVA, OEE belongs to which metric group?
A: GPC-M (equipment control)
OEE expresses equipment effectiveness, so it is a GPC-M metric (target ≥ 85%).

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Statistics
chunks.x:
Basic Statistics
Understand mean, range, standard deviation, coefficient of variation, histograms and the normal distribution from calculator-level examples — the base for talking about variation with numbers.
Explain population vs sample
Calculate mean, median, range, variance and standard deviation by hand
Compare variation of data with different means using CV
Read histogram shapes and the 68-95-99.7 rule
Describe data with both centre and spread
σ measures typical distance from the mean; divide by n − 1 for samples
CV = σ ÷ μ compares data with different means — same as ZEVA V.Score
Histogram shape hints at causes (two peaks = mixture, island = temporary abnormality)
Normal distribution: 68/95/99.7% within ±1σ/±2σ/±3σ

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Statistics › Why statistics?
chunks.x:
Why statistics?
Shop-floor data differ a little every time, even for the same job on the same machine. Measure once and call it "CT = 30 s" and it may have been a lucky fast cycle. Statistics is the toolkit for describing the whole picture of varying data with a few numbers.
Centre (location)
Where do the data gather? → mean, median
Spread (variation)
How widely do they spread? → range, σ, CV
Population and sample
The whole group you want to know about (e.g. every part this process will make) is the population; the part you actually measure (e.g. 20 parts today) is the sample. We infer the population from the sample, so a biased measurement or an unstable process leads to wrong conclusions.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Statistics › Centre: mean and median
chunks.x:
Centre: mean and median
Mean x̄ = Σx ÷ n
Sum of the data
Number of data
The Mean is the sum divided by the count. The Median is the middle value when sorted (for an even count, the average of the middle two).
Which is robust to outliers?
CT: 30, 31, 29, 30, 80 s (the last cycle waited for missing parts)
Mean = 200 ÷ 5 = 40 s
Sorted: 29, 30, 30, 31, 80 → median = 30 s
The mean is pulled strongly by one abnormal value. But that 80 s is a signal of an abnormality — investigate its cause rather than just deleting it.
The danger of managing by averages
A process at 29–31 s and one at 20–40 s can both average 30 s, yet they are completely different. The mean speaks only about the centre — always pair it with a measure of spread.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Statistics › Spread: range, variance, standard deviation
chunks.x:
Spread: range, variance, standard deviation
Range R = Max − Min
Range: simple, but uses only two extreme values, so it is sensitive to outliers.
Standard deviation s = √{ Σ(x − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1) }
Deviation (difference from the mean)
Variance (square of σ)
When estimating population spread from a sample, divide by n − 1 (divide by n for a whole population). In spreadsheets, STDEV.S uses n − 1 and STDEV.P uses n.
Variance is the average of squared deviations; the Standard deviation is its square root. We square so that positive and negative deviations do not cancel out, then take the root to return to the original unit (seconds, mm).
Calculate by hand: 10, 12, 11, 9, 13
Mean = 55 ÷ 5 = 11; range = 13 − 9 = 4
Deviations: −1, +1, 0, −2, +2 (they always sum to 0)
Squared: 1, 1, 0, 4, 4 → sum 10
Variance s² = 10 ÷ (5 − 1) = 2.5
Standard deviation s = √2.5 ≈ 1.58
"Mean 11, standard deviation about 1.6" — two numbers convey both centre and spread.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Statistics › Coefficient of variation (CV): comparing different means
chunks.x:
Coefficient of variation (CV): comparing different means
CV = σ ÷ μ (standard deviation ÷ mean)
Coefficient of variation: a unit-free "relative spread", sometimes shown as %.
A standard deviation of 2 s is large for a 10 s job but tiny for a 100 s job. CV gives 2 ÷ 10 = 0.20 versus 2 ÷ 100 = 0.02, so they can be compared fairly.
Operators A and B (both average 30 s)
A: 30, 31, 29, 30, 30 s → sum of squared deviations 2 → s = √(2 ÷ 4) ≈ 0.71 → CV ≈ 0.024
B: 25, 36, 28, 34, 27 s → sum of squared deviations 90 → s = √(90 ÷ 4) ≈ 4.74 → CV ≈ 0.158
Same average, but B varies about 6.7 times more than A — B’s method likely has unstandardised parts.
ZEVA connection: CV = V.Score
V.Score, the core metric for human work (GPC-H) in ZEVA, is exactly the coefficient of variation of work time (σ/μ). ZEVA guide: < 0.1 extremely stable, 0.1–0.3 stable, 0.3–0.5 slightly unstable, 0.5–1.0 unstable, ≥ 1.0 very unstable. Above, A is extremely stable and B is in the stable band, but the gap to A is obvious.
A process has mean 60 s and σ 9 s. CV?
0.15
6.7
0.54
9 ÷ 60 = 0.15 — "stable" (0.1–0.3) on the ZEVA scale.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Statistics › Seeing the shape with histograms
chunks.x:
Seeing the shape with histograms
A Histogram groups data into intervals and draws the count in each as a bar. It shows the shape of the distribution that mean and σ alone cannot. Use at least 30–50 data points and about √n intervals.
Shape
What it suggests
Bell-shaped
Only chance variation; likely stable
Two peaks
Two different conditions mixed (2 operators, 2 machines, 2 lots)
Skewed (long tail on one side)
Common for quantities with a lower limit, like work time; occasional delays on the long side
Cliff (cut off)
Out-of-spec items have been sorted out
Isolated island
A temporary abnormality (measurement error, wrong material)
Guess the cause from the histogram shape
Bell
Two peaks
Island
CTs of a veteran and a newcomer plotted together
Two different distributions overlap, giving two peaks.
A different material lot got mixed in on one day
A temporary abnormality forms a small separate bump.
Dimensions from a process with established standard work
With only common causes, a symmetric bell is typical.
Parts from two machines measured together
If each machine has a different centre, two peaks appear.
The gauge was dropped once and a few readings jumped high
Measurement problems also create islands.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Statistics › Normal distribution and the 68-95-99.7 rule
chunks.x:
Normal distribution and the 68-95-99.7 rule
Variation produced by many small chance causes tends toward a symmetric bell — the Normal distribution. Its shape is fully determined by just two numbers: mean μ and standard deviation σ.
About 68% within μ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, 99.7% within ±3σ
Range
Share inside
Share outside
about 1 in 3
about 1 in 22
about 1 in 370
Try it
Part length: μ = 50.0 mm, σ = 0.1 mm (assume normal)
±3σ = 49.7–50.3 mm contains about 99.7%
If the spec is 49.7–50.3 mm, about 0.27% (≈3 per 1,000) fall outside
Halve σ to 0.05 mm and the same spec gives ±6σ of margin — defects become practically zero.
ZEVA connection
Centring the mean on the spec alone cannot eliminate defects; shrinking σ is the fundamental fix. That is why ZEVA shifts evaluation from managing averages to managing variation. Note that distribution shape and σ are meaningful only when the process is stable (ie-09).

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Statistics › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Data 4, 6, 8: mean and range?
A: Mean 6, range 4
Mean = 18 ÷ 3 = 6; range = 8 − 4 = 4.
Q: Sample standard deviation (n − 1) of 4, 6, 8?
A: 2
Deviations −2, 0, +2 → squares sum 8 → 8 ÷ 2 = 4 → √4 = 2. (Dividing by n gives 1.63.)
Q: Which centre measure is least affected by outliers?
A: Median
The median is the middle value, so extreme values at the ends barely affect it.
Q: Process X: mean 20 s, σ 3 s. Process Y: mean 100 s, σ 5 s. Which varies more relatively?
A: Process X (CV 0.15)
X: 3 ÷ 20 = 0.15; Y: 5 ÷ 100 = 0.05. Y has larger σ, but X varies three times more relatively.
Q: A two-peaked histogram most likely indicates…
A: Data from different conditions are mixed
Two groups with different centres (operators, machines, lots) produce two peaks. Stratify the data to check.
Q: In a normal distribution, about what share lies within μ ± 2σ?
A: 95%
±1σ ≈ 68%, ±2σ ≈ 95%, ±3σ ≈ 99.7%.
Q: ZEVA V.Score is the same as which statistic?
A: Coefficient of variation (σ/μ)
V.Score is the coefficient of variation of work time, σ/μ. Below 0.1 is extremely stable.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Control Charts and Process Capability
chunks.x:
Control Charts and Process Capability
Learn the X̄-R control chart, which separates common causes from special causes, and the capability indices Cp and Cpk, which show performance against the specification. Rule: stability first, capability second.
Explain common causes vs special causes
Calculate X̄-R control limits and read out-of-control signals
Explain the difference between control limits and spec limits
Calculate Cp and Cpk and judge them
Explain why capability cannot be defined without stability
Variation has common and special causes; the control chart separates them
X̄-R (n = 5): X̿ ± 0.577R̄; R upper limit 2.114R̄
Control limits = voice of the process; spec limits = voice of the customer
Cp = spec width ÷ 6σ; Cpk includes centring; ≥ 1.33 is the usual target
No stability, no capability: stabilise first, then assess capability

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Control Charts and Process Capability › Two kinds of variation: common and special causes
chunks.x:
Two kinds of variation: common and special causes
In the 1920s, W. A. Shewhart split process variation into two kinds. This distinction is the starting point of control charts and of quality control as a whole.
Common causes (chance)
Many small causes that are always present
e.g. tiny material differences, small room-temperature swings
Variation stays within a predictable band
Reducing it needs system change (4M, standards) — a management job
Special causes (assignable)
Occasional, identifiable, larger causes
e.g. a chipped tool, a skipped step, a different material lot
Variation becomes unpredictable
Find and remove the cause on the shop floor
When special causes are removed and only common causes remain, the process is in State of statistical control (stable). A stable process can be predicted to produce a similar distribution tomorrow.
A process that is not in a state of statistical control has no definable capability.
Shewhart principle
Two mistakes
① Reacting to every chance fluctuation by adjusting the machine (over-adjustment) increases variation. ② Ignoring a special-cause signal as "normal" lets defects continue. The control chart exists to prevent both mistakes.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Control Charts and Process Capability › Building an X̄-R chart
chunks.x:
Building an X̄-R chart
A Control chart plots data in time order with a centre line and upper/lower Control limits. In the common X̄-R chart, small subgroups (e.g. 5 parts) are sampled at intervals, and each subgroup’s mean X̄ and range R are plotted. The X̄ chart watches shifts in the centre; the R chart watches changes in within-subgroup spread.
1. Sample subgroups
e.g. 5 parts every hour, 20–25 subgroups
2. Compute X̄ and R
Mean and range of each subgroup
3. Centre lines
X̿ (mean of X̄), R̄ (mean of R)
4. Control limits
Use the constants table
5. Plot and judge
Look for out-of-control signals
X̄ chart: UCL = X̿ + A2R̄, CL = X̿, LCL = X̿ − A2R̄
R chart: UCL = D4R̄, CL = R̄, LCL = D3R̄
For subgroup size n = 5: A2 = 0.577, D3 = 0 (no lower limit), D4 = 2.114, d2 = 2.326. The limits correspond to mean ± 3σ.
Worked example (n = 5, 25 subgroups)
X̿ = 10.00 mm and R̄ = 0.20 mm
X̄ UCL = 10.00 + 0.577 × 0.20 = 10.115 mm
X̄ LCL = 10.00 − 0.115 = 9.885 mm
R UCL = 2.114 × 0.20 = 0.423 mm; no LCL
Estimated σ of individual values = R̄ ÷ d2 = 0.20 ÷ 2.326 ≈ 0.086 mm
From now on, if subgroup X̄ stays within 9.885–10.115 mm, R stays at or below 0.423 mm, and no patterns appear, the process is judged stable.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Control Charts and Process Capability › Reading the chart: out-of-control signals
chunks.x:
Reading the chart: out-of-control signals
Even when all points are inside the limits, a pattern that does not look random suggests a Special cause. Typical rules are below (point counts differ slightly between standards).
Rule
Pattern
Example cause
One point outside a control limit
Tool breakage, bad material, measurement error
A run of points on one side of the centre line (e.g. 9 in a row)
Setting change, lot change, operator change
Steady rise or fall (e.g. 6 in a row)
Tool wear, heating up, operator fatigue
2 of 3 points beyond ±2σ on the same side
Early stage of a shift
Cyclical up-and-down
Shift change, morning/afternoon temperature, alternating two machines
Points hug the centre line too closely
Wrong subgrouping, mixed streams, altered data
When you find a signal
Check records and the actual parts for "when, where, what changed" (4M change points). After removing the cause, build the countermeasure into the standard so the same abnormality cannot recur.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Control Charts and Process Capability › Control limits ≠ specification limits
chunks.x:
Control limits ≠ specification limits
Control limits (UCL/LCL)
Spec limits (USL/LSL)
Who decides
The process data (voice of the process)
Design / customer (voice of the customer)
Meaning
Line to judge whether the process is stable
Line to judge good vs defective product
Applied to
Subgroup means and ranges
Individual products
Neither "inside control limits means good product" nor "inside spec means stable" is true. A stable process can consistently miss the spec (not capable), and a process can be inside spec yet unstable, so defects may appear at any time.
ZEVA connection: GPC band
ZEVA adds a third kind of line: the GPC band — the range of process conditions (X) verified by physical experiments to produce good products. It differs from both statistical control limits and product spec limits (covered in z2-01).

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Control Charts and Process Capability › Capability indices Cp and Cpk
chunks.x:
Capability indices Cp and Cpk
Process capability is how comfortably a stable process can meet the specification. It compares the spec width with the process spread (6σ).
Process capability index Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6σ
Looks only at spread; unchanged even if the centre is off.
Process capability index Cpk = min{ (USL − μ) ÷ 3σ , (μ − LSL) ÷ 3σ }
Includes centring; evaluates the side closer to a spec limit. Cpk ≤ Cp (equal when centred).
Worked example: spec 10.0 ± 0.5 mm
LSL = 9.5, USL = 10.5, process μ = 10.1, σ = 0.12
Cp = 1.0 ÷ (6 × 0.12) = 1.0 ÷ 0.72 ≈ 1.39
Upper: (10.5 − 10.1) ÷ 0.36 ≈ 1.11; lower: (10.1 − 9.5) ÷ 0.36 ≈ 1.67
Cpk = the smaller = 1.11 → about 430 ppm expected above USL
Centre at 10.0 → Cpk = Cp = 1.39; also cut σ to 0.10 → 1.67
Raise Cp by reducing variation; bring Cpk up to Cp by centring. The fundamental lever is variation reduction.
Cpk
Judgement (common guide)
Action
≥ 1.67
More than sufficient
Consider simplifying inspection, cutting cost
1.33 – 1.67
Sufficient
Maintain and monitor
1.00 – 1.33
Barely adequate
Manage carefully; plan improvement
< 1.00
Insufficient
Contain (e.g. 100% inspection) and improve urgently
ZEVA does not use capability indices as metrics

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Control Charts and Process Capability › Capability indices Cp and Cpk
chunks.x:
ge carefully; plan improvement
< 1.00
Insufficient
Contain (e.g. 100% inspection) and improve urgently
ZEVA does not use capability indices as metrics

Cp and Cpk are common IE language, so they are taught here, but they are not part of the ZEVA metrics system (Defect rate, Overall Equipment Effectiveness, V.Score (Variation Score), X̄-R chart). ZEVA holds the conditions (X) inside the GPC band and reads the result through the defect rate and OEE, rather than through an index of the result (see the metrics-system module).

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Control Charts and Process Capability › Golden rule: stability first, then capability
chunks.x:
Golden rule: stability first, then capability
Collect data and draw a control chart
If signals appear, remove causes to reach stability
Once stable, estimate σ from that data
Calculate Cp and Cpk to judge capability against spec
Cpk of an unstable process can be calculated, but it does not predict tomorrow — it is a meaningless number.
ZEVA connection: the root logic
ZEVA’s root logic says data-based action needs reliable data, and reliable data has little variation and no bias. Its theoretical foundation is the Shewhart principle. In ZEVA too, process stability is confirmed with an X̄-R chart before evaluating Cpk or V.Score (GPC-M target: Cpk ≥ 1.33).
A process with many out-of-control signals shows Cpk = 1.5. What is the right conclusion?
It is capable, no problem
Not stable, so Cpk is not trustworthy; remove special causes first
Just widen the spec
A process not in statistical control has no definable capability (Shewhart principle).

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Control Charts and Process Capability › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Dimensions grow gradually due to tool wear. This is…
A: A special cause
It is a systematic change from an identifiable cause, appearing as a steady rise on the chart.
Q: n = 5, X̿ = 50.0, R̄ = 2.0. X̄ chart UCL? (A2 = 0.577)
A: 51.15
50.0 + 0.577 × 2.0 = 51.154 ≈ 51.15.
Q: All points are inside the limits, but 10 in a row are above the centre line. Conclusion?
A: The centre may have shifted; suspect a special cause
A run on one side signals a shift, e.g. from a setting or lot change.
Q: Which statement about control and spec limits is correct?
A: Control limits are calculated from process data
Control limits are the voice of the process (data); spec limits are customer/design requirements.
Q: LSL = 10, USL = 20, σ = 1, μ = 16. Cpk?
A: 1.33
Upper (20 − 16) ÷ 3 = 1.33; lower (16 − 10) ÷ 3 = 2.0. The smaller gives Cpk = 1.33. (Cp = 10 ÷ 6 = 1.67.)
Q: Cp = 1.5 and Cpk = 0.9. What is the most effective first action?
A: Centre the distribution on the spec midpoint
Cp is good but Cpk is low: spread is small but the centre is off. Centring brings Cpk toward Cp.
Q: What does the Shewhart principle state?
A: A process not in statistical control has no definable capability
Data from an unstable process does not predict tomorrow, so capability cannot be defined. This underpins ZEVA’s root logic.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Improvement Tools
chunks.x:
Basic Improvement Tools
5S & 3-tei, standard work, ECRS, PDCA, 5-Why, fishbone, Pareto, the QC 7 tools and poka-yoke — the basic tools that form the common language of shop-floor improvement.
Explain 5S and 3-tei and check a workplace
Explain the three elements of standard work
Generate improvement ideas in ECRS order
Narrow down causes with 5-Why, fishbone and Pareto
Explain how PDCA and poka-yoke make improvements stick
5S and 3-tei build a workplace where abnormalities are visible and inconsistency cannot arise
Standard work: takt time, work sequence, standard WIP
In ECRS, Eliminate comes first
Pareto to prioritise, fishbone to list candidates, 5-Why to reach the root cause
Run with PDCA; lock in with standardisation and poka-yoke

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Improvement Tools › 5S and 3-tei: the base of all improvement
chunks.x:
5S and 3-tei: the base of all improvement
5S keeps the workplace in a state where anyone can work under the same conditions at any time. The goal is not just tidiness but an environment where abnormalities are instantly visible and searching and mistakes do not happen.
S
Meaning
Example
Sort (Seiri)
Separate needed from unneeded; remove the unneeded
Red-tag and remove tools unused for a month
Set in order (Seiton)
Give needed items a place where they can be taken at once
Shadow boards cut to the tool shape
Shine (Seiso)
Clean and inspect at the same time to find dirt and faults
Finding an oil leak during cleaning
Standardise (Seiketsu)
Make rules to maintain the first three S
5S checklist and duty roster
Sustain (Shitsuke)
Build the habit of following the rules
Five-minute 5S before every shift end
3-tei: fixed position, fixed item, fixed quantity
Fixed position
Decide where it goes and label the address
Fixed item
Decide what goes there and label the item
Fixed quantity
Decide how many; mark max and min
When 3 Fixes (3-tei) is kept, "missing parts", "searching for tools" and "wrong counts" are obvious at a glance, so work sequence and time stop fluctuating.
ZEVA connection: 5S & 3-tei are the foundation

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Improvement Tools › 5S and 3-tei: the base of all improvement
chunks.x:
hing for tools" and "wrong counts" are obvious at a glance, so work sequence and time stop fluctuating.
ZEVA connection: 5S & 3-tei are the foundation

ZEVA groups 5S, 3-tei, 4M standards and standard work as "standardisation — the foundation of everything". If management gaps like searching and hesitation remain, work-time data scatter and cannot be trusted. Securing basic reproducibility is the starting point of data-based improvement (the virtuous cycle).

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Improvement Tools › Standard work
chunks.x:
Standard work
Standard work is the current best way (quality, safety, efficiency) that everyone follows. "Without standards, no improvement" — without a baseline you cannot even tell whether something improved.
① Takt time
How many seconds per unit (customer pace)
② Work sequence
In what order and how to move
③ Standard WIP
Minimum work-in-process kept in the process
Vague instruction
"Tighten the screw firmly"
"Apply neatly"
Interpretation differs by person → results vary
Instruction with only one interpretation
"Tighten with the torque driver set to X N·m until it clicks"
"One back-and-forth brush stroke over the area in the photo"
With photos, video and judgement criteria
Standards exist to be changed
Standardisation does not kill creativity. A standard is "today’s best"; when a better way is found, the standard is updated. Decide → follow → revise, again and again.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Improvement Tools › ECRS: four angles for improvement
chunks.x:
ECRS: four angles for improvement
ECRS is the order of questions for reviewing work or processes. Eliminate first; only what cannot be eliminated is then combined, rearranged or simplified. Later steps usually give less effect for more effort.
Order
Angle
Question
Example
E: Eliminate
Can this work be removed?
Guarantee quality in-process and remove later inspection
C: Combine
Can it be done together?
Drill and chamfer at once with one tool
R: Rearrange
Can order or place be swapped?
Prepare setup before stopping (external setup)
S: Simplify
Can it be made easier?
A locating jig removes the need to align
Is this improvement E, C, R or S?
E Eliminate
C Combine
R Rearrange
S Simplify
Stop placing a part down and picking it up again; assemble directly
The temporary placing step itself is removed.
Label and visually check in a single lift
Two tasks are merged into one motion.
Move the most-used parts rack in front of the operator
This rearranges the location.
Add a guide shaped so orientation cannot be wrong
It makes the work easier and surer.
Abolish a double-check record that is no longer needed
Non-value work is removed.
Swap process order so drilling happens before painting to prevent scratches
Order is rearranged.
Merge two people’s separate trips into one cart run
Multiple transports are combined.
Change hand screwing to an electric driver

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Improvement Tools › ECRS: four angles for improvement
chunks.x:
Order is rearranged.
Merge two people’s separate trips into one cart run
Multiple transports are combined.
Change hand screwing to an electric driver

It simplifies by making the work easier.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Improvement Tools › Finding causes: 5-Why, fishbone, Pareto
chunks.x:
Finding causes: 5-Why, fishbone, Pareto
Pareto chart: where to start
A Pareto chart chart sorts items by count as bars and overlays a cumulative percentage line. Often a few items account for most of the total, so attacking the top items gives the biggest effect.
Breakdown of 100 defects (illustrative)
Scratch 45 (45%) → cumulative 45%
Misalignment 25 (25%) → cumulative 70%
Missing screw 15 (15%) → cumulative 85%
Stain 10 (10%) → cumulative 95%
Other 5 (5%) → cumulative 100%
The top two items make up 70%. Focus the cause analysis on scratches and misalignment first.
Fishbone diagram: listing candidate causes
A Fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram diagram writes the effect (problem) at the head, major cause categories (such as 4M) on the big bones, and specific causes on the small bones. Teams use it to list candidate causes without gaps.
Man
Poor understanding of steps, force differences
Machine
Jig play, driver torque drop
Material
Size differences by lot
Method
No rule on how to place parts
Effect: misalignment
Result (Y)
5-Why analysis: digging to the root cause
5 Whys repeats "why?" on an observed fact until reaching a root cause you can act on. Five is only a guide; what matters is checking with facts and reaching a system-level cause.
Why misaligned? → The part was not seated correctly in the jig
Why not seated? → The part can be placed even when reversed

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Improvement Tools › Finding causes: 5-Why, fishbone, Pareto
chunks.x:
ching a system-level cause.
Why misaligned? → The part was not seated correctly in the jig
Why not seated? → The part can be placed even when reversed

Why can it be reversed? → The jig has no shape that restricts orientation
Why no such shape? → Mis-assembly was not considered in jig design
Countermeasure: add a guide so a reversed part will not fit (poka-yoke), and add "mis-assembly prevention" to the jig design checklist.
Common 5-Why mistakes
Stopping at "operator carelessness" or "lack of attention" is a mistake. Blaming people does not prevent recurrence. Dig into "why does the system allow a careless moment to become a defect?"

chunks.x:

The QC seven tools are the basic set for visualising and analysing problems with data. Most can be used without advanced statistics.

A correlation between torque and defect rate does not prove torque is the cause. A third factor (e.g. operator skill) may affect both. Use correlation as a hint for hypotheses and confirm by experiment.

chunks.t: IE Fundamentals › Basic Improvement Tools › PDCA and poka-yoke: run and lock in improvement
chunks.x:
PDCA and poka-yoke: run and lock in improvement
PDCA
Plan
Target, cause analysis, countermeasure plan
Do
Try it as planned, small first
Check
Verify the effect with data
Act
Standardise if good; otherwise try the next idea
PDCA cycle is the basic cycle that stops improvement from being "done and forgotten". In Check, judge by repeated data rather than a single result — with large variation you cannot tell a real improvement from chance.
Poka-yoke: preventing slips by design
Poka-yoke is a mechanism that makes it impossible to make or pass on a defect even when someone slips. Instead of "be careful", it prevents errors physically with shapes, sensors or sequence control.
Level
Function
Example
Prevention (best)
The mistake cannot be made
A jig shape that rejects reversed parts
Stop
Equipment stops when a mistake occurs
Cannot send to next process if screw count is short
Warning
Signals the mistake with sound or light
A lamp lights when a part is not picked
ZEVA connection
ZEVA adds "S (Standardize)" to PDCA as PDCA+S — one of its principles — so every improvement is fed back into a new standard. Poka-yoke is also a typical application of ZEVA’s third law of motion stability (constraint & guide: limiting freedom structurally blocks variation).

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › What is ZEVA? › Definition of ZEVA
chunks.x:
Definition of ZEVA
ZEVA (Zero Variation Production System) (Zero Variation Production System) is the general name for a next-generation production system that uses the idea of the theoretical value as its purpose foundation, GPC (Good Process Conditions) (Good Process Conditions) as its method foundation, and places "control of variation" at its core.
In one sentence
"Cut off the root of variation, converge toward the theoretical value, and sustain it through the cycle of standardization" — this is the core principle of ZEVA.
What the name means
Zero
Aim for a state where variation is under control and keeps converging to the theoretical value
Variation
Shift the focus of improvement from "waste" to "variation (mura)"
Production System
Not a temporary activity but a "system" that designs and runs all of production
ZEVA is a production system, not an improvement tool
Improvement tools (e.g. 5-Why analysis, Pareto charts) are "instruments you pick up when needed". ZEVA, in contrast, is a framework for designing and operating all production activities based on a unified philosophy and methodology. It defines, as one system, which problem to improve, at what speed, with what method, and how to sustain the result.
Analogy

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › What is ZEVA? › Definition of ZEVA
chunks.x:
ilosophy and methodology. It defines, as one system, which problem to improve, at what speed, with what method, and how to sustain the result.
Analogy

If the theoretical value is the "destination (the ideal state)", ZEVA is the navigation system that gets you there reliably. It not only shows the destination but also clears the "fog (variation)" that hides the road and builds a solid "road (reproducibility)" as it goes.

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › What is ZEVA? › Background: why ZEVA was needed
chunks.x:
Background: why ZEVA was needed
ZEVA was born from a wall encountered when trying to spread theoretical-value thinking into a plant where people do most of the work. Working from the theoretical value means deciding what to improve based on "the gap between the theoretical value (ideal state) and the current state". But on a floor where process variation was large, that gap itself could not be measured correctly.
Work variation
Experienced and new operators differ by nearly 2× in work time. Quality shifts slightly every time. The "current value" used as the baseline is not stable.
Vague instructions
Expressions like "tighten firmly" or "apply neatly" are interpreted differently by each person. Same instruction, different results.
Weak standardization
It is impossible to measure what the real loss is, so improvement activity itself cannot work.
A good average is not enough
Even if the average meets the target, a process with large variation "cannot be evaluated", because today’s average does not guarantee tomorrow’s. Yet we still pursue the theoretical value — ZEVA was designed to achieve both.
Before improvement, we must first secure "reproducibility", the premise of everything. For that, variation is the root of all evil.
Conclusion at the birth of ZEVA

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › What is ZEVA? › Background: why ZEVA was needed
chunks.x:

Conclusion at the birth of ZEVA

The more a site depends on people — for example where automation investment does not pay back easily — the more important variation countermeasures become. ZEVA started on such floors by making work instructions concrete enough that "anyone who reads them can interpret them only one way".

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › What is ZEVA? › The 4 components and the 4-layer structure
chunks.x:
The 4 components and the 4-layer structure
ZEVA consists of the following 4 elements. Each has a different role, and together they work as one production system.
Element
Role
Content
Theoretical value
Purpose foundation
Define the ideal state physically and technically
GPC control theory
Method foundation
Control variation with the dual structure GPC-M (machine) / GPC-H (human)
Hybrid triage
Improvement engine
Route each issue to Quick GPC or Deep GPC according to its nature
Staged digitalisation
Accelerator
3-level design that works in analog and accelerates with digitalisation
Components of ZEVA
4 layers: upper layers guide lower layers
The ZEVA 4-layer structure
Layer 1
Theoretical value — purpose foundation
Defines the ideal and sets priorities by the gap to the theoretical value
Layer 2
Hybrid triage — routing
Routes issues to Quick GPC (H-T-C-A) or Deep GPC (DMAIC)
Layer 3
GPC control — method foundation
Controls variation through GPC-M (machine) and GPC-H (human)

Daily operation and the mechanism to identify causes structurally

ZEVA works fully in an analog environment with paper, stopwatches and whiteboards. Digitalisation is an "accelerator" that raises speed and coverage.

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › What is ZEVA? › Definition of "zero"
chunks.x:
Definition of "zero"
Important
The "zero" in ZEVA does not mean "complete disappearance".
Making variation literally zero is impossible in the physical world. Even the most precise machine shows differences if you measure finely enough. ZEVA therefore defines Definition of "Zero" as: "a state in which variation is under control, good products are guaranteed, and convergence toward the theoretical value continues".
Stage 1 (must)
Bring all parameters inside the GPC band — Variation Under Control
Stage 2 (aim)
Move the center of the distribution toward the Target (theoretical value) — Center-Aiming
Archery analogy
Stage 1 is "getting every arrow onto the target". Stage 2 is "moving the center of the arrow group to the bullseye". While some arrows still miss the target, discussing the bullseye is meaningless.
Which is Stage 1 (must) of "zero" in ZEVA?
Eliminate variation completely
Bring all parameters inside the GPC band
Make the average equal the target
First, being "under control (inside the band)" is required; then the center is moved to the theoretical value. Complete elimination is not the goal.

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › What is ZEVA? › Mindset shift: from average to variation
chunks.x:
Mindset shift: from average to variation
Traditional improvement focused on "removing waste", and evaluation tended to use the average of results. ZEVA shifts the focus to Mura (unevenness) (variation) and changes the evaluation axis from "how good the average is" to "how stably it can be reproduced".
Traditional view
OK if the average CT is within target
Find waste and subtract it
Chase results (defect rate, OEE) directly
Improvements tend to be temporary
ZEVA view
Even with a good average, large variation = "unstable" = improvement target
Design targets backward from the theoretical value
Control causes (X) to change results (Y)
Sustain as a new standard with PDCA+S
Same average, different processes (illustrative numbers)
Operator A CT (s): 30, 31, 29, 30, 30 → average 30 s
Operator B CT (s): 22, 40, 25, 38, 25 → average 30 s
By average they are the same. But in B you cannot predict how long the next unit will take, and downstream suffers waiting and piling up.
ZEVA treats B as a priority improvement target. Variation is quantified with V.Score (σ/μ).
Next module
Why does variation make it impossible to even judge whether an improvement worked? The logic behind this (the root logic) is covered in the next module.

JIT, jidoka, kanban
DMAIC, SPC, DOE

ZEVA does not reject other theories; it uses them complementarily
What makes ZEVA unique
① Aligns all improvement toward one point: controlling variation ② Works backward from the theoretical value instead of subtracting from the current state ③ Chooses improvement speed by the nature of the issue (Quick / Deep) ④ Runs in analog and accelerates with digitalisation.

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Root logic: why eliminate variation to the limit?
chunks.x:
Root logic: why eliminate variation to the limit?
Data-based action needs reliable data — learn the logical chain behind all of ZEVA and its theoretical basis, Shewhart’s principle.
Explain the 5-step chain of the root logic in order
Explain Shewhart’s principle and its effect on interpreting the defect rate and V.Score
Distinguish 3 kinds of variation (object, measurement, intentional)
Explain data reliability = precision + accuracy
Explain why the virtuous cycle starts from the foundation and is not a deadlock
Action is based on data → needs reliable data → reliable = low variation and no bias
Shewhart: an unstable process has no definable capability
Remove "uncontrolled change"; measurement issues → MSA/calibration; DOE change → learning
Data reliability = precision (low variation) + accuracy (no bias)
The virtuous cycle starts from the foundation; start it while moving, do not wait

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Root logic: why eliminate variation to the limit? › The logical chain of the root logic
chunks.x:
The logical chain of the root logic
The basic idea of ZEVA is to "eliminate all variation to the limit". This is not a slogan like "let’s improve quality". It rests on the logic that makes improvement activity possible at all — the Root logic.
Improvement actions must be based on data, not on intuition or experience
Data-based action requires highly reliable data
Reliable data is data with little variation and no bias
Therefore large uncontrolled variation = unreliable data = you cannot (easily) act
Hence eliminating all variation (uncontrolled change) to the limit is the fundamental premise of data-based action
Removing variation is both a "goal" and the "precondition" that makes improvement possible
Root logic with virtuous and vicious cycles
Bathroom scale analogy
You want to check whether your diet works, but the scale changes ±3 kg every time you step on it. You cannot tell whether you lost 1 kg, so you cannot decide whether to change your meals. Process data works the same way.

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Root logic: why eliminate variation to the limit? › Theoretical basis: Shewhart’s principle
chunks.x:
Theoretical basis: Shewhart’s principle
A process that is not in a stable state (statistical control) has no definable process capability.
Shewhart’s principle
Control chart theory (Shewhart / Deming) divides variation into common causes (many small factors always present) and special causes (sudden, identifiable factors such as a broken tool, a material lot change, or a deviation from the procedure). The state where special causes are removed and only common causes remain is called State of statistical control.
Unstable process (special causes)
Today’s data does not predict tomorrow’s process
The defect rate and V.Score can be calculated but mean nothing
Before/after comparisons depend on luck
Stable process (in statistical control)
Data is reproducible and predicts the future
What the process can do can be judged from the metrics
Improvement effects can be judged correctly
In the root logic, "large variation = unreliable data" strictly means the process is not in statistical control and its data is not reproducible. That is why ZEVA first confirms stability with a control chart before evaluating the Defect rate or V.Score (Variation Score).
Common pitfall
"The defect rate is 0.05% this month, so we are fine" — if you have not confirmed the process is stable, that number may just be a coincidence.
When a process is not in statistical control, what is true about its metrics?

When a process is not in statistical control, what is true about its metrics?

It cannot be calculated, so treat it as 0
It can be calculated but has no meaning as process capability

Shewhart’s principle: an unstable process has no definable capability. Remove special causes first.

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Root logic: why eliminate variation to the limit? › Defining "variation": three kinds of change
chunks.x:
Defining "variation": three kinds of change
The "variation" that the root logic asks us to remove is uncontrolled change. Not all change is bad. Distinguishing the following three prevents confusing "measurement problems", "process problems" and "intentional experiments".
Kind
Content
Treatment
Variation of the object
Uncontrolled change remaining in the process or work
To be removed. "Variation" in ZEVA normally means this
Measurement variation & bias
Error of the measurement system itself (precision, accuracy)
Removed via Measurement System Analysis and calibration to directly guarantee data reliability
Intentional experimental change
Change created on purpose by varying conditions, e.g. in Design of Experiments
Not to be removed. A source of learning to identify causes
Distinguishing three kinds of change
Which kind of change is this?
Object variation (remove)
Measurement variation/bias (MSA, calibration)
Intentional experiment (learning)
Screw-tightening time differs greatly between operators
Uncontrolled change remaining in the work.
Two people measure the same part and get different sizes
The object is the same, so it is a measurement system (reproducibility) issue.
Trial production at 3 temperature levels to find the optimum
Planned change for experiment — a source of learning.
The caliper always reads 0.05 mm too large
Measurement bias (accuracy). Fixed by calibration.

chunks.x:

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Root logic: why eliminate variation to the limit? › Data reliability = precision + accuracy
chunks.x:
Data reliability = precision + accuracy
Data reliability is the degree to which data can be trusted in terms of both variation (precision) and bias (accuracy), so that it can be the basis for action. One without the other is not enough.
Precision and accuracy: four targets
Precision (small variation)
How closely repeated measurements of the same thing agree. Small random error.
Accuracy (trueness) (no bias)
How close the center of the values is to the true value. Small systematic error (bias).
Data that is "consistent but wrong"
A precise but biased gauge is wrong the same way every time. It looks trustworthy because variation is small, but actions go in the wrong direction. That is why "absence of bias" is part of the definition of data reliability.
Measurement variation (repeatability, reproducibility) and bias (calibration) are evaluated and removed through Measurement System Analysis in the Measure phase of Deep GPC.

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Root logic: why eliminate variation to the limit? › Virtuous and vicious cycles, and the starting point

ZEVA’s guiding principles form a hierarchy: three principles stand on a foundation of standardization. Like a house, without a foundation even the finest pillars (principles) will lean.
ZEVA principle system (foundation + 3 principles)

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Principle system: foundation + 3 principles › Foundation: standardization — guaranteeing reproducibility
chunks.x:
Foundation: standardization — guaranteeing reproducibility
The Foundation: standardization is the precondition for the principles to work. Without it, neither measurement nor improvement is possible — as the root logic showed, data has no meaning on a floor without reproducibility.
5S / 3 Fixes (3-tei)
Organizing the physical environment and standardizing how things are managed. Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize, Sustain / fixed position, fixed item, fixed quantity. An environment where anyone can work under the same conditions at any time.
4M standards
Standards for Man (work instructions), Machine (maintenance criteria), Material (receiving/storage criteria), Method (procedures, inspection criteria).
Standard work
Establish procedures that "anyone can interpret only one way". Not "tighten firmly" but "tighten to 2.0 N·m, until the click".
Securing reproducibility

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Principle system: foundation + 3 principles › How to standardize: Quick and Deep standardization
chunks.x:
How to standardize: Quick and Deep standardization
Standardization follows three stages as its frame: "decide → keep → revise". The first standard you decide is the Initial standard. It is not the optimum; it exists to create a "measurable state" where the same method and the same way of measuring allow comparison.
Standardizing every process in detail stops improvement from starting
If every process gets a detailed procedure, improvement cannot start until standardization is finished. You would create, at the standardization stage, the very deadlock ("cannot act until the data is reliable") that the root logic rejects. So, just like Quick / Deep GPC, you normally decide fast with Quick standardization and use Deep standardization only where you need to dig deep.
Quick standardization (normal)
Decide: pick the single best method known now as the initial standard, on the same day or within 3 days at most as a guide
Keep: everyone on every shift works and measures the same way
Revise: correct it from data and compliance, and put improvements into the outcome standard
Deep standardization (local)
Decide: collect the basis from specifications and drawings, break down to element tasks and conditions X, and build the initial standard (Steps 0–6)
Keep: several people run it to confirm reproducibility, and measurement conditions are fixed (Steps 7–8)

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Principle system: foundation + 3 principles › The three principles
chunks.x:
The three principles
Principle ①: variation countermeasure — cut the root of loss
Variation is the root of every loss in quality, cost, delivery and safety. Quality drops, repair, excess inventory, disrupted plans — all come from variation. By controlling causes (X) instead of results (Y), QCDS improves at the same time. This "single focus" is the source of ZEVA’s improvement efficiency.
Q Quality
Fewer defects and repairs
C Cost
Less safety stock and spare staff
D Delivery
Flows as planned
S Safety
Fewer unexpected motions
Principle ②: theoretical-value thinking — work backward from the ideal
Instead of "a bit better than now", define "the ideal state theoretically reachable", visualize the gap and identify improvement targets. This is Absolute-value thinking based on the theoretical-value formula "site theoretical value = value work + semi-value work (minimum necessary)". Targets are set by working backward from the theoretical value, not by subtracting from the current state.
Principle ③: PDCA+S — return improvement to the standard and evolve it
P Plan
Decide
D Do
Do it
C Check
Is it followed? Any gap?
A Act
Close the gap
S Standardize
Revise into a new standard
The "S" in PDCA-S (PDCA+S) keeps improvements from being temporary and fixes them as new standards. The cycle "decide → keep → revise" keeps evolving the foundation itself.
Initial standard
Creates a measurable state

chunks.x:
Theoretical value
The theoretical value is the purpose foundation of ZEVA. Learn the 3 work categories and their "boundaries", site vs technical theoretical value, management vs technical loss, and the value-work ratio.
Explain the difference between the analytic approach and the design approach (absolute-value thinking)
Classify work into value, semi-value and non-value and explain their "boundaries"
Calculate site/technical theoretical values and management/technical loss
Calculate the value-work ratio and explain target levels
Explain how required quality, required cost and over-quality relate, and judge where process variation must sit
Theoretical value = flow only value work at top speed and cut everything else as loss
Absolute-value thinking: theoretical value + semi-value = ideal (not subtracting from now)
Boundaries: value = design, semi-value = method, non-value = management; moving boundaries is improvement
Management loss = current − site theoretical value; technical loss = site theoretical value − technical theoretical value
Value-work ratio: typically 10–30%, target 50–60%+
The required quality is set after confirming mass-production feasibility; anything beyond it is over-quality and only adds cost
Keep process variation inside the required quality within the required cost; lowering the slope needs a change of technical theory and product design

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Theoretical value › What the theoretical value is: flow only value work, at top speed
chunks.x:
What the theoretical value is: flow only value work, at top speed
Theoretical value is the idea of "flowing only value work at top speed and cutting everything else as loss". It is not just a productivity technique but continuous reform and improvement activity that builds shop-floor capability contributing to the business.
The core of the theoretical-value approach that ZEVA inherits
Clarify the theoretical value
Define the ideal state physically and technically
Absolute-value thinking
Work backward from the theoretical value, not subtract from the current state
Priority by gap
Start where the gap to the theoretical value is largest
Two approaches
Analytic approach (subtraction)
Current − waste = after improvement
Steady, step by step
Hard to escape the extension of the current state
You never know "how far is enough"
Design approach (absolute value)
Theoretical value + semi-value = ideal state
Design backward from the ideal
Encourages radical improvement ideas
The destination (goal) is clear
Analogy: planning a trip
Subtraction thinking is "take the usual road and avoid spots likely to be jammed". Absolute-value thinking is "first draw the shortest route on the map, then add only the detours you really need". The latter shows clearly how much of a detour your current road is.

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Theoretical value › The 3 work categories and their boundaries
chunks.x:
The 3 work categories and their boundaries
Theoretical-value thinking strictly classifies all work into 3 categories. The essence of the classification is "what determines that the work exists (its boundary)".
The 3 categories and their boundaries
Category
Boundary (what decides)
Definition
Examples
Value work
Product design — always needed unless the design changes
The "moment" that changes the shape or properties of the item for its required function
The moment a drill makes the hole, a bolt reaching the specified torque, applying paint
Semi-value work
Method/process — can be reduced or removed by changing the method
Accompanying work that is the minimum necessary given the current method
Grasping a part, setting it in a jig, pressing start, changeover
Non-value work
Execution/management — can be zero under proper management
Pure loss that creates no added value
Walking, waiting, searching, re-grasping, repair, transport between processes
Focus on the "moment"
The whole screw-tightening task is not value work. Grasping the screw, placing it in the hole and positioning the driver are semi-value; the moment the screw reaches the tightening torque is value. The higher the resolution, the more you realize how surprisingly short value work is.
Which is it? Value, semi-value, non-value
Value
Semi-value
Non-value

Moving a boundary is improvement itself
The boundaries of the 3 categories are not fixed. Change the boundary and the classification changes — this shows the direction of improvement.
Boundary change
Example
Effect
Change the design → value boundary moves
4 screws → snap-fit design; the value work "screw tightening" itself disappears
Redefine value work (how the essential function is achieved changes)
Change the method → semi-value boundary moves
Manual setting → automatic feeder; semi-value work "grasping the part" disappears
Reduce/remove semi-value (site theoretical value approaches technical theoretical value)
Improve management → non-value decreases
Apply 3-tei to parts so "searching" disappears / optimize layout so "walking" disappears
Thorough removal of non-value (can act immediately with ECRS)

Much non-value work comes from poor management, a breeding ground for variation. "Searching", "waiting" and "re-grasping" take a different time each cycle and create CT variation. Removing non-value work reduces loss and variation at the same time.

Two theoretical values and two losses
Site theoretical value = value work + semi-value work (minimum under current method)
Site theoretical value: the ideal reachable while accepting current equipment, tools and methods. The first destination.
Technical theoretical value = value work only (semi-value also removed by new technology/method)
Technical theoretical value: the ideal that guides future technology development and investment.
Current
Current work time
Value + semi-value + non-value
↓ Management loss

Solved by removing non-value work (start now with management and ECRS)

The first destination

Solved by method improvement or investment
Technical theoretical value

The ultimate ideal
Worked example (illustrative numbers)
Video analysis of a 60 s assembly cycle: value 12 s, semi-value 18 s, non-value 30 s
Site theoretical value = 12 + 18 = 30 s → management loss = 60 − 30 = 30 s
Assume a new method can cut semi-value to 6 s → ideal under it = 12 + 6 = 18 s. Technical theoretical value with all semi-value removed = 12 s → technical loss = 30 − 12 = 18 s

Example: fill time in injection moulding
The same view applies to process conditions, not just time. In injection moulding, the fill time at the machine’s maximum injection speed is the technical theoretical value. Fill too fast and you get jetting, flow marks, air traps, burn marks and flash; too slow and you get a short shot (incomplete filling). Only the range in between yields good parts, and that range changes with part shape, mould specification and so on.

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Theoretical value › Value-work ratio: the core improvement metric
chunks.x:
Value-work ratio: the core improvement metric
Value-work ratio (%) = value work time ÷ total work time × 100
Value-work ratio is the share of time that truly creates value.
On typical floors the value-work ratio is only about 10–30%. Theoretical-value thinking targets 50–60% or more. Manual processes usually start from a low value. A low number is not a shame; it means "the room for improvement has become visible".
With variation, even the theoretical value cannot be measured
If the same task is done in a different way each time, you cannot decide "what is the minimum semi-value". Theoretical-value analysis becomes accurate only after reproducibility is secured through standardization. This is exactly why ZEVA puts the foundation (standardization) first.
Total work 80 s, value work 20 s. Value-work ratio?
20%
25%
40%
20 ÷ 80 × 100 = 25%.

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › Theoretical value › Quiz

Q: Which formula expresses the design approach of the theoretical value?
A: Theoretical value + semi-value = ideal state
Absolute-value thinking: add only the needed semi-value to the ideal.
Q: What is the boundary of semi-value work?
A: Method / process
Semi-value is required by the current method and can be removed by changing it.
Q: How is "searching for parts" classified?
A: Non-value
Pure loss caused by poor management; removable with 3-tei.
Q: Changing screw fastening to a snap-fit design does what?
A: The value boundary moved and the value work "screw tightening" disappeared
Changing design changes the definition of value work itself.
Q: Current 60 s, site theoretical value 35 s. Management loss?
A: 25 s
Management loss = current − site theoretical value = 60 − 35 = 25 s.
Q: Main way to eliminate technical loss?
A: Method improvement / investment
The gap between site and technical theoretical value is closed by new methods/technology.
Q: Target level of value-work ratio for the theoretical value?
A: 50–60% or more
Typical current level is 10–30%; the target is 50–60%+.
Q: Why does theoretical-value analysis become inaccurate with large variation?
A: Procedures differ each time, so minimum semi-value and current values cannot be fixed
Without reproducibility the gap cannot be evaluated — the very reason ZEVA was born.

From 4M to 7 factors
The well-known 4M (Man, Machine, Material, Method) is the starting point for tracing the sources of variation. ZEVA extends it with Measurement, Management and Environment, and controls the Seven variation factors.
Why add three more?
Measurement: if the data itself varies, even a stable process looks unstable (root logic). Management: disorder in planning or changeovers creates variation even when people and machines are right. Environment: temperature, humidity and lighting directly affect materials and human motion. These sources are easy to miss with 4M alone.

Performance and condition of equipment and tools
3. Material
Lot differences, dimensions, properties
4. Method
Ambiguity in procedure, standard, know-how
5. Measurement
Errors of gauges and measuring methods
6. Management
Disorder in plans, changeovers, instructions
7. Environment
Temperature, humidity, lighting, vibration

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › The 7 variation factors and XY thinking › XY thinking: control causes, not results
chunks.x:
XY thinking: control causes, not results
Core principle
OEE, time and quality are "results (Y)", not "causes (X)".
X (7 variation factors) → process → Y (OEE, time, quality)
Y = f(X1, X2, … Xn)
Result (output): defect rate, CT, OEE, etc.
Cause (input): parameters/conditions belonging to the 7 factors
To change Y, you can only change X.
In XY thinking, when you want a better result you control the upstream causes (the 7 factors). In cooking terms, when the taste (Y) is weak you do not "taste more often"; you decide and keep the amount of salt, heat and time (X).
Link to the root logic
Controlling variation in causes (X) also raises the reliability of the data obtained as results (Y). XY thinking is the tool that brings the root logic — "low-variation data makes action possible" — into daily thinking.
Which of these is a "cause (X)"?
Defect rate
Soldering iron temperature setting
OEE
The temperature setting is an input condition = X. Defect rate and OEE are results = Y.

chunks.t: ZEVA Foundations › The 7 variation factors and XY thinking › Don’ts: manipulating Y directly
chunks.x:
Don’ts: manipulating Y directly
A typical prohibition in ZEVA is trying to manipulate the result (Y) directly. The numbers may look better for a while, but the cause remains — and new variation and loss appear.
NG: manipulating Y directly
Defect rate is high → make inspection stricter
CT is slow → rush the operators
OEE is low → make up numbers with overtime
OK: controlling X
Defect rate is high → optimize machine parameters (X) → defect rate (Y) drops
CT is slow → improve the work procedure (X) → CT (Y) shortens
OEE is low → remove the cause of breakdowns (X) → OEE (Y) rises
NG action
Why it fails
Stricter inspection
Defects are only "found after being made". Nothing stops them being made; inspection cost and inspector variation increase
Rushing operators
Creates overburden (muri), increasing mistakes, quality variation and safety risk; CT returns unless the procedure changes
Overtime to make up numbers
The cause of breakdowns remains; cost and fatigue increase, and fatigue becomes a new Man variation factor
Is this countermeasure OK or NG?
OK: controls X
NG: manipulates Y
Many scratch defects, so add 2 more final visual inspectors
It only catches results afterward; the cause of scratches remains.

"Is that Y or X?" "Which of the 7 factors is that X?" "Is that data reliable?" — just asking these three in meetings and morning huddles changes the quality of discussion.
Case: adhesive defects suddenly increased
In an assembly process, adhesive peeling defects have increased this week (illustrative). As team leader, what do you do?

Strengthen final inspection so no defects escape

GPC Control Theory

Explain the two stages: range control and Center-Aiming

GPC = the range of process conditions that guarantees good products, verified by physical experiments. The method foundation of ZEVA
GPC band = GPC_min to GPC_max; Target matches the theoretical value

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC Control Theory › What is GPC?
chunks.x:
What is GPC?
GPC (Good Process Conditions) (Good Process Conditions) is the control theory that forms the method foundation of ZEVA (Zero Variation Production System). While the theoretical value shows where to aim (the ideal state), GPC shows how to bring variation under control.
Definition of GPC
The range of process conditions that guarantees good products, verified by physical experiments.
The core of GPC is to actually try (physically experiment) and confirm that "within this width of conditions, good products are made", and then to produce within that range. This range is called the GPC band.
Layer 1
Theoretical value (purpose foundation)
Defines the ideal state = Target
Layer 2
Hybrid Triage
Routes issues to Quick / Deep
Layer 3
GPC control (method foundation) ← this module
Controls variation within range by GPC-M / GPC-H
Layer 4
PDCA-S + 7 factors + XY thinking
Daily operation and cause identification

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC Control Theory › The three elements of the GPC band
chunks.x:
The three elements of the GPC band
GPC band: good products are guaranteed between GPC_min and GPC_max; Target matches the theoretical value
Element
Meaning
How it is set
The physically best efficiency and quality point. It matches the theoretical value
Defined from theory, physics and experiments
Lower limit of conditions where good products are guaranteed
Confirmed by physical trials
Upper limit of conditions where good products are guaranteed
Confirmed by physical trials
Structure of the GPC band
Example: GPC band for soldering temperature (illustrative numbers)
Vary the temperature from 320°C to 380°C in 10°C steps and make 20 pieces at each condition
At 330°C or below, wetting was insufficient; at 370°C or above, components were heat-damaged
From 340°C to 360°C all pieces were good. The best joint was at 350°C
Set GPC_min = 340°C, GPC_max = 360°C, Target = 350°C

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC Control Theory › Core ideas: range control and physical basis
chunks.x:
Core ideas: range control and physical basis
Range Control
If the value is inside the GPC band it is regarded as "under control". Instead of chasing one perfect point, we keep the range where good products are guaranteed. Chasing a single point invites over-adjustment (tampering), which can actually increase variation.
Physical basis
The GPC band is not a statistical control limit but a good-product range verified by physical experiments. Because it has been confirmed by real trials that "this range makes good products", the shop floor can keep it with confidence.
GPC band vs specification limits vs control limits
Item
Range of what
Who / how it is set
Main use
Specification limit (USL/LSL)
Result (Y) = product characteristic
Set by design / customer requirement
Pass/fail judgment, tallying the Defect rate
Control limit (UCL/LCL)
Statistical behaviour of process data
Calculated from actual data (±3σ)
Judging stability (X̄-R chart)
GPC band
Cause (X) = process condition
Condition width verified by physical experiment
Daily condition control, stop on deviation
Link to XY thinking
Specification limits look at the result (Y); the GPC band controls the cause (X). Rather than reacting after Y goes out of spec, keeping X inside the GPC band creates a state where only good products can be made.
Own-process completion: the state of a process where GPC holds

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC Control Theory › Core ideas: range control and physical basis
chunks.x:
ec, keeping X inside the GPC band creates a state where only good products can be made.
Own-process completion: the state of a process where GPC holds

A process whose conditions (X) are inside the GPC band and whose standard work is followed can hand only good products to the next process without adding inspection. This state is called Own-process completion. It is not a new principle or method. It is the state that appears in a process as a result of GPC-M (Machine) / GPC-H (Human) holding, and a way of placing responsibility at the exit of the process.
Do not accept, do not make, do not pass on: do not accept defects from the previous process, do not make them in your own, and do not pass them to the next. The boundary of responsibility sits at the exit of the process.
It does not mean adding inspection in your own process: inspection only sorts the result (Y), and adding it pushes you past the Required cost. Keep the conditions (X) inside the band and create a state where inspection is not needed.
The standard for good or bad is the Required quality: stacking extra criteria on top leads to Over-quality, which only adds cost.
What makes it hold: for machines, the GPC band and an immediate stop on deviation; for people, standard work, Judgment criteria and a hold rule. Whether it holds is measured with the Outflow rate.
Which statement about own-process completion is correct?

chunks.x:
work, Judgment criteria and a hold rule. Whether it holds is measured with the Outflow rate.
Which statement about own-process completion is correct?

Adding an inspection at the exit of each process to sort out defects
A state where conditions (X) are kept in the band so that only good products are handed on without added inspection
Setting your own criteria stricter than the required quality
Inspection only sorts the result (Y), and adding it exceeds the required cost. Option 3 is over-quality. Own-process completion is the state that appears in a process where GPC holds.
Which statement about the GPC band is correct?
A statistical range calculated as mean ±3σ of past data
A range of process conditions confirmed by physical experiment to guarantee good products
The product dimension tolerance specified by the customer on the drawing
The GPC band is a physically grounded range of process conditions (X). Option 1 describes control limits; option 3 describes specification limits.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC Control Theory › GPC is not a quality-only method
chunks.x:
GPC is not a quality-only method
The name "conditions that guarantee good products" makes GPC look like a quality method. But the width of the band is set by the good-part range (quality), while the Target inside it is set by the theoretical value — the point of physically highest efficiency and quality. GPC is therefore condition control that moves toward the theoretical value within a constraint of quality.
What sets the width of the band
The Good-part range (quality). Physical trials confirm "inside this range we get good parts"
Outside it you get defects, so you stop when a condition leaves the band
What sets the Target inside the band
The theoretical value (efficiency): the point of physically highest efficiency and quality
So GPC pursues speed and stability too, while protecting quality
What handles each of the five losses in the loss structure
The five losses inside non-value work (Loss structure chart) are not all received by the GPC band. What can be set as a range of conditions goes to the GPC band; what is decided by work sequence and layout goes to standard work and ECRS. Standard work and ECRS are both means of GPC-H (Human), so neither falls outside GPC.
Loss
Mainly handled by
How it is set
Motion loss
GPC-H (Human) (standard work, motion-stability principles)
Set the distance, count and freedom of motions. Decided by procedure and layout, not by a range
Stop loss

chunks.x:
(standard work, motion-stability principles)
Set the distance, count and freedom of motions. Decided by procedure and layout, not by a range
Stop loss

GPC-M (Machine) (operating errors go to GPC-H (Human))
Keep equipment conditions inside the band and remove the seeds of minor stops and breakdowns. Breakdowns and material waiting go to equipment and material management
Speed loss
GPC-M (Machine) (human work goes to GPC-H (Human))
Equipment holds the standard speed with the band; human work holds the standard CT with standard work
Quality loss
GPC-M (Machine) / GPC-H (Human)
Confirm the good-part range by physical trials and fix it as the band. This is where GPC starts
Flow loss
GPC-H (Human) (standard work and management; outside the GPC band)
Set the WIP cap and the frequency of transport between processes. Handled by the design of the flow between processes
Semi-value work is shortened by method, equipment and product design: not by the band, but managed as technical loss against the theoretical value
Quick GPC / Deep GPC are not only for quality problems
Quick GPC and Deep GPC are names for how improvement is run. They apply to slow CT, frequent minor stops and piled-up WIP just as much as to defects.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC Control Theory › The two stages of "Zero": in-band and Center-Aiming
chunks.x:
The two stages of "Zero": in-band and Center-Aiming
In ZEVA, "Zero Variation" does not mean variation disappears completely. It means "variation is under control, good products are guaranteed, and convergence toward the theoretical value continues". GPC realises this in two stages.
Current state
Conditions sometimes leave the band (defect risk)
Stage 1 (must)
All parameters converge inside the GPC band = Variation Under Control
Stage 2 (aim)
Move the distribution centre toward Target (theoretical value) = Center-Aiming
Why does the order matter? If you only move the centre while variation is still large, the tails of the distribution spill out of the band and defects occur. Also, data from an unstable process is unreliable, so you cannot even know correctly where the centre is (Root logic). First shrink variation to fit inside the band, then perform Center-Aiming.
How to use the simulator
First reduce the variation and watch the conformance rate rise, then move the centre toward Target. Also try the reverse order and see what happens.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC Control Theory › Evaluating with the band conformance rate
chunks.x:
Evaluating with the band conformance rate
Band conformance rate = measurements inside GPC band ÷ total measurements × 100%
ZEVA target: ≥ 99%. A key metric of GPC-M (machine control).
Worked example (illustrative numbers)
Temperature was recorded 3 times a day for 20 days: 60 records in total
57 records were inside the GPC band (340–360°C), 3 were outside
57 ÷ 60 × 100 = 95%
Below the 99% target. Investigate the cause (X) of the deviations and run triage
Rule on band deviation
When the GPC band is exceeded, stop production immediately and investigate the cause. Then run triage: if there is a cause hypothesis and low risk, adjust immediately with Quick GPC; if the root cause is unknown, start Deep GPC.
GPC is not only for machines
The GPC idea is used in a dual structure: GPC-M (Machine) controls machine parameters by range, and GPC-H (Human) eliminates human work variation through standardization. You will learn the details in the next module.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC Control Theory › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: What does GPC stand for?
A: Good Process Conditions
GPC = Good Process Conditions: the range of process conditions that guarantees good products.
Q: The Target of the GPC band matches what?
A: The theoretical value
Target is the physically best efficiency/quality point and matches the theoretical value.
Q: Which is a correct difference between the GPC band and control limits?
A: The GPC band is verified by physical experiment; control limits are calculated statistically from data
The GPC band has a physical basis; control limits have a statistical basis. There is no fixed rule about which is wider.
Q: Which describes "range control" correctly?
A: If within the GPC band it is under control; keep the range
Chasing one point can cause over-adjustment and more variation. Range control keeps the guaranteed range.
Q: Which is Stage 1 (must) of ZEVA "Zero"?
A: Make all parameters converge inside the GPC band
Stage 1 is Variation Under Control (in-band); Stage 2 is Center-Aiming.
Q: 196 of 200 records were inside the band. What is the conformance rate and judgment?
A: 98%, below target (≥ 99%)
196 ÷ 200 = 98%, below the 99% target.
Q: What is the first response when the GPC band is exceeded?
A: Stop production immediately, investigate and run triage
The protocol is stop → investigate → triage. Tightening inspection manipulates Y directly and is a "don’t".

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC-M / GPC-H Dual Structure and Metrics
chunks.x:
GPC-M / GPC-H Dual Structure and Metrics
Learn the dual structure that uses machine control (GPC-M) and human control (GPC-H) according to the source of variation, and the metrics and targets of each.
Explain why ZEVA controls people and machines separately
Describe the method flow of GPC-M and GPC-H
State each metric and its target value
Calculate V.Score and judge it by the ZEVA scale
Use GPC-M (machine) or GPC-H (human) according to the source of variation
GPC-M: experiment → GPC band → record & monitor. Metrics: band conformance ≥ 99%, OEE ≥ 85%, X̄-R within limits, defect rate against a per-product target
GPC-H: ECRS + motion stability → 4M standards → CT measurement. Metrics: V.Score < 0.1, CT achievement ≥ 95%
V.Score = σ/μ — reveals variation differences even when means are equal
Interpreting metrics requires confirming stability first (Shewhart’s principle)

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC-M / GPC-H Dual Structure and Metrics › Why a dual structure?
chunks.x:
Why a dual structure?
Core
ZEVA designs input control as a dual structure: GPC-M (Machine) and GPC-H (Human).
Machines and people create variation in completely different ways. Machine variation appears as fluctuation of parameters such as temperature, pressure and speed, which can be tracked as numbers with sensors or records. Human variation appears as differences in interpreting procedures, motion order, hand position, habituation and fatigue — it cannot be solved just by setting a parameter.
Therefore ZEVA inherits the view of treating people and machines as separate control elements, so the best method can be chosen for each cause.
Machine-caused variation → GPC-M
Parameter range control
Set the GPC band by physical experiment
Sensors, records, interlocks
Human-caused variation → GPC-H
Define standard work through 4M standardization
Design work with ECRS and motion stability principles
Evaluate with CT measurement and V.Score

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC-M / GPC-H Dual Structure and Metrics › GPC-M: machine control
chunks.x:
GPC-M: machine control
GPC-M (Machine) is the method specialised in range control of machine parameters. Among the seven variation factors, it mainly handles Machine, Material and Environment; Measurement spans both GPC-M and GPC-H.
① Physical experiment
Vary conditions, confirm the good range, set the GPC band
② Record & monitor
Continuous monitoring by sensors or fixed-time sampling
③ Evaluate
Band conformance, OEE, defect rate, control chart
Metric
Definition
Target

(Rework + Repair + Scrap) ÷ total production (excluding Trial)

Within control limits

OEE expresses the overall production effectiveness of equipment. Human work variation is evaluated directly with V.Score and CT achievement rate, so OEE belongs to GPC-M (older versions once placed it under GPC-H, but in the current system it is GPC-M).

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC-M / GPC-H Dual Structure and Metrics › GPC-H: human control
chunks.x:
GPC-H: human control
GPC-H (Human) is the method specialised in eliminating human work variation. Based on the idea that "variation = evidence of insufficient standardization", it removes work variation through 4M standardization. It mainly handles Man, Method and Management.
① Design the work
Build stable work with ECRS and Principles of motion stability
② Standardize
Define Standard work with 4M standards (only one interpretation)
③ Measure
Quantify variation with CT measurement (stopwatch, video)
④ Evaluate
V.Score (σ/μ) and CT achievement rate
Metric
Definition
Target
V.Score (Variation Score) (σ/μ)
Coefficient of variation of work time
CT achievement rate
Share of cycles finished within the standard CT
GPC-H metrics

GPC-M (machine)
GPC-H (human)

A layout/motion issue — redesign with the motion stability principles.
