chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC-M / GPC-H Dual Structure and Metrics › Calculating and judging V.Score
chunks.x:
Calculating and judging V.Score
V.Score = σ ÷ μ
Standard deviation of work time (CT)
Mean of work time (CT)
Same as the coefficient of variation (CV). Because it is relative to the mean, processes with different CT lengths can be compared fairly.
V.Score
Judgment
Meaning
< 0.1
Extremely stable
The line runs at the pace it was designed for
0.1 – 0.3
Stable
Standard work is working
0.3 – 0.5
Slightly unstable
There is room to improve
0.5 – 1.0
Unstable
Revisit the standard work
≥ 1.0
Very unstable
Every cycle is done differently
How to read V.Score (spec v29, 16.4). The GPC-H target is < 0.1
Worked example: two operators (illustrative)
Operator A: 30, 31, 29, 30, 32, 29, 30, 31 s → μ ≈ 30.3, σ ≈ 1.0
V.Score(A) = 1.0 ÷ 30.3 ≈ 0.03 → Extremely stable
Operator B: 19, 42, 23, 39, 17, 45, 22, 35 s → μ ≈ 30.3, σ ≈ 11.2
V.Score(B) = 11.2 ÷ 30.3 ≈ 0.37 → Slightly unstable
The means are almost the same, but B lacks standardization. Looking only at averages would miss it.
CT achievement rate = cycles finished within standard CT ÷ all cycles × 100%
Target ≥ 95%. With a standard CT of 32 s in the example above, A = 8/8 = 100%, B = 4/8 = 50%.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › GPC-M / GPC-H Dual Structure and Metrics › Before reading metrics: stability
chunks.x:
Before reading metrics: stability
A process that is not in a stable state (statistical control) has no definable process capability.
Shewhart’s principle
The defect rate and V.Score can be calculated whenever you have data. But in an unstable process with special-cause variation remaining, today’s data does not predict tomorrow’s process, so the numbers themselves have no meaning. In ZEVA, first confirm the process is in State of statistical control with an X̄-R chart or similar, then evaluate the defect rate and the other metrics.
Metrics = visualising data reliability
Metrics are also a mechanism that visualises Data reliability by quantifying variation. When V.Score or the defect rate improves, you are getting closer to a state where data-based actions are possible.
A process shows a defect rate of 0.05%, but its control chart has many points outside the control limits. Correct interpretation?
It is below target, so the process is fine
The process is not stable, so this figure has no meaning
Just widen the control limits
By Shewhart’s principle, the metrics cannot be interpreted until stability is confirmed. Remove special causes first.

Q: CT mean 40 s, standard deviation 6 s. V.Score and judgment?
A: 0.15, Stable
6 ÷ 40 = 0.15. 0.1–0.3 is "stable (standard work is working)".
Q: Main reason V.Score uses σ/μ rather than σ alone?
A: Processes with different CT lengths can be compared fairly
σ = 2 s means different things for a 10 s and a 100 s mean. σ/μ allows relative comparison.
Q: Correct order of the GPC-M method?
A: Set GPC band by experiment → continuous monitoring by records → evaluate with conformance, OEE, etc.
Option 3 is the GPC-H flow; option 4 ignores the physical basis of the GPC band.
Q: "Operators pick parts in different ways, so CT varies." Suitable control?
A: GPC-H: 4M standardization and motion stability
Human-caused variation is handled by GPC-H through work design and standardization.
Q: What must be confirmed before evaluating the metrics?
A: That the process is in a stable state (statistical control)
A process not in statistical control has no definable capability (Shewhart’s principle).

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Principles of Motion Stability
chunks.x:
Principles of Motion Stability
Learn the three laws used in GPC-H to structurally eliminate human work variation: distance/displacement, sequence accumulation, and constraint & guide.
Explain what "every motion is a source of variation" means
Explain the content and reasoning of each of the three laws
Show the relation between number of motions and success probability by calculation
Check a workstation by applying the three laws
Every motion is a source of variation — block it by work design, not by willpower
Law 1: shorter distance leaves no room to drift
Law 2: fewer motions = fewer dice rolls. (1−p)ⁿ
Law 3: limiting freedom with guides/stoppers brings variation close to zero
Confirm the effect with CT measurement and V.Score

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Principles of Motion Stability › Every motion is a source of variation
chunks.x:
Every motion is a source of variation
Core
Every motion is a source of variation.
People are not machines, so even when repeating the same motion, it differs slightly each time. The reach distance, grasp position, placing angle and motion order — each of these creates variation in time and quality. Principles of motion stability is not a "please be careful" mindset; it builds a structure where variation hardly arises, through the design of the work itself.
Law 1: Distance / displacement
Shortening motion distance physically shrinks the room for variation
Law 2: Sequence accumulation
Reducing the number of motions eliminates opportunities for variation
Law 3: Constraint & guide
Limiting degrees of freedom structurally blocks variation
Position within GPC-H
GPC-H flows as: design the work with ECRS and motion stability → define standard work with 4M standards → measure CT → evaluate with V.Score. Motion stability is used before writing the standard, when designing the work itself to be hard to vary.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Principles of Motion Stability › Law 1: Distance / displacement
chunks.x:
Law 1: Distance / displacement
Law
Law of distance and displacement: shortening motion distance physically shrinks the allowable range of variation.
Short distance = no room to drift. The spread of where the hand stops is very different for a part 10 cm away and one 60 cm away.
Minimising the movement vector forcibly reduces the physical spread. The longer the movement, the more acceleration, deceleration and positioning errors add up.
In terms of time too, long-distance motions vary in speed with the person and their condition, becoming CT variation.
Application example (illustrative)
Parts bins sit 50 cm in front on shelves of different heights; pick time varies 2–5 s
Move the most frequently used parts into the range reachable with elbows bent (golden zone)
Change to inclined shelves with openings facing the operator
Pick time stabilised at 1.5–2.0 s (spread reduced)

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Principles of Motion Stability › Law 2: Sequence accumulation
chunks.x:
Law 2: Sequence accumulation
Law
Law of sequence accumulation: reducing the number of motions eliminates the opportunities for variation to occur.
Each motion carries a small chance of an error or a time deviation. Many motions are like rolling a die many times. Even if the failure chance per motion is small, total failures surely accumulate as the count grows.
Probability all motions succeed = (1 − p)n
Probability of error (deviation) per motion
Number of motions
A simplified model to grasp the idea (assumes independent motions).
Motions n
The more motions, the lower the chance of finishing a cycle without deviation
Eliminate re-grasping: can passing a part from right hand to left hand be removed entirely?
Eliminate searching/selecting: make searching zero with 3-teii (fixed position, item, quantity)
Replace checking motions with structure: jigs and poka-yoke make visual checks unnecessary

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Principles of Motion Stability › Law 3: Constraint & guide
chunks.x:
Law 3: Constraint & guide
Law
Law of constraint and guide: limiting degrees of freedom structurally blocks variation from occurring.
Free motion → maximum variation
Place the part "roughly around here" on the bench
Stick a label straight by eye
The operator decides insertion direction
Constrained motion → variation approaches zero
Place it against a locating jig / stopper
Fix position and angle with a guided labelling jig
Shape it so it cannot be inserted the wrong way
The more you demand "accuracy" from people, the more you depend on skill, concentration and physical condition. Guides and stoppers reduce the options of motion themselves, so the result is the same position and orientation whoever does it. This is the same idea as Poka-yoke.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Principles of Motion Stability › Relation to motion economy and application
chunks.x:
Relation to motion economy and application
ZEVA motion stability
Counterpart in IE Principles of motion economy
Difference in viewpoint
Distance / displacement law
Optimal/shortest distance, workplace layout
Seen not only as time saving but as shrinking spread
Sequence accumulation law
Eliminate / reduce motions
Probabilistic reason: fewer opportunities for variation
Constraint & guide law
Use of jigs and tools
Guarantee reproducibility by structurally limiting freedom
Order of application
First remove motions with the E of ECRS (can it be eliminated?). For the remaining motions, think in the order: reduce count (Law 2) → shorten distance (Law 1) → constrain freedom (Law 3).
Workstation checklist
Are reaching and walking completed within elbow-bent range? (Law 1)
Are there remaining re-grasp, search, select or re-orient motions? (Law 2)
Are placing positions and insertion directions determined by jigs, stoppers or shape? (Law 3)
Can steps saying "be careful" or "check" be replaced by structure?
After the change, did you measure CT and confirm V.Score went down?
A step says "place the part roughly in the centre of the tray" and misplacement defects occur. Most effective countermeasure?
Add "place exactly in the centre" in bold to the instruction
Add a locating guide matching the part shape to the tray
Hold a daily morning reminder meeting for operators

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Principles of Motion Stability › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Motion stability principles are used in which?
A: GPC-H (human control)
It is a GPC-H principle to structurally eliminate human work variation.
Q: "Reducing the number of motions eliminates opportunities for variation" is which law?
A: Sequence accumulation law
If motions are dice rolls, this means rolling fewer times.
Q: Error probability 1% per motion, 20 motions. Probability all succeed is about?
A: About 82%
(0.99)^20 ≈ 0.818. It accumulates by power, not simple multiplication.
Q: Which describes the distance/displacement law?
A: Shorter motion distance physically reduces spread
The shorter the distance, the less room to drift; minimising the movement vector lowers spread.
Q: Which is an application of the constraint & guide law?
A: Fix the placing position with a jig that has a stopper
Law 3 limits freedom so the part "can only go there". Option 1 is Law 1.
Q: Which is NOT consistent with motion stability?
A: Telling operators to "pay close attention" is the most reliable method
Relying on attention depends on people and cannot guarantee reproducibility. The essence is blocking variation by structure.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Hybrid Triage
chunks.x:
Hybrid Triage
Learn triage (Phase 0), the entrance to every improvement issue, which routes issues to Quick GPC (fast) or Deep GPC (deep).
Explain three reasons why triage is needed
Evaluate an issue with the four criteria
Decide Quick / Deep by following the flowchart
Explain how to handle the gray zone
Triage (Phase 0) is the entrance to all improvement; it prevents the three problems of uniform handling
Four criteria: ① cause idea ② number of variables ③ risk ④ data (availability + reliability)
Quick = hypothesis AND low risk AND single variable / Deep = unknown OR high risk OR many variables
Flow order: cause → risk → variables (3 or more) → data
Gray zone: try one Quick cycle, escalate to Deep if no effect. Modes can run in parallel

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Hybrid Triage › Why triage is needed
chunks.x:
Why triage is needed
Improvement issues on the shop floor range from those with an obvious cause that can be fixed at once, to those where many factors interact and statistical analysis is needed. Handling them all with one uniform improvement process causes three problems.
Over-quality
Applying heavy DMAIC to minor issues wastes resources
Lack of solving power
Applying intuitive trials to complex multi-factor issues never reaches the root cause
Speed contradiction
Forcing "just try it" and "prove it statistically" together kills the strengths of both
Concept
Instead of handling every issue with the same procedure, route issues at the entrance to Quick GPC mode (fast) or Deep GPC mode (deep).
Hybrid triage is inspired by medical triage (sorting patients by urgency). Just as an emergency room does not treat a light scratch and a severe injury with the same procedure, improvement issues get the best "speed (gear)" for their nature.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Hybrid Triage › The two modes
chunks.x:
The two modes
Mode
Target issues
Duration
Cycle
Approach
Quick GPC mode (fast improvement)
Cause hypothesis, low risk, single variable
1 day – 1 week
Think while running. Mass-produce small trials
Deep GPC mode (deep analysis)
Unknown cause, high risk, multiple variables
1 – 3 months
Stop and think deeply. Statistical root-cause identification
Digitalisation is an accelerator
Triage can be done with a paper checklist. Digitalisation is not a prerequisite but an optional accelerator: at Level 2 it can be an interactive web form, at Level 3 AI-assisted judgment and recommendation.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Hybrid Triage › The four criteria
chunks.x:
The four criteria
Criterion
Question
Toward Quick GPC
Toward Deep GPC
① Cause idea
Do you have an idea of the cause?
Yes (hypothesis possible)
Completely unknown
② Number of variables
How many related parameters?
Specific 1–2
Compound (many variables)
③ Risk
Impact if it fails?
Easy to revert (Low)
Equipment damage / injury risk (High)
④ Data
Data availability?
Available right now
Long collection needed
Triage criteria
Criterion ④ and the root logic
The "data" of criterion ④ includes not only availability but also reliability (degree of variation). If the data varies so much that it cannot be trusted, first secure data reliability through standardization and stabilising measurement (Root logic).
Decision logic
Route A: Quick GPC
Condition: cause hypothesis AND low risk AND single variable
Chosen only when all are met
Try floor insights at once; mass-produce successes and knowledge
Route B: Deep GPC
Condition: unknown cause OR high risk OR many variables
Chosen if any one applies
Identify root cause statistically and solve fundamentally
There is a cause idea and one variable, but failure could damage a press die. Decision?
Quick GPC (two conditions are met)
Deep GPC (because risk is high)
No triage needed, just try
Route B is an OR condition — high risk alone means Deep GPC.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Hybrid Triage › Decision flowchart
chunks.x:
Decision flowchart
Triage flow: if any of Steps 1–4 triggers, Deep GPC; if all pass, Quick GPC
Step 1: Any idea of the cause? (criterion ①) → No: Deep GPC; Yes: go to Step 2
Step 2: Is the risk on failure high? (criterion ③) → High: Deep GPC; Low: go to Step 3
Step 3: Are there 3 or more related variables? (criterion ②) → Yes: Deep GPC; No: go to Step 4
Step 4: Can data be obtained right now? (criterion ④) → No (long collection): Deep GPC; Yes: Quick GPC
Why this order?
Without a hypothesis you cannot even write the "H" of H-T-C-A. Next, check safety and equipment impact to decide whether trying is acceptable. Then look at the number of variables and data availability to confirm you can try small and fast.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Hybrid Triage › Gray zone and linking the modes
chunks.x:
Gray zone and linking the modes
If the decision is unclear, first try one cycle (1 day – 1 week) in Quick GPC mode. If there is no effect, Escalation to Deep GPC mode follows. This stepwise "Quick → Deep" approach heads surely to a solution while minimising wasted resources.
But safety comes first
"Try first" in the gray zone applies only when failure is easy to revert (low risk). If there is a risk of equipment damage or injury, choose Deep GPC even if unclear.
Unclear decision
(low risk)
One Quick GPC cycle
Try in 1 day – 1 week
Effective → standardize
Temporary standard → PDCA-S
No effect → Deep GPC
Escalation
The modes are not mutually exclusive. If, during a Deep GPC analysis, an idea comes up that meets the Quick GPC conditions (low risk, single variable), you may run a Quick GPC trial in parallel with the analysis.
Exercise: triage three issues
You are a line leader. Route the issues reported this week (fictional illustrative cases).
Issue 1: "Tape position varies in packing. I think it is because each operator puts the tape cutter in a different place."
Quick GPC
Correct. Hypothesis, one variable, low risk, measurable now. Fix the location and try a few cycles.
Deep GPC
DMAIC would be over-quality here. All four criteria point to Quick.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Hybrid Triage › Gray zone and linking the modes
chunks.x:
ariable, low risk, measurable now. Fix the location and try a few cycles.
Deep GPC
DMAIC would be over-quality here. All four criteria point to Quick.

Issue 2: "Paint film thickness defects occur a few times a month. Temperature, humidity, paint lot, gun distance, pretreatment… no idea which is the cause."
Quick GPC
Unknown cause, many variables, low frequency so data takes time. Intuitive trials will not reach the root cause.
Deep GPC
Correct. "Unknown cause" at Step 1 already means Deep GPC. Start with MSA and analyse with DMAIC.
Issue 3: "Assembly CT seems a bit slower since last week. Maybe the new part supply method, but CT records are inconsistent and cannot be compared."
Revert the supply method immediately and conclude
With unreliable data you cannot even tell whether reverting made it faster.
First standardize measurement to secure data reliability, then try with Quick GPC
Correct. Criterion ④ includes data reliability. Once measurement is aligned, it is a low-risk hypothesis for Quick GPC.
Triage means judging the nature of an issue. A wrong decision leads to wasted resources or lack of solving power.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Hybrid Triage › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Which is NOT a problem triage aims to prevent?
A: Insufficient investment in digitalisation
Digitalisation is an accelerator, not the purpose of triage.
Q: Typical duration of Quick GPC mode?
A: 1 day – 1 week
Quick: 1 day – 1 week; Deep: 1 – 3 months.
Q: Decision condition for Route A (Quick GPC)?
A: Hypothesis AND low risk AND single variable
Quick requires all (AND); Deep needs any one (OR).
Q: What is checked at Step 1 of the flowchart?
A: Whether there is an idea of the cause
Order: Step 1 cause → Step 2 risk → Step 3 variables → Step 4 data.
Q: At Step 3, what leads to Deep GPC?
A: 3 or more related variables
Specific 1–2 leans Quick; 3 or more means Deep GPC.
Q: Which is correct about criterion ④ "data"?
A: It includes reliability (degree of variation) as well as availability
If data is unreliable, first secure reliability through standardization and stable measurement (root logic).
Q: Recommendation when the decision is unclear (low risk)?
A: Try one Quick GPC cycle first; escalate to Deep GPC if no effect
The stepwise approach minimises waste while heading surely to a solution.
Q: During Deep GPC analysis, a low-risk single-variable idea appears. What do you do?
A: You may run a Quick GPC trial in parallel
The modes are not exclusive and can run in parallel when conditions are met.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Quick GPC: H-T-C-A
chunks.x:
Quick GPC: H-T-C-A
Learn the fast improvement cycle H-T-C-A, which tries floor insights immediately and mass-produces small successes and knowledge.
Explain what is done in each of the four H-T-C-A steps
Write a one-sentence hypothesis with the template
Explain the rules of a temporary standard (deadline, scope, rollback)
Judge the escalation criteria to Deep GPC
Quick GPC = H-T-C-A, 1 day – 1 week, no statistics, analog OK
H: one-sentence hypothesis with the template; search past cases in the knowledge base
T: try immediately with small N / C: near-binary better/worse (keep measurement consistent)
A: success → update WI, temporary standard (formalise within 30 days, one line, rollback) / failure → change conditions
Escalate to Deep GPC after 3 failures, no hypotheses, recurrence, or larger impact

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Quick GPC: H-T-C-A › Purpose and mindset of Quick GPC
chunks.x:
Purpose and mindset of Quick GPC
Purpose
Try shop-floor insights immediately and mass-produce small successes and knowledge. Duration: 1 day – 1 week.
Quick GPC mode drives improvement with H-T-C-A cycle, a four-step fast cycle without the heaviness of DMAIC. No statistical knowledge is required, and it runs fully in an analog environment (paper and stopwatch). Instead of "move after making a perfect plan", it thinks while running, raising improvement speed and floor participation.
H-T-C-A
H: Hypothesis
Put "changing this should improve it" in one sentence
T: Trial
Test right away with small N
C: Check
Better or worse?
A: Standardize or retry
If good, update WI now; if not, change conditions
Not a simplified PDCA
H-T-C-A is an improvement cycle — hypothesis → experiment → verification → standardization — starting from a hypothesis. PDCA-S is a maintenance cycle — plan → do → check → act → standardize — starting from a plan. Their roles differ.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Quick GPC: H-T-C-A › Step 1: Hypothesis
chunks.x:
Step 1: Hypothesis
Set the "best 5M": no complex analysis needed. Put into words the intuition "changing this in this way should make it better".
Search the knowledge base: check recommended parameters and failed trials from similar past cases to avoid wasted re-experiments.
Simplify it so it fits in one sentence. If it does not, there may be too many variables (revisit triage).
Hypothesis template
"If we change [target parameter] from [current value] to [new value], we should get [expected result]."
Poor hypotheses
"Defects drop if operators are more careful" → the X to change is vague
"Reviewing various things will help" → cannot be verified
"Double inspection reduces escapes" → manipulates Y directly
Good hypotheses
"Moving the parts tray from left to right should cut pick time by 2 s."
"Raising solder temperature from 345°C to 350°C should eliminate poor wetting."
"Laying felt on the bench should bring scratch defects to zero."
Which best follows the hypothesis template?
We want to improve quality in the screw-tightening process
Changing the driver torque from 1.0 N·m to 1.2 N·m should eliminate lifted screws
Investigate the cause of lifted screws statistically
It has target, current value, new value and expected result. Option 1 is a goal; option 3 is a Deep GPC activity.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Quick GPC: H-T-C-A › Step 2: Trial and Step 3: Check
chunks.x:
Step 2: Trial and Step 3: Check
Trial: small and immediate
Set a small N (sample size) and test right away. "Try 5 units first" is enough.
A perfect experimental design is unnecessary (that is the job of Deep GPC).
For GPC-M: change the parameter and produce a small lot
For GPC-H: change the standard work and try several cycles
Check: a near-binary judgment
The judgment is close to binary: "better or worse?". No statistical test is needed; decide with the senses of the floor and simple measurement.
Analog alternative
No sensors? "Visual check" and "handwritten check sheet" are fine.
Digital level
Check method
Level 1 (analog)
Visual check + handwritten record
Level 2 (digitisasi)
Spreadsheet summary + graph
Level 3 (digitalisation)
Real-time dashboard
Check methods by Staged digitalisation model
Simple, but consistent measurement
Even without statistics, you must keep the measurement method the same before and after (same break points, same person, same tool). If measurement varies, you cannot tell whether there was an effect (Root logic). Data reliability rises with each improvement — this is how the virtuous cycle starts.

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › Quick GPC: H-T-C-A › Step 4: Action (standardize or retry)
chunks.x:
Step 4: Action (standardize or retry)
If it worked
Update the Work instruction immediately
Apply it on the floor the same day as a Temporary standard
Register briefly in the knowledge base (one photo + comment)
Move to daily monitoring in PDCA-S
If it did not work
Change the conditions the next day
Run H-T-C-A again with another hypothesis
Register the failure as knowledge too (avoid repeating it)
If escalation criteria apply, move to Deep GPC
Rules of the temporary standard
Waiting for the formal revision process (approval flow) delays the benefit reaching the floor, and people may drift back to the old way. So a temporary standard is used as an "express lane" with a simplified approval flow — with constraints to keep it safe.
Validity: max 30 days
Obtain formal approval within 30 days
Scope: single line only
Horizontal deployment to other lines only after formal approval
Rollback possible
Back up the previous state so it can be restored any time

chunks.x:
Q: What is done in the "C" of H-T-C-A?

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › PDCA-S and the Three Cycles
chunks.x:
PDCA-S and the Three Cycles
Learn the different roles and connections of H-T-C-A, DMAIC and PDCA-S, and the GPC-M / GPC-H daily operation protocols that sustain improvement results.
Distinguish the purpose, duration and output of the three cycles
Explain how the cycles connect (hand-over)
Correctly explain four common confusions
Explain daily operation, abnormality response and periodic review for GPC-M / GPC-H
H-T-C-A and DMAIC "solve"; PDCA-S "maintains". Complements, not alternatives
H-T-C-A success → PDCA-S; 3 failures → DMAIC; DMAIC Control → hands over to PDCA-S Plan

chunks.t: ZEVA Practice › PDCA-S and the Three Cycles › Positioning of the three cycles
chunks.x:
Positioning of the three cycles
ZEVA uses three kinds of cycles. They are not alternatives but complements for different phases. Choose not by "which one do I like" but by "which phase am I in now".
Improvement phase: find and solve issues
H-T-C-A cycle (Quick GPC)
DMAIC (Deep GPC)
Maintenance phase: sustain results in daily operation
PDCA-S (PDCA+S) (daily operation)
H-T-C-A (Quick GPC)
DMAIC (Deep GPC)
PDCA-S (daily operation)
Purpose
Solve issues by fast hypothesis testing
Find root cause statistically and solve fundamentally

After triage (Route B)
After improvement (continuous)
Duration
1 day – 1 week
1 – 3 months
Continuous (no end)
Steps
Statistics
Not needed
Needed
Not needed

Temporary standard (formalise within 30 days)
GPC band reset, SOP revision
Maintain/update standards, early abnormality detection
Comparison of the three cycles
Point
H-T-C-A and DMAIC are cycles to solve issues; PDCA-S is the cycle to maintain the solved state. Executing and sustaining improvement are separate phases; combining them makes the effect stick.

Common confusions and correct understanding
Confusion
Correct understanding
"Are DMAIC and PDCA-S not basically the same?"
DMAIC solves a problem; PDCA-S maintains the solved state. Their purposes are fundamentally different.
"Can we not improve with PDCA-S alone?"
PDCA-S works for fine-tuning existing standards but is unsuitable for root-cause identification or fundamental improvement. Complex issues need DMAIC.
"Are DMAIC Control and PDCA-S Check the same?"
Control is the "close" of an improvement project, building the control system. Check is routine confirmation in daily operation. Control results hand over to PDCA-S.
"Is H-T-C-A not a simplified PDCA?"
H-T-C-A is an improvement cycle: hypothesis → experiment → verification → standardization. PDCA-S is a maintenance cycle: plan → do → check → act → standardize. The starting point differs (hypothesis vs plan).
"If we run PDCA-S, chronic defects of unknown cause will also be solved." This idea is…
Correct. PDCA-S is an all-purpose improvement cycle
Wrong. Unknown-cause issues go to Deep GPC (DMAIC) through triage
Wrong. Unknown-cause issues are outside improvement scope
PDCA-S is a maintenance cycle. Use DMAIC to identify root causes.

When the criteria are not met or the work could not be done to standard → hold the item instead of passing it on, and tell the team leader. chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Theoretical-Value Improvement Methods: The Four Boxes and ECRS › The Theoretical-Value Thinking Process: Hypothesis and Verification
chunks.x:
The Theoretical-Value Thinking Process: Hypothesis and Verification
Improvement based on the theoretical value is a systematic, shop-floor version of something we do unconsciously every day: decide the destination, think about the route, act, and evaluate the result. At its core is the attitude of working backward from the theoretical value, instead of subtracting waste from the current state.
① Recognise the need
Why improve? (capacity, cost, ...)
② Grasp the current state
Current value, theoretical value, the gap (loss)
③ Design the desired state
Measurable targets benchmarked on the theoretical value
④ Build the scenario
Improvement themes and steps to get there
Hypothesise and verify with 5W1H
Running through the whole process is the habit of thinking logically with 5W1H (why, what, where, when, who, how) and always forming and testing hypotheses. You do not need the right answer on the first try — each loop sharpens it.

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Theoretical-Value Improvement Methods: The Four Boxes and ECRS › The Compass of Improvement: The Four Boxes
chunks.x:
The Compass of Improvement: The Four Boxes
The Four boxes is a framework for logically building everything from current-state analysis to the design of the desired state and the scenario to reach it. The top row is the result side (values), the bottom row the cause side (ways of working); the left column is the current state, the right column the desired state.
Figure: structure and thinking loop of the Four Boxes
Box
Conclusion (what to write)
Grounds (how to support it)
① Current value (result)
Quantify current performance: OEE, CT, defect rate, headcount, inventory
Understand the theoretical value (essential function) and visualise OEE and CT losses structurally
② Current way (cause)
Describe the weaknesses that cause ①, concretely (e.g. processes split apart, lots of waiting)
Analyse variation causes from the 4M (seven-factor) viewpoint
③ New way (cause)
Countermeasures that overcome ② and achieve ④ (e.g. connect processes, one-person completion)
Reason from the theoretical value and explain why it works using ECRS etc.
④ Target value (result)
Performance targets to achieve (e.g. one fewer operator, half the lead time)
Stack up the losses to be removed and show logically that the target is valid
Loop back and forth

chunks.x:
chieve (e.g. one fewer operator, half the lead time)

Think in the loop “② current way → ③ new way → ④ target value → compare with ① current value” many times. If the numbers in ④ do not match the story in ② and ③, some hypothesis is still weak.
The Four Boxes in ZEVA
In ZEVA, box ① must contain metrics such as V.Score (Variation Score) and the Defect rate, not just averages. If ① is written while variation is large, the values themselves are unreliable (Root logic), and the target in ④ loses its grounds.

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Theoretical-Value Improvement Methods: The Four Boxes and ECRS › Analysis Methods that Make Losses Visible
chunks.x:
Analysis Methods that Make Losses Visible
To fill the four boxes you must grasp the current state accurately and pin down the nature of the losses. Theoretical-value thinking combines the following four analyses.
Loss structure chart
Splits total actual time into value, semi-value and non-value work, then breaks non-value work into five losses — motion, stop, speed, quality and flow — and shows the proportions, so you see at a glance where the biggest impact is.
CT (cycle time) analysis
Break work into elements and time each repeatedly. You capture not just the total but the variation of each element. Line-balance analysis adds the neck CT and balance efficiency.
Value-work analysis
Watch video frame by frame and classify every motion as value, semi-value or non-value using a value-work definition. Non-value is further split by loss axis: reaching, walking, re-gripping, etc.
OEE analysis
Split into availability, performance and yield rate and drill into stop, speed and quality losses. For example, speed-loss causes are found by continuous on-site observation.
Variation is “evidence of missing standards”
When element times vary in a CT analysis, it proves the work is not standardised or some problem is hidden. ZEVA looks at variation before the average CT to decide the GPC-H (Human) targets.
Loss structure chart: the five losses inside non-value work

Loss structure chart: the five losses inside non-value work

Non-value work is not a single kind of loss. Besides wasted motions such as walking and searching, it includes time stopped, time running slow, time spent on defects and repair, and time stuck between processes. Semi-value work corresponds to Technical loss and non-value work to Management loss.
Loss
What it is
Examples
Motion loss
Extra motions during work
Walking, searching, re-gripping, reaching
Stop loss
Time not producing
Time actually stopped by breakdowns, waiting for material, operating errors, etc. (breakdowns and such are causes X)
Speed loss (Slow)
Time producing but below the standard speed
Short stops not counted as stoppages in the records (minor stops), reduced speed, CT delays
Quality loss (Defect)
Time that does not yield good product
Defects, rework, repair, scrap
Flow loss
Time goods or people are held or moved between processes
Work in process, waiting, stagnation, jams and transport between processes
Classify losses by result Y (stopped, slowed, did not yield good product). Quality-loss time counts as non-value work whatever its cause; trace the cause separately as X. Changeover kept to the necessary minimum is semi-value work
Link to OEE

Link to OEE

The stop, speed and quality losses show up as drops in the availability, performance and yield rate of equipment OEE. In manual work, motion and flow losses are harder to see, so pick them up with video analysis and records of WIP and waiting.
Example: reading a loss structure chart (illustrative numbers)
Video analysis of one 60 s cycle: value 12 s, semi-value 18 s, non-value 30 s
Value-work ratio = 12 ÷ 60 = 20%
Site theoretical value = 12 + 18 = 30 s → management loss 30 s (non-value work)
Break the 30 s of non-value work down by loss: motion 18 s (walking 10, searching 5, re-gripping 3), quality 6 s (repair), flow 4 s (waiting), stop 2 s (waiting for material). Speed loss is 0 s in this process
The 6 s of repair is non-value work too. Count it as a loss instead of saying “it's fine because inspection catches and fixes it”
The biggest loss (walking, in motion loss) becomes the first theme for ③ new way; the quality loss goes to GPC by tracing its cause X

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Theoretical-Value Improvement Methods: The Four Boxes and ECRS › The ECRS Principle: E Comes First
chunks.x:
The ECRS Principle: E Comes First
ECRS gives four viewpoints for improving work and processes, and the order matters a great deal. Theoretical-value thinking puts E (Eliminate) first, going back to the essential function and asking relentlessly: “Is this work really needed?” Starting from S (Simplify) traps you into making work faster that could have been removed entirely.
Order
Principle
Question
Example
Can we remove it?
Guarantee quality inside the process and abolish the downstream inspection step
Can we combine it?
Use a combined tool that drills and chamfers at once
Can we change the order or place?
Convert internal setup into external setup
Can we make it simpler?
Introduce a jig that makes positioning easy
Which ECRS type is this idea?
E Eliminate
C Combine
R Rearrange
S Simplify
Stop placing a part temporarily and picking it up again; assemble it directly
The temporary placement itself disappears, so it is E.
Do labelling and visual check in the same posture at the same moment
Two tasks are merged into one, so it is C.
Move frequently used tools to the operator's right side, in order of use
It changes place and order, so it is R.
Use a tray that feeds screws in the same orientation so they are easy to pick
The task remains but becomes easier, so it is S.
Quality is now guaranteed in-process, so the 100% re-inspection is abolished

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Theoretical-Value Improvement Methods: The Four Boxes and ECRS › Pursuing Shortest, Simultaneous, Fastest
chunks.x:
Pursuing Shortest, Simultaneous, Fastest
For work that ECRS decides to keep, pursue efficiency at the motion level. Combine the following three principles without muda, muri or mura. They point in the same direction as the classic principles of motion economy.
Shortest
Bring everything to hand. Place parts and tools in the low-strain value-work zone (gold / silver / bronze areas) and eliminate reaching and walking.
Simultaneous
Use both hands and coordinate people with machines. Remove one-hand idling; while the machine processes, the person prepares the next step.
Fastest
Combine shortest and simultaneous into a rhythmic, continuous motion. Not by rushing people, but by building a structure that is naturally fast.
Zone
Rough range
What to place
Gold
Reachable with elbows kept at the sides
Parts and tools used every cycle
Silver
Reachable by extending the arm
Items used occasionally
Bronze
Reachable by moving the upper body
Rarely used items (avoid if possible)
Value-work zone concept (guideline)
“Fastest” does not mean rushing operators
Rushing operators is a “Don't” that manipulates Y (CT) directly and increases variation and quality problems. ZEVA changes X (layout, sequence, jigs) so that CT shrinks as a result.
The parts box is on a shelf behind the operator, who turns around every cycle. Which principle should you think of first?
Shortest (bring to hand)

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Theoretical-Value Improvement Methods: The Four Boxes and ECRS › Making It Stick: 4M Standards and PDCA+S
chunks.x:
Making It Stick: 4M Standards and PDCA+S
Improvement does not end with execution. Document the best state achieved as standards and procedures for Man, Machine, Material and Method (4M standards), then maintain and update it with PDCA-S (PDCA+S). This lets anyone get the same result and becomes the foundation of the next improvement.
Decide → Keep → Revise
Design with 4 boxes
Backward from theoretical value
ECRS & shortest/simul./fastest
Execute countermeasures
Verify the effect
CT, V.Score, OEE
4M standardisation
Feed back into the foundation
No improvement without standards
The “④ target value” drawn in the four boxes is reproduced every day only after it is standardised. Improvement without S slides back to the old way within weeks.

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Theoretical-Value Improvement Methods: The Four Boxes and ECRS › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Which boxes are on the “cause” side of the four boxes?
A: ② current way and ③ new way
Values (①④) are results; ways (②③) are causes. ①② are current, ③④ desired.
Q: What is the most appropriate “grounds” for ④ target value?
A: The sum of the losses removed by the countermeasures
Targets are justified logically by stacking up the losses removed — design from the theoretical value, not arbitrary subtraction.
Q: Which ECRS viewpoint should be considered first?
A: Eliminate
Speeding up work that could be removed is pointless, so E comes first.
Q: In a CT analysis, element times vary widely. How does ZEVA interpret this?
A: Evidence of missing standardisation or hidden problems
Variation is evidence of missing standards and a GPC-H target. The average alone cannot be trusted.
Q: In a 50 s cycle, value work is 10 s and semi-value 15 s. Value-work ratio and site theoretical value?
A: 20%, 25 s
10 ÷ 50 = 20%. Site theoretical value = value + semi-value = 25 s; the other 25 s is management loss.
Q: Which improvement fits the “simultaneous” principle?
A: Prepare the next part while the machine processes automatically
Coordinating people and machines to remove waiting is “simultaneous”. Tools to hand is “shortest”; removing inspection is ECRS E.
Q: What must ZEVA include in box ① current value?
A: Metrics such as V.Score and the defect rate

Deep GPC mode is the deep-analysis mode applied to issues that Hybrid triage judged as “unknown cause OR high risk OR multi-variable”. It uncovers chronic defects and tangled causes with the Six Sigma DMAIC framework and statistics, and solves them at the root. Typical duration is 1–3 months.

Cause hypothesis, low risk, single variable
1 day – 1 week
No statistics needed; senses and simple measurement

Deep GPC (DMAIC)
Unknown cause, high risk, multi-variable
1 – 3 months

Define decides unambiguously what is to be solved. If the problem definition wobbles here, all later measurement and analysis will miss the mark.
Define Y (result): what the problem is and which metric to improve to what level (e.g. the dimensional Defect rate from 2% to ≤ 0.2%)
List X (cause) candidates: brainstorm with a Fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram diagram from the Seven variation factors viewpoint
Set scope: target line, product, period — and what is out of scope
Quantify the gap to the theoretical value: show project value as the gap to the theoretical value
Supporting tools: project charter, identify CTQ (Critical to Quality), confirm process boundaries with SIPOC
SIPOC
Meaning
Example (soldering, illustrative)
Supplier
Upstream board & parts process
Input
Board, solder, temperature setting, operator
Process
Preheat → solder → cool
Output
Soldered board
Customer
Assembly (downstream)
Do not plan to manipulate Y directly
“Tighten inspection to reduce escapes” manipulates Y directly. From Define onward, phrase the theme as “which X must we control so that Y changes?” (XY thinking).

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Deep GPC: DMAIC › Measure: First Make the Data Trustworthy
chunks.x:
Measure: First Make the Data Trustworthy
The first job in Measure is to confirm that the data used for analysis can be trusted. Unreliable data leads to neither correct conclusions nor correct actions (Root logic). That is why we perform Measurement System Analysis (measurement system analysis).
Data reliability = precision (low variation) + accuracy (no bias)
MSA check item
Meaning
Aspect of reliability
Repeatability
Same person, same gauge, same part — same value every time?
Precision (variation)
Reproducibility
Same value when a different person measures?
Precision (variation)
Bias
Is there an offset from the reference (true) value?
Accuracy
Calibration
Is the gauge regularly checked against a standard?
Accuracy
%GRR = measurement-system variation (σGRR) ÷ total variation (σtotal) × 100
Combined repeatability and reproducibility variation
Part-to-part variation + measurement variation
Common rule of thumb: 30% not acceptable (fix the measurement system first)
A Gage R&R study gives %GRR = 38%. What should you do next?
Collect data as is and move on to regression
Review method, fixture, gauge and training; improve the measurement system and re-evaluate
Just increase the sample size
Above 30% the measurement noise is too large to separate from process variation. More samples do not remove measurement error — fix the measurement system first.

Measure baseline variation and defects: calculate the standard deviation and the Defect rate, but interpret them only after confirming State of statistical control with an X̄-R chart
Analog alternative
Sensors are not required for data collection. Manual measurement plus a spreadsheet is enough for solid analysis. What matters is the reliability of the measurement system, not the tools.

chunks.x:
Analyze: Identify the Root Cause Statistically
Analyze is where statistical tools are used in earnest. You verify with data which X candidates really move Y. The basic combination is digging logically with 5 Whys and confirming with statistics.
Method
What it tells you

By defect mode, lot, time slot

Reading a p-value (basics)
A p-value is “the probability of seeing a difference this large by chance if there were really no difference”. Commonly below 0.05 we judge the difference unlikely to be chance. But a statistically significant effect that is practically small still has low priority.
Correlation is not causation
A relationship in a scatter plot may just be a third factor moving both. Proof of cause comes from deliberately changing conditions in Improve (DOE).

chunks.x:
Exercise: Run a DMAIC Project
Chronic dimensional variation (illustrative numbers)
On a machining line, the defect rate of a dimension has stayed high at 2% for six months. No one knows why, and wrong machine settings could break expensive tooling. You are the project leader.
What is the triage result?
Deep GPC (unknown cause, high risk)
Correct. Either unknown cause or high risk alone is enough for Deep GPC.
Quick GPC (just try raising the temperature)
There is no hypothesis and a risk of tool breakage, so Quick GPC is inappropriate.
What should be written in Define?
Y = dimensional accuracy (defect rate 2% → ≤ 0.2%), X candidates = temperature, humidity, tool wear, material lot; scope and the gap to the theoretical value
Y, X candidates and the goal are clear.
“Inspect 100% so no defects escape”
This manipulates Y directly and never touches the cause (X).
What comes first in Measure?
Run regression right away on six months of inspection records
The measurement system's reliability is unconfirmed; if measurement error is large, the analysis will mislead.
Do MSA (Gage R&R, bias, calibration) and make a data collection plan
Correct. Secure data reliability, then collect four weeks of stratified data.
Regression shows the interaction “tool wear × temperature” is the main cause. What do you do in Improve?

Regression shows the interaction “tool wear × temperature” is the main cause. What do you do in Improve?

Use DOE to find the optimum tool-change interval and temperature, reset the GPC band, verify with a pilot run
Correct. Interactions are confirmed efficiently with DOE.
Change only temperature and see
With an interaction, changing one factor at a time can miss the optimum.
The defect rate improved to 0.2%. What happens in Control?
Project is done, no need to monitor
Without a control system it will slide back. Improvement without S is do-and-forget.
Monitor with an X̄-R chart, control plan, SOP revision and training, hand over to PDCA-S Plan
Correct. Control connects to PDCA-S so the effect sticks.
Asking “is the data reliable?” and “are we controlling X?” at every step from Define to Control is the key to Deep GPC success.

Q: Which condition routes an issue to Deep GPC?
A: Unknown cause OR high risk OR multi-variable
Deep GPC uses OR: any one condition triggers it. Quick GPC requires all conditions (AND).
Q: Which aspect of data reliability do “bias” and “calibration” check in MSA?
A: Accuracy
Repeatability/reproducibility check precision (variation); bias/calibration check accuracy (offset from true value).
Q: What is the common judgment for a measurement system with %GRR = 8%?
A: Good
Rule of thumb: 30% not acceptable.
Q: You want to know whether mean dimensions differ between three part lots. Which method fits?
A: ANOVA
ANOVA tests mean differences among three or more groups.
Q: How does ZEVA treat the variation created by deliberately changing conditions in DOE?
A: Intentional experimental variation — a source of learning to identify causes
ZEVA separates object variation, measurement variation/bias and intentional experimental variation; DOE variation is not eliminated.
Q: Which correctly describes the relation between DMAIC Control and PDCA-S?
A: Control charts and monitoring items set in Control are handed over to PDCA-S Plan
Control closes the project by building the management system, whose results connect into daily PDCA-S.

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › The Metrics System and Statistical Stability
chunks.x:
The Metrics System and Statistical Stability
ZEVA metrics are a way of making data reliability visible. Learn to confirm stability before interpreting the defect rate and V.Score, the GPC-M / GPC-H metrics and targets, and how to read metrics in combination.
Explain “a process not in statistical control has no definable capability”
Follow the procedure: confirm stability with a control chart, then evaluate the metrics
Use GPC-M and GPC-H metrics and targets correctly
Combine OEE and V.Score to judge improvement priority
Metrics quantify variation and show whether data-based action is possible
An unstable process has no definable capability: confirm stability with a control chart before evaluating the metrics
GPC-M: band conformance ≥ 99%, OEE ≥ 85%, X̄-R within limits, defect rate against a per-product target
GPC-H: V.Score < 0.1, CT achievement ≥ 95%. Never evaluate by averages alone
Combine metrics such as OEE × V.Score to set priority and direction

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › The Metrics System and Statistical Stability › Metrics Mirror Data Reliability
chunks.x:
Metrics Mirror Data Reliability
The ZEVA metrics system is not just for scoring results. By quantifying variation it shows whether the data is good enough to act on. When V.Score (Variation Score) or the Defect rate improves, you are moving closer to the state the Root logic calls “able to take data-based action”.
Variation is small
Data is reliable
Metrics (defect rate, V.Score) are meaningful
The right action can be chosen
Better metrics = greater ability to act
A process that is not in a state of statistical control has no definable process capability.
Shewhart's principle
In an unstable process where special-cause variation remains, today's data does not predict tomorrow's process. The defect rate and V.Score can be calculated, but mean nothing until stability is confirmed.

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › The Metrics System and Statistical Stability › Procedure: Stability First, Then Metrics
chunks.x:
Procedure: Stability First, Then Metrics
1. Check the measurement system
Secure precision and accuracy with MSA (remove measurement variation and bias)
2. Confirm stability with a control chart
Any points outside control limits or abnormal patterns on the X̄-R chart?
3a. If unstable
Find and remove special causes (Quick/Deep GPC). Treat the metrics as reference only
3b. If stable
Calculate the defect rate and V.Score and compare with targets
4. Monitor continuously
Watch the trend with PDCA-S to prevent backsliding
In the simulator below, inject special causes (a mean shift or increased spread). When the chart signals an abnormality, metrics calculated from that data cannot be used to predict the next lot.
Common mistake: reporting numbers from an unstable process as real ability
Reporting “defect rate 0.05%, target met” from a week that happened to be quiet, then seeing defects spike the next week, is the classic result of skipping the stability check. Even if the number looks good, if the chart shows abnormalities the correct report is “this figure does not yet show what the process can do”.

chunks.x:

Quality categories: the units for counting quality loss (spec v29, 16.3)
Categories in pieces, losses in time

Quality categories are recorded in pieces, while the quality loss shown on the loss-structure diagram is counted in time. The Defect rate is a ratio of pieces; quality loss is a ratio of time.
Record both where a defect was made and where it was found
For each defect, record both the process of origin (where it was made) and the process of detection (where it was found). A defect found later than where it was made counts as outflow. Outflow rate = defects made in the process and found in a later process ÷ total production of that process (excluding Trial). Even with the same defect rate, a process with a lot of outflow has not achieved Own-process completion. Do not stop outflow by adding inspection; go back to the conditions (X) and the Judgment criteria of the process of origin (spec v30, 16.3).
GPC band vs specification
The defect rate is a metric of the result (Y); band conformance is a metric of the conditions (X). The band is the experimentally verified range of process conditions that guarantee good parts, so the better you hold conditions inside it, the lower and steadier the defect rate becomes — watch both in that relation.

Computing V.Score: per model, then weighted by output

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › The Metrics System and Statistical Stability › GPC-H (Human Control) Metrics
chunks.x:
re (spec v29, 16.4). The GPC-H target is < 0.1; these five bands say where the line stands today
Computing V.Score: per model, then weighted by output

Take the interval between completion times as the cycle time, keep the shift window, drop breaks, and exclude anything under 0.5 min or over 60 min. On a line that runs several models a day, compute σ ÷ μ per model and take a weighted average by output. Mixing all models counts the speed difference between models as variation. Total variation splits into within-model variation and between-model difference; the one to control is the first.
Same average, different evaluation
Even if the average CT meets the target, a large V.Score makes it an “unstable process” and an improvement target. Never evaluate by averages alone — this is ZEVA's shift in evaluation criteria.

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › The Metrics System and Statistical Stability › Read line balance against the takt time
chunks.x:
Read line balance against the takt time
V.Score looks at the variation in the work time itself — the scatter when the same work is repeated — and can be taken per process or for a whole line. What it does not show is the balance between processes. The basic Line balance efficiency formula uses the neck CT as its reference, but ZEVA measures line balance against the takt time, and switches to the neck time only when the neck exceeds takt. Measuring a line that cannot run at takt against the takt time would not describe reality.
Line balance efficiency = Σ standard CT ÷ (reference time × number of processes)
Reference time
The larger of the takt time and the neck time
Standard CT
What the process does when it runs normally (the smallest value after outliers are removed)
Worked example: a 10-process line (measured)
Standard CT per process: 32 / 57 / 34 / 32 / 31 / 33 / 70 / 59 / 54 / 34 s (total 436 s)
Neck time = 70 s, takt time = 98 s → the neck is within takt, so the reference time is 98 s
Efficiency = 436 ÷ (98 × 10) = 44.5%, line balance loss = 55.5%
If takt were 60 s, the neck of 70 s exceeds it, so the reference time is 70 s. Line balance efficiency = 436 ÷ (70 × 10) = 62.3%
The same line gives a different figure when the reference time changes. Always say which one the reference was: the takt time or the neck time.
Reference = takt time (neck ≤ takt)

Efficiency says how much of the takt window is used
The remainder is waiting between processes, or capacity beyond demand
Where to act: revisit the takt, merge processes
Reference = neck time (neck > takt)
Efficiency says how even the load is against the pace the line can run
The remainder is time spent waiting for the neck process
Where to act: split the neck process, move work across
Move all three at once: the hybrid score
Balance, within-process variation and the takt gap do not tell you what to do first when you read them separately. The hybrid score normalises all three to 0–1, weights them and reports one number out of 100. Zero is the worst state, 100 the ideal one. ZEVA puts the heaviest weight on variation, because until variation is cut neither balance nor the takt gap can be measured properly (spec v29, 16.5).
What to try with the sliders
Set within-process variation to 0 and the score jumps: the only losses left are balance and the takt gap. Then set spread between processes to 0 and the efficiency approaches 100%. Conversely, set the weights to γ1 : α1 : β1 and even the measured line keeps some points — which shows the weight on variation is a choice, not an accident.

Both the neck time and the standard CT come from what the process does when it runs normally, with outliers removed. That is a different number from the actual pace (the mean cycle time). When two figures disagree on the floor, check which one is being quoted.

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › The Metrics System and Statistical Stability › Reading Metrics in Combination
chunks.x:
Reading Metrics in Combination
A single metric can mislead. Combining efficiency (OEE) with stability (V.Score), for example, shows priority and direction (a way of thinking for comparing lines; set the thresholds for your own site).
High OEE × low V.Score: best
Efficient and stable. Keep the standard, continue center-aiming toward the theoretical value. A model for rollout.
High OEE × high V.Score: stabilise
Output is fine now but unstable — maybe reliant on experts. Lock in reproducibility with standard work and motion stability.
Low OEE × low V.Score: raise effectiveness
Stable, so the data can be trusted. Find the causes (X) of stop, speed and quality losses via OEE analysis and improve.
Low OEE × high V.Score: top priority
Both efficiency and stability are poor. First suppress variation with the foundation (5S, 3-tei, standard work) so reliable data can be collected.
Why stabilise first for low OEE × high V.Score?
Analysing OEE losses while variation is large gives unreliable data, so you misjudge which loss is the real cause. The virtuous cycle starts from the foundation (standardisation).

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › The Metrics System and Statistical Stability › Exercise: Interpreting a Report
chunks.x:
Exercise: Interpreting a Report
Monthly KPI review (illustrative numbers)
In a monthly review you receive reports on two processes. Read them and judge using ZEVA thinking.
Process A: “The defect rate this month is 0.05%, target met.” But the X̄-R chart has three points outside the control limits. Your judgment?
Target met, no problem
Numbers from an unstable process do not predict the next week or the next lot; 0.05% may be a coincidence.
The process is unstable. Investigate special causes and hold the defect-rate evaluation until stability is confirmed
Correct — a judgment based on Shewhart's principle.
Process B (manual assembly): “OEE rose from 80% to 86%.” The work-time V.Score is 0.42. How do you evaluate?
OEE exceeds target, so human work is good too
OEE is a GPC-M metric. Human work is judged by V.Score, and 0.42 is in the slightly-unstable band.
High OEE × high V.Score = stabilise. Advance GPC-H with standard work and motion stability
Correct. Make today's result reproducible.
Process B's team leader proposes “next month we rush operators to shorten CT”. How do you respond?
Not allowed — it manipulates Y directly. Replace it with changes to layout, sequence, jigs (X)
Correct. Rushing increases variation and quality problems, worsening V.Score further.
Adopt it if CT gets shorter
“CT is slow → rush operators” is exactly a ZEVA “Don't” example.

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › The Metrics System and Statistical Stability › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Which statement is Shewhart's principle?
A: A process not in statistical control has no definable capability
With special causes present, today's data does not predict tomorrow, so capability cannot be defined.
Q: What should be done before evaluating the defect rate or V.Score?
A: Confirm process stability with a control chart
Confirm stability with an X̄-R chart etc. before interpreting the metrics. Deleting outliers hides special causes.
Q: Which metric group does OEE belong to?
A: GPC-M
OEE represents equipment effectiveness, so it is a GPC-M metric.
Q: Mean work time 60 s, standard deviation 9 s. V.Score and judgment?
A: 0.15, stable
9 ÷ 60 = 0.15. 0.1–0.3 is “stable (standard work is working)”.
Q: What is the target for GPC band conformance rate?
A: ≥ 99%
Band conformance ≥ 99%, CT achievement ≥ 95%, OEE ≥ 85%.
Q: On a line with low OEE × high V.Score, what should be tackled first?
A: Suppress variation with the foundation (5S, 3-tei, standard work) so reliable data can be collected
With large variation even loss-analysis data is unreliable. The virtuous cycle starts at the foundation.
Q: Which use of metrics is consistent with ZEVA?
A: Watch the weekly V.Score trend and check standard-work adherence when it worsens
Trend monitoring to prevent backsliding is correct; the others are pitfalls.

chunks.x:
Staged Digitalisation and the ZEVA System
Digitalisation is not a prerequisite but an accelerator. Learn how digital levels 1–3 speed up a ZEVA that already works on paper, when to move up a level, which functions a ZEVA system needs, and where AI fits.
Explain the design idea “Digitalisation is an optional accelerator”
Describe digital levels 1–3 and how improvement activities differ at each
Judge from site conditions whether to move to the next digital level
Explain the four ZEVA system functions and why AI is positioned as a weapon to absorb and visualise variation
Digitalisation is an accelerator, not a prerequisite. ZEVA works fully at Level 1 (analog)
The digital level is independent of improvement quality; raise it to match the pain (aggregation load → Level 2, real-time → Level 3)
Four ZEVA system functions: intelligent triage, integrated knowledge DB, agile standard update, analysis support
Temporary standards: max 30 days, single line only, rollback possible
AI is a weapon to absorb and visualise variation; ZEVA stays at the centre

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Staged Digitalisation and the ZEVA System › Design Idea: Works in Analog, Faster with Digitalisation
chunks.x:
Design Idea: Works in Analog, Faster with Digitalisation
ZEVA positions digitalisation not as a prerequisite but as an optional accelerator. It works fully on a site with only a whiteboard and a stopwatch, and as digitalisation matures, speed and coverage increase.
Digital level ≠ quality of improvement
Raising the digital level is independent of the quality of improvement. Excellent improvement is possible at Level 1. Digitalisation is only a tool for speed and coverage.
We do not use the word “DX”
DX (digital transformation) reaches all the way to changing the business model. ZEVA is about accelerating shop-floor improvement, which is narrower. This site therefore talks about digitisation (Level 2), turning paper records into data, and digitalisation (Level 3), changing how the process runs with digital technology.
Common misunderstanding
No sensors or system, so we cannot start ZEVA
Building a dashboard will drive improvement
Adding AI solves the variation problem
ZEVA thinking
Spread ZEVA thinking in analog first; add digitalisation later
The mechanism for acting on data (triage, PDCA-S) comes first
ZEVA is always at the centre; technology is the means

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Staged Digitalisation and the ZEVA System › Deciding When to Move Up a Level
chunks.x:
Deciding When to Move Up a Level
A higher digital level is not automatically better; you raise it to match a real pain on the shop floor. Guidelines for moving up:
Level 1
Spread the thinking first
→ Level 2 when
Manual input is heavy and aggregation takes too long
→ Level 3 when
Real-time response is needed, or anomaly detection must be automated
A process spends 30 minutes daily aggregating handwritten CT records, but abnormalities are rare and next-day response is fast enough. What is the right decision?
Jump to Level 3 and introduce real-time monitoring
Consider Level 2 (input template, automatic aggregation) to reduce the aggregation load
Digitalisation is unnecessary, so stop aggregating altogether
The pain is aggregation effort, not real-time need — the Level 1 → 2 condition.
Order of introduction
In the ZEVA implementation steps, clarifying the theoretical value, building triage and starting Quick GPC all work at Level 1. Level 2 is recommended for Deep GPC projects, and you raise to Level 2–3 gradually during rollout.

chunks.x:
Four Functions a ZEVA System Needs
To support the Hybrid triage model as a mechanism, a ZEVA system needs the following functions. They can also be substituted with paper or spreadsheets; their form changes with the digital level.
Intelligent triage
For inputs like “defects appeared” or “CT is slow”, asks the four criteria (cause idea, number of variables, risk, data) interactively, recommends Quick or Deep, and presents the right template and guide.
Integrated knowledge database
Manages small (Quick) and large (Deep) improvements in one Knowledge base while keeping them distinct. Similar trials — including failures — can be found instantly, preventing wasted re-experiments. Organised by GPC-M/GPC-H with cross search.
Agile standard update (for Quick GPC)
A fast lane to apply a successful improvement the same day as a Temporary standard. Valid for up to 30 days (formal approval within that time), limited to a single line, with automatic backup of the previous state for rollback at any time.
Analysis support (for Deep GPC)
Automatic correlation visualisation when data is loaded, automatic sampling plans, automatic X̄-R charts, automatic defect rate and V.Score with trends — making DMAIC easier for people new to statistics.
Failures are assets too

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Staged Digitalisation and the ZEVA System › Where AI Fits: A Weapon to Absorb and Visualise Variation
chunks.x:
Where AI Fits: A Weapon to Absorb and Visualise Variation
In ZEVA, AI and digitalisation are not mere automation tools. They are weapons to absorb and visualise the variation that cannot be removed when people are involved. They are most effective where work depends heavily on human senses and skill and standard procedures alone cannot remove variation. On people-centred sites where automation is hard to justify financially, they also offer the option “keep human work, absorb variation with technology”.
Technology (generic example)
Variation targeted
Effect
AI visual inspection (object detection)
Judgment variation (Man), interpretation variation (Method)
Objectifies checks such as part presence, position, type and packing contents — quality assurance not dependent on people
Video-based work analysis
Method variation, hidden waste
Classifies value/semi/non-value frame by frame, times elements, compares experts and newcomers
Motion analysis by skeleton (pose) estimation
Skill variation (Man) = knacks and intuition
Visualises tacit knowledge as motion data for skill standardisation and training
IoT and sensors
Machine and environment variation
Real-time monitoring of operation and temperature/humidity, anomaly detection, early warning
Do not let technology become the goal

A: An optional accelerator that speeds up improvement

Level 1 → 2 is about aggregation load; Level 2 → 3 about real-time response and automated anomaly detection.

A: To prevent wasted re-experiments and improve triage accuracy
Failures are important knowledge that stops the same failure recurring.
Q: What is the correct position of AI in ZEVA?
A: A weapon to absorb and visualise variation that cannot be removed, with ZEVA always at the centre
The goal is realising ZEVA, not introducing technology.

A: Human judgment variation and method interpretation variation

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Implementation Process and Success Factors › Don'ts: Never Manipulate Y Directly
chunks.x:
Don'ts: Never Manipulate Y Directly
As implementation progresses, KPI pressure grows and it becomes tempting to push the result numbers (Y) directly. But that leaves the causes (X) untouched and makes variation and data reliability even worse (XY thinking).
NG: manipulating Y
Defect rate high → tighten inspection
CT slow → rush operators
OEE low → make up numbers with overtime
OK: controlling X
Defect rate high → optimise machine parameters (X) → defect rate (Y) falls
CT slow → improve work procedure (X) → CT (Y) shortens
OEE low → remove the cause of breakdowns (X) → OEE (Y) rises

chunks.x:
Case 1: CT Variation in Manual Assembly (Quick GPC × GPC-H)
Case 1: Picking parts takes too long
A manual assembly process for a small product. Standard CT is 40 s, but 10 timed cycles range from 38 to 52 s, V.Score 0.11. Observation shows the operator reaches to a parts box at the far left every cycle and sometimes re-grips. The team leader thinks “moving the box to the front right should make it faster”.
What is the triage decision?
Quick GPC: hypothesis exists (layout), low risk, single variable, data available now
Correct. All four steps point to Quick.
Deep GPC: because V.Score exceeds 0.1
A metric value alone does not decide the route; use the four criteria.
GPC-M or GPC-H?
GPC-H: variation in human motion and work method
Correct. Use ECRS and motion stability (distance/displacement law).
GPC-M: the parts box is equipment
The source is human motion — reaching and re-gripping.
Which is the best hypothesis?
“If the operator concentrates more, CT will stabilise.”
It is willpower; the X, current value and new value are unclear.
“If the parts box moves from far left (~50 cm) to front right (~25 cm), picking time shortens and CT variation falls.”
Correct. It follows the template “change [target] from [current] to [new] to get [result]”.
After 5 trial cycles, stopwatch shows CT 2 s shorter on average and the max fell from 48 to 42 s. Next action?

Case 2: Soldering Temperature (Quick GPC × GPC-M)
Case 2: Soldering defects are increasing
In a soldering process, defects from insufficient melting have increased since last week. The engineer suspects “since the material changed it melts less easily; raising the setting by 5 °C should stabilise it”. The current setting is near the lower edge of the GPC band, and +5 °C stays within the upper limit.
Triage decision?
Quick GPC: hypothesis, single variable (temperature), low risk within the band, data available now
Correct. A change within the band is easy to reverse if it fails.
Deep GPC: defects are quality problems, so always DMAIC
Even for quality issues, a hypothesis + low risk + single variable means Quick GPC. Unneeded DMAIC wastes resources.
How do you run the trial?
Raise temperature by 5 °C, run just 10 units and check melting
Correct. Test immediately with a small N.
Change temperature, speed and flux amount at the same time
Changing several variables at once hides which one worked. Quick GPC tests a single variable.
Digitalisation is Level 1 (no sensors). How do you check?
Visual check + handwritten check sheet recording OK/NG for the 10 units
Correct. Analog alternative: you can judge without sensors.
Hold the check until sensors are installed
Digitalisation is not a prerequisite.
Zero defects in all 10 units and no recurrence over 3 days. Action?

chunks.x:
Case 3: Chronic Dimensional Variation (Deep GPC × GPC-M)
Case 3: Machined part dimensions are unstable
On a machining line, the defect rate of a bore diameter has hovered around 2% for a long time. It gets better or worse by season and time of day, and no one can explain why. Large condition changes could damage expensive tools or equipment.
Triage decision?
Deep GPC: unknown cause, multi-variable, high risk
Correct. One condition is enough; here all three apply.
Quick GPC: just try lowering cutting speed
No grounds for the hypothesis and high risk; intuitive trials will not reach the root cause.
After Define, past inspection records show different tendencies by inspector. What first?
Evaluate the measurement system with MSA (Gage R&R, bias, calibration)
Correct. %GRR was 22% (conditional); after standardising how the fixture is applied it became 9%, then data collection began.
Inspector differences are just error, so average them
Leaving measurement variation and bias hides the true process. Secure data reliability first.
For four weeks you recorded temperature, humidity, tool usage count and material lot. What in Analyze?
Use regression to examine each factor's contribution and interactions, and confirm the physical reason with 5-Why
Correct. The analysis showed the tool wear × temperature interaction as the main cause (wear matters more in warm hours).

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Integrated Case Studies › Case 4: Hypotheses Keep Failing (Quick → Deep Escalation)
chunks.x:
Case 4: Hypotheses Keep Failing (Quick → Deep Escalation)
Case 4: A 3% assembly defect rate will not fall
An assembly line has about 3% fitting defects. At first it was thought to be “an operator procedure problem”, and Quick GPC was started.
Cycle 1: changed procedure → no change. Cycle 2: changed jig → improved a few days then recurred. What next?
Try a third hypothesis (how materials are placed) while watching the escalation criterion (recurrence)
Reasonable. Recurrence is already an escalation sign, so decide quickly based on cycle 3.
Increase warnings to operators
Warnings do not control X.
Cycle 3: changed material placement → no change. No more hypotheses. Decision?
Escalate to Deep GPC (DMAIC), handing over the results of all three trials including failures
Correct. Three failures, no hypotheses and recurrence all meet the criteria. Failed results are valuable “X that did not work” information.
Keep going with a 4th and 5th Quick GPC hypothesis
Ignoring escalation criteria exhausts the floor and delays the solution.
In Define and Measure, X candidates were operator, time slot, part lot and jig, and data was collected. What do you use in Analyze?
ANOVA to compare differences between groups

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Integrated Case Studies › Reflection: Lessons Common to All Four Cases
chunks.x:
Reflection: Lessons Common to All Four Cases
The entrance is always triage
The route was chosen by the four criteria — cause idea, variables, risk, data — not by how bad a metric looked or the problem type.
Secure data reliability first
As with the MSA in Case 3, removing measurement variation is what made the root cause reachable.
Control X; let Y move as a result
Every case rejected direct manipulation of Y: more inspection, warnings, rushing.
End with S (standardise) and knowledge
Hand-over to PDCA-S through temporary standards, band updates and SOP revisions, recording failures too.
Keep the virtuous cycle turning
Reduce variation → data becomes reliable → accurate action becomes possible → variation falls further. All four cases are records of one turn of this virtuous cycle. Try drawing the same flow for an issue on your own site.

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Integrated Case Studies › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Why was Case 1 (parts box position) Quick GPC?
A: There was a hypothesis, low risk, a single variable and data available now
The route is set by the four criteria; manual work with unknown cause or high risk goes to Deep.
Q: In Case 2, why not change temperature, speed and flux at once?
A: You could not tell which variable worked
Quick GPC trials are single-variable; if multiple variables must be studied together, it is Deep GPC (DOE) territory.
Q: In Case 3, why was MSA done before data collection?
A: Values differed by inspector, so data reliability was doubtful
Unreliable data yields neither correct conclusions nor actions (root logic).
Q: In Case 3, why was humidity not declared the cause despite high correlation?
A: Correlation is not causation; it may just move with temperature
Causation is confirmed via regression interactions and deliberate DOE changes. Humidity belongs to the Environment factor.
Q: Which was NOT a reason for escalation in Case 4?
A: The digital level was Level 1
digital level is not an escalation criterion. The criteria are 3 failures, no hypotheses, recurrence and bigger impact.
Q: Case 4's root cause (differences between part lots) belongs to which factor and control side?
A: Material / GPC-M
Material is on the GPC-M side, controlled by acceptance criteria and lot control.
Q: What was always done at the end of improvement in all four cases?

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Integrated Case Studies › Quiz
chunks.x:
Material is on the GPC-M side, controlled by acceptance criteria and lot control.
Q: What was always done at the end of improvement in all four cases?

A: Standardisation (temporary standard, GPC band, SOP), hand-over to PDCA-S and knowledge registration
Improvement without S is do-and-forget; connecting to the maintenance cycle makes it stick.

Fill the four boxes from the data that was collected

The process, and what hurts
Machine M-07 moulds a resin cover in a two-cavity tool. It runs a 420-minute shift (loading time, breaks removed). Two things hurt, and the floor treated them as two separate problems.
Quality: 3.2% warp defects
Of 402 shots, 13 are scrapped for warp. It behaves differently in the morning and the afternoon.
Efficiency: OEE 64.8%
CT scatters between 44 and 63 s. 62 minutes are lost to changeover and mould cleaning.
ZEVA questions the order here
Splitting "cut defects" and "shorten CT" into two activities splits the owners and the countermeasures too. ZEVA starts by collecting one set of data, because the cause (X) of both may sit in the process conditions.

Q: Why fix an initial standard before collecting data?
A: Unless measurement and settings match, the data describes the people, not the process

Q: Where did the OEE target of 77.7% in box ④ come from?

Q: Why did quality (warp) and efficiency (CT, stops) improve together?
A: Both traced back to the same X: the mould temperature after start-up
The warp, the stretched CT and the cleaning stops all tied back to the mould warming up.
Q: How was the GPC band of 58–66 °C decided?
A: A physical trial varying pre-heat time confirmed the range that yields good parts
A GPC band is the good-part range confirmed by physical trials, not by statistics alone (spec v29, 3.1).
Q: What comes first after the improvement?
A: Write the 40-minute pre-heat and the GPC band into the work instruction and control plan
Unless it is frozen as an outcome standard, the line reverts when the people change (principle ③).

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Case: flow across processes (lead time) › No process is slow, yet the delivery slips
chunks.x:
No process is slow, yet the delivery slips
Product K passes through six processes: cutting, bending, welding, painting, drying, and assembly-plus-inspection. Output is 180 a day and the lead time from order to shipment is 9.5 days, with 78% on-time delivery. Yet look process by process and none of them is short of capacity.
The mix-up that usually happens here
Hearing "the lead time is long", people go and time the cycle of each process, assuming some process is slow. Here, the time the product actually spends being worked on is under 2% of the lead time. The other 98% is spent waiting between processes.

Where the 12-minute changeover comes from
Splitting the 45 minutes showed that only 12 are internal — work that truly needs the machine stopped. The other 33 are preparing the next colour and its jigs, which can be done while the previous lot still runs. Nothing was made faster; work that never needed the stop was simply moved out of it.

Step 4: the improvement plan
Dropping every ceiling at once means that when something starves, you cannot say which change did it. The plan was to lower one place at a time, from upstream down, and watch for two weeks.

Lowering a ceiling always exposes a problem
WIP is also the stock that hides a process in trouble. Lower the ceiling and the stoppages and defects that were hidden surface as idle time downstream. That is not a failure — it is the point. Fix what surfaces, then lower the next ceiling.

Not one process got a second faster here. OEE and V.Score look inside a process, so this improvement does not show up in either. To see flow, measure lead time and WIP.
