chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Case: flow across processes (lead time) › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Of the 9.5-day lead time, how much was the product actually being worked on?
A: About 65.9 minutes (1.7%)
The six processes take 65.9 minutes net against a 3,990-minute lead time. All the rest is waiting between processes.
Q: With daily output fixed at 180, what WIP gives a 3.4-day lead time?
A: About 620
Lead time = WIP ÷ daily output, so 3.4 × 180 = about 620.
Q: What really caused 640 pieces to pile up before painting?
A: A 45-minute colour change dictated a lot of 600
Painting takes 2.8 minutes net, the shortest of the six. What is slow is the lot size the changeover dictates, not the process.
Q: Why did the changeover go from 45 minutes to 12?
A: 33 minutes of paint and jig prep were moved out of the stop
The internal setup — work that truly needs the machine stopped — was 12 minutes all along. Nothing got faster; work simply moved out.
Q: Lowering a WIP ceiling caused idle time downstream. What now?
A: Fix the stoppage or defect that surfaced, then lower the next ceiling
WIP is the stock that hides a troubled process. Exposing the problem is the purpose, and the idle time is the signal.

chunks.x:
Case: the paint line (Deep GPC)
Three years of 4.2% dirt-inclusion defects brought to 0.5% with Deep GPC (DMAIC). Quick GPC had failed three times because the cause was not one factor but two acting together. The numbers describe an illustrative process.
Decide when to escalate from Quick GPC to Deep GPC
Question the measurement itself and start with MSA
Find an interaction by stratifying, and explain why one factor at a time cannot reach it
Turn the condition into a GPC band in Control and hand it to PDCA-S
Three Quick GPC cycles that fall short suggest the cause is not one factor; escalate to Deep GPC
Data collected while inspectors disagree forces the whole analysis to be redone; Measure starts with MSA
Crossing two conditions in a stratification exposes an interaction that addition cannot explain
Stratification finds the neighbourhood; cutting inside the band is the job of DOE
In Control the conditions become a GPC band, handed to PDCA-S through the chart and standard work

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Case: the paint line (Deep GPC) › Three tries, three failures
chunks.x:
Three tries, three failures
Paint line P-2 coats a resin cover, 600 units a day. Dirt inclusions — specks in the paint film — have sat at around 4.2% for three years. A rejected part is sanded and resprayed, which costs 25 minutes each.
Try
Hypothesis (X)
What was done
Result
1st
The booth is not clean enough
Added 30 minutes of cleaning before the shift
4.2% → 4.0%. No change
2nd

Changed the interval from 30 to 20 days

3rd
Operator skill
Assigned the experienced operator permanently
4.2% → 4.1%. No change
Three H-T-C-A cycles fell short. That is the escalation criterion
After three failures, question the shape of the failure
All three followed the same shape: pick one X and change only that. Quick GPC is the fast route when you have a hypothesis and one variable. Guesses that keep missing may be telling you the cause is not one thing. That is the moment to move to Deep GPC (DMAIC).

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Case: the paint line (Deep GPC) › Measure: question the measurement first
chunks.x:
Measure: question the measurement first
Before collecting anything, an MSA was run. Three inspectors judged the same ten parts twice each; 14 of the 60 judgments disagreed. Agreement was 46 ÷ 60 = 77%. This is a pass/fail judgement, so it is read as an agreement rate rather than a Gage R&R (%GRR), which is for variable data (see the Deep GPC procedure).
Four weeks collected on judgements that agree 77% of the time is four weeks wasted
While inspectors disagree, a moving defect rate cannot tell you whether the process moved or the judgment moved. Analysis stacked on unreliable data has to be redone from the start.

The number of units only
The number of units, plus where the speck sits and how big it is
Agreement rate

97% (they agree)
With the measurement fixed, four weeks — 20 days × 600 units = 12,000 — were recorded. Dirt inclusions: 504, and 504 ÷ 12,000 = 4.2%. The figure quoted for three years finally had something behind it.

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Case: the paint line (Deep GPC) › Analyze: the cause was not one thing
chunks.x:
Analyze: the cause was not one thing
The 12,000 units were stratified by each candidate X. Two stood out on their own: days since the filter change and booth humidity. Neither explained the whole picture. Crossing the two gives the table below.
Humidity ≥ 55%
Humidity < 55%
Filter 1–15 days
1.2%
2.4%
Filter 16–30 days
3.2%
10.0%
The four cells average 4.2%. Only the bottom-right is in another league
The gap that addition cannot reach is the interaction
Humidity alone costs 2.4 − 1.2 = 1.2 pt; the filter alone 3.2 − 1.2 = 2.0 pt. A day with both should be 1.2 + 1.2 + 2.0 = 4.4% if the effects simply added. It was 10.0%. The 5.6 pt difference is the interaction. Dry air pulls dust in by static electricity, and an old filter does not stop it. It only happens when the two coincide.
Why Quick GPC fell short three times
The second try — filter 30 → 20 days — left humidity alone. On the table it moves from bottom-right to top-right, where the best you can reach is 2.4%. And 20 days does not reach the 1–15 day band, so in practice it only fell to 3.6%. Chasing one variable at a time, the best you reach is 2.4% or 3.2%. The 1.2% shows up only on days when both are right.

chunks.t: ZEVA Advanced › Case: the paint line (Deep GPC) › Quiz
chunks.x:
Q: Three Quick GPC cycles fell short. What comes next?
A: Suspect the cause is not one factor and move to Deep GPC
All three took the same shape: pick one X and change it. Guesses that keep missing signal that the cause is not one thing.
Q: What was done first in Measure?
A: MSA — evaluating the measurement system
When inspectors agree only 77% of the time, a moving defect rate cannot tell you whether the process or the judgment moved.
Q: Humidity alone accounts for 1.2 pt and the filter alone 2.0 pt. If a day with both is 10.0%, how large is the interaction?
A: 5.6 points
Addition predicts 1.2 + 1.2 + 2.0 = 4.4%. The 5.6 pt gap to the actual 10.0% is the interaction.
Q: What took the case from the best cell, 1.2%, down to the 0.5% in ④?
A: A DOE cut inside the band and found a filter within 7 days and 55–65% humidity
The 1.2% is the average of a coarse band, 1–15 days × ≥ 55%. Cutting inside it was the job of DOE.
Q: Where does Control hand the conditions on to?
A: PDCA-S — the day-to-day maintenance cycle
It is frozen as a control chart, a GPC band and standard work, then moved into the PDCA-S of daily operation.

chunks.t: Glossary › Industrial Engineering
chunks.x: Industrial Engineering (IE): An engineering discipline that designs, improves and operates production systems made of people, equipment, materials and information. It uses time study, motion study and process analysis to remove waste, overburden and unevenness.

chunks.t: Glossary › Productivity
chunks.x: Productivity: The ratio of output (quantity or added value) to input (labour, time, equipment, material). Productivity = Output ÷ Input.

chunks.t: Glossary › QCDS
chunks.x: QCDS (QCDS): Quality, Cost, Delivery and Safety — the basic evaluation axes of manufacturing. Environment is sometimes added (QCDSE).

chunks.t: Glossary › 4M
chunks.x: 4M (4M): The four basic elements of production: Man, Machine, Material and Method. Used as a framework to sort the causes of variation in quality and time.

chunks.t: Glossary › Value added
chunks.x: Value added: Value created by activities that change the shape, properties or function of a product in a way the customer pays for. Activities that add no value are regarded as waste.

chunks.t: Glossary › Muda (waste)
chunks.x: Muda (waste): Any activity or state that adds cost but no value. The "seven wastes" are typical examples.

chunks.t: Glossary › Muri (overburden)
chunks.x: Muri (overburden): A state in which people or equipment are loaded beyond their capability. It causes fatigue, breakdowns, defects and safety problems.

chunks.t: Glossary › Mura (unevenness)
chunks.x: Mura (unevenness): Unevenness in work time, quality, load or output. Mura breeds muda and muri, and corresponds directly to the "variation" that ZEVA focuses on.

chunks.t: Glossary › Seven wastes
chunks.x: Seven wastes: Overproduction, waiting, transportation, over-processing, inventory, motion and defects. Used as a checklist for finding waste on the shop floor.

chunks.t: Glossary › Takt time
chunks.x: Takt time (TT): The time in which one unit should be produced to match customer demand. TT = Available time ÷ Required quantity. It is set by demand, not by production capability.

chunks.t: Glossary › Cycle time
chunks.x: Cycle time (CT): The actual time a process (or operator) takes to complete one cycle of work. It shows real capability and is compared with TT to judge over- or under-capacity.

chunks.t: Glossary › Lead time
chunks.x: Lead time (LT): The total elapsed time from order or material input to product completion or shipment. It includes waiting, transport and inspection time, not only processing time.

chunks.t: Glossary › Available time
chunks.x: Available time: The net time available for production: shift time minus planned non-production time such as breaks and meetings. It is the numerator of the takt-time formula.

chunks.t: Glossary › Capacity
chunks.x: Capacity: The maximum quantity that can be produced in a given time. Line capacity is limited by the neck process: Capacity = Available time ÷ Neck CT.

chunks.t: Glossary › Time study
chunks.x: Time study: A method that breaks work into elements and repeatedly measures and analyses their time with a stopwatch or video. Used to set standard time and to reveal time variation.

chunks.t: Glossary › Work element
chunks.x: Work element: A unit of work with a clearly defined start and end point (e.g. pick part, set, tighten). It is the unit for time measurement and improvement.

chunks.t: Glossary › Standard time
chunks.x: Standard time (ST): The time required for a qualified operator working at a normal pace to do a job by the specified method. Standard time = Observed time × Rating × (1 + Allowance).

chunks.t: Glossary › Rating (performance rating)
chunks.x: Rating (performance rating): A factor that compares the observed operator's pace with the normal pace (normal = 100%). It adjusts observed time to obtain normal time.

chunks.t: Glossary › Allowance
chunks.x: Allowance: The extra time for personal needs, fatigue and unavoidable delays, expressed as a percentage of normal time.

chunks.t: Glossary › Predetermined Time Standards
chunks.x: Predetermined Time Standards (PTS): A method that builds work time from pre-set time values for basic motions. MTM and WF are typical; time can be estimated at design stage without stopwatch measurement.

chunks.t: Glossary › Therblig
chunks.x: Therblig: About 18 basic motion elements (grasp, transport, search, etc.) defined by Gilbreth. Used to separate value-adding motions from wasteful ones for motion improvement.

chunks.t: Glossary › Principles of motion economy
chunks.x: Principles of motion economy: A set of principles for efficient, low-fatigue motion, covering use of the body, arrangement of the workplace and design of tools and equipment. Core idea: eliminate, reduce, do simultaneously, make easier.

chunks.t: Glossary › Work area
chunks.x: Work area: The reach of an operator's hands. The normal work area (forearm reach) and maximum work area (full-arm reach); frequently used parts and tools belong in the normal area.

chunks.t: Glossary › Process analysis
chunks.x: Process analysis: A method that records and analyses the sequence of steps a product or worker goes through, classified into operation, transport, delay, inspection, etc. It makes waste in the flow visible.

chunks.t: Glossary › Process chart symbols
chunks.x: Process chart symbols: Symbols used in process analysis: operation (○), transport (⇨), delay/storage (▽ / D) and inspection (□). Only operation adds value.

chunks.t: Glossary › Flow diagram
chunks.x: Flow diagram: A layout drawing on which the movement paths of people or materials are drawn as lines. It reveals long transport distances, crossings and backtracking.

chunks.t: Glossary › Man-machine chart
chunks.x: Man-machine chart: A time-scaled chart showing working and idle time of a person and a machine side by side. Used to find operator waiting or machine idle time and to plan multi-machine handling.

chunks.t: Glossary › Work sampling
chunks.x: Work sampling: A statistical method that observes the state of workers or machines at many random moments and estimates utilisation or activity ratios from the frequency. More observations mean smaller error.

chunks.t: Glossary › Line balancing
chunks.x: Line balancing: Distributing work so that each process's CT is as even as possible and close to TT. Poor balance causes waiting at all processes except the neck.

chunks.t: Glossary › Neck (bottleneck) process
chunks.x: Neck (bottleneck) process: The process with the longest CT, which limits the output of the whole line. Improving it directly raises line capacity.

chunks.t: Glossary › Line balance efficiency
chunks.x: Line balance efficiency: An index of how well a line is balanced. Line balance efficiency = Σ standard CT ÷ (reference time × number of processes) × 100%. Closer to 100% means more even load. The basic IE formula puts the neck CT in the reference time; ZEVA measures against the takt time and switches to the neck time only when the neck exceeds takt (spec v29, 16.5). Line balance loss = 100% − line balance efficiency.

chunks.t: Glossary › Neck (bottleneck) time
chunks.x: Neck (bottleneck) time: The standard cycle time of the slowest process (the maximum of the per-process standard cycle times). It sets the pace the line can actually run. The reference time for line balance is whichever is larger, the takt time or the neck time (spec v29, 16.5).

chunks.t: Glossary › Yamazumi chart
chunks.x: Yamazumi chart: A stacked bar chart of work elements per process or operator, compared with a TT line. It shows the neck and the line balance loss at a glance and is used to rebalance work.

chunks.t: Glossary › Overall Equipment Effectiveness
chunks.x: Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE): An index of how effectively equipment is used. OEE = Availability × Performance × Yield rate. In ZEVA it is a GPC-M metric (target ≥ 85%) and a result (Y) indicator.

chunks.t: Glossary › Availability
chunks.x: Availability: The share of loading time in which the equipment actually runs. Reduced by stop losses such as breakdowns, setup and adjustment.

chunks.t: Glossary › Performance
chunks.x: Performance: How much was produced at the ideal speed during running time. Performance = Ideal CT × Output ÷ Operating time. Reduced by minor stops and speed loss.

chunks.t: Glossary › Yield rate
chunks.x: Yield rate: The share of pieces that came out good with no repair or rework (Good) against total production excluding Trial. Yield rate = Good ÷ total production (excluding Trial). Pieces recovered by repair or rework do not count. It is a component of OEE.

chunks.t: Glossary › Six big losses
chunks.x: Six big losses: Six losses that reduce equipment effectiveness: breakdowns and setup/adjustment (availability), minor stops and reduced speed (performance), defects/repair and start-up losses (quality).

chunks.t: Glossary › Mean
chunks.x: Mean (μ / x̄): The sum of the data divided by the count; it represents the centre of a distribution. Symbol μ (population) or x̄ (sample). The mean alone says nothing about variation.

chunks.t: Glossary › Median
chunks.x: Median: The middle value when data are sorted. It is robust against outliers.

chunks.t: Glossary › Range
chunks.x: Range (R): The difference between the maximum and minimum (R = Max − Min). Easy to calculate; used as R (within-subgroup variation) in the X̄-R chart.

chunks.t: Glossary › Variance
chunks.x: Variance (σ²): The average of squared deviations from the mean; a measure of spread. When estimating population variance from a sample, divide by n−1.

chunks.t: Glossary › Standard deviation
chunks.x: Standard deviation (σ): The square root of the variance; it expresses how far data spread from the mean, in the same unit as the data. Symbol σ (sample: s).

chunks.t: Glossary › Coefficient of variation
chunks.x: Coefficient of variation (CV): The standard deviation divided by the mean (CV = σ ÷ μ). It lets you compare relative variation between data with different units or averages. ZEVA's V.Score uses this idea.

chunks.t: Glossary › Histogram
chunks.x: Histogram: A bar chart of frequencies of data grouped into intervals. It shows the centre, spread and shape (bimodal, skewed, etc.) of a distribution. One of the QC seven tools.

chunks.t: Glossary › Normal distribution
chunks.x: Normal distribution: A symmetric bell-shaped distribution around the mean. About 68.3% of data fall within ±1σ, 95.4% within ±2σ and 99.7% within ±3σ.

chunks.t: Glossary › Common cause
chunks.x: Common cause: The many small, ever-present causes that produce natural variation in a process. A process with only common causes is stable and predictable.

chunks.t: Glossary › Special cause
chunks.x: Special cause: An identifiable cause of unusual variation such as a broken tool, a new material lot or a deviation from procedure. Detected on a control chart as out-of-limit points or abnormal patterns and removed.

chunks.t: Glossary › Control chart
chunks.x: Control chart: A time-series chart with a centre line and upper/lower control limits used to judge whether a process is in statistical control. Invented by Shewhart.

chunks.t: Glossary › X̄-R chart
chunks.x: X̄-R chart: The typical variables control chart that monitors subgroup averages (X̄) and ranges (R) of small subgroups (e.g. n = 5). The X̄ chart detects shifts in the mean; the R chart detects changes in within-group variation.

chunks.t: Glossary › Control limit
chunks.x: Control limit (UCL / LCL): Boundaries calculated statistically from the process's own data (usually centre line ± 3σ). They are the "voice of the process" and are different from specification limits.

chunks.t: Glossary › Specification limit
chunks.x: Specification limit (USL / LSL): The upper (USL) and lower (LSL) tolerance of a product characteristic set by design or customer requirements. They are the "voice of the customer".

chunks.t: Glossary › Process capability index Cp
chunks.x: Process capability index Cp (Cp): The ratio of the specification width to the process spread (6σ). Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6σ. It ignores off-centring.

chunks.t: Glossary › Process capability index Cpk
chunks.x: Process capability index Cpk (Cpk): A capability index that accounts for off-centring. Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL) ÷ 3σ. ≥ 1.33 is generally sufficient; it presupposes a process in statistical control. It is taught here as general IE knowledge: ZEVA does not use it as a process metric (ZEVA uses control charts, OEE, V.Score and the defect rate).

chunks.t: Glossary › State of statistical control
chunks.x: State of statistical control: A state in which variation from special causes has been removed and only common causes remain. A process not in this state has no definable capability (Shewhart's principle).

chunks.t: Glossary › 5S
chunks.x: 5S (5S): Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardize and Sustain. By removing unnecessary items and keeping needed items ready to use, it builds the foundation of a reproducible workplace.

chunks.t: Glossary › 3 Fixes (3-tei)
chunks.x: 3 Fixes (3-tei): Fixed position (where), fixed item (what) and fixed quantity (how many). It physically removes non-value work such as searching and the variation it causes.

chunks.t: Glossary › Standard work
chunks.x: Standard work: The currently best, safe, quality-assured and waste-free way of doing the work. It consists of takt time, work sequence and standard in-process stock, and serves as the baseline for improvement.

chunks.t: Glossary › ECRS
chunks.x: ECRS (ECRS): Eliminate, Combine, Rearrange, Simplify — consider improvement ideas in this order. The top priority is E: "is this work really needed?"

chunks.t: Glossary › PDCA cycle
chunks.x: PDCA cycle (PDCA): A management cycle for continuous improvement: Plan → Do → Check → Act, repeated.

chunks.t: Glossary › 5 Whys
chunks.x: 5 Whys: An analysis method that repeatedly asks "why?" (about five times) to move from the symptom to the root cause.

chunks.t: Glossary › Fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram
chunks.x: Fishbone (cause-and-effect) diagram: A fish-shaped diagram organising the relationship between an effect and its possible causes, using main bones such as 4M. One of the QC seven tools.

chunks.t: Glossary › Pareto chart
chunks.x: Pareto chart: A bar chart of categories sorted by size combined with a cumulative-percentage line. It finds the "vital few" to set priorities.

chunks.t: Glossary › QC seven tools
chunks.x: QC seven tools: Pareto chart, fishbone diagram, check sheet, histogram, scatter diagram, control chart and graphs (or stratification): the basic tools for data-based quality improvement.

chunks.t: Glossary › Poka-yoke
chunks.x: Poka-yoke: A mechanism or jig that prevents human error from creating defects or from passing defects to the next process.

chunks.t: Glossary › ZEVA (Zero Variation Production System)
chunks.x: ZEVA (Zero Variation Production System) (ZEVA): A next-generation production system with the theoretical value as its purpose foundation and GPC as its method foundation, centred on controlling variation. It is a production system for designing and running all production activity, not an improvement tool.

chunks.t: Glossary › Definition of "Zero"
chunks.x: Definition of "Zero": "Zero" in ZEVA does not mean variation has vanished; it means variation is under control, good quality is guaranteed and convergence to the theoretical value continues. Stage 1: all parameters within the GPC band; Stage 2: move the distribution centre toward the theoretical value.

chunks.t: Glossary › Center-Aiming
chunks.x: Center-Aiming: Moving the centre of a distribution that is already within the GPC band toward the Target (theoretical value). It is Stage 2 (the aspiration) of "Zero".

chunks.t: Glossary › ZEVA four-layer structure
chunks.x: ZEVA four-layer structure: The implementation structure: Layer 1 theoretical value (purpose), Layer 2 Hybrid Triage (routing), Layer 3 GPC control theory (method), Layer 4 PDCA-S + 7 factors + XY thinking (execution). Upper layers guide lower layers.

chunks.t: Glossary › Root logic
chunks.x: Root logic: The chain of logic that improvement must be data-based action, which requires reliable data (low variation, no bias). Therefore eliminating uncontrolled variation as far as possible is the prerequisite for data-based improvement.

chunks.t: Glossary › Shewhart's principle
chunks.x: Shewhart's principle: "A process that is not in statistical control has no definable process capability." In an unstable process today's data do not predict tomorrow, so the defect rate or V.Score can be calculated but mean nothing. It is the theoretical basis of ZEVA's root logic.

chunks.t: Glossary › Data reliability
chunks.x: Data reliability: The degree to which data can be trusted in both variation (precision) and bias (accuracy) and used as a basis for action. It requires the process to be in statistical control.

chunks.t: Glossary › Precision
chunks.x: Precision: How small the spread is when the same thing is measured repeatedly. High precision = small variation. It is a different concept from accuracy.

chunks.t: Glossary › Accuracy (trueness)
chunks.x: Accuracy (trueness): How close the average of measurements is to the true value, i.e. how small the bias is. Ensured by calibration.

chunks.t: Glossary › Foundation: standardization
chunks.x: Foundation: standardization: The precondition for ZEVA's three principles, including 5S/3-tei, 4M standards, standard work and ensured reproducibility. "No improvement without standards" — without reproducibility neither measurement nor improvement works. It is also the starting point of the virtuous cycle.

chunks.t: Glossary › Initial standard
chunks.x: Initial standard: The first standard decided when standardizing. It is not the optimum; its purpose is to create common conditions (a measurable state) where the same method and the same way of measuring allow comparison.

chunks.t: Glossary › Outcome standard
chunks.x: Outcome standard: A standard that locks in the state improved through improvement activities. It becomes the starting line for the next improvement and keeps updating the foundation that began with the initial standard.

chunks.t: Glossary › Quick standardization
chunks.x: Quick standardization: The normal way of standardizing: running "decide → keep → revise" quickly. The initial standard is decided on the same day, or within 3 days at most as a guide, and the "five questions" and the specification check are always done.

chunks.t: Glossary › Deep standardization
chunks.x: Deep standardization: Standardization that builds the standard from the specification basis with Steps 0–8, only where the criteria apply (safety, critical quality characteristics, specification requirements, etc.). The team leader decides which mode applies (Quick or Deep), and the process engineer confirms it.

chunks.t: Glossary › ZEVA's three principles
chunks.x: ZEVA's three principles: ① Variation countermeasures (what to focus on), ② theoretical-value thinking (where to aim), ③ PDCA+S (how to sustain and evolve). They stand on the foundation of standardization and drive the cycle "foundation → principles → improvement → updated foundation".

chunks.t: Glossary › Theoretical value
chunks.x: Theoretical value (Theoretical value): An improvement philosophy: "flow only value work at the fastest speed and cut everything else as loss". It defines the physically and technically ideal state (theoretical value) and designs targets backward from it. It is ZEVA's purpose foundation (Layer 1).

chunks.t: Glossary › Value work
chunks.x: Value work: The "moment" of work that changes the shape or properties of a product for its required function. Its boundary is set by product design; it is always needed unless the design changes (e.g. the moment a bolt reaches the specified torque).

chunks.t: Glossary › Semi-value work
chunks.x: Semi-value work: The minimum work accompanying value work under the current method. Its boundary is set by the process/method and can be reduced or removed by changing the method (e.g. grasping a part, setting it in a jig).

chunks.t: Glossary › Non-value work
chunks.x: Non-value work: Pure loss that adds no value. Its boundary is set by execution/management, and it can in principle be made zero under proper management (e.g. walking, waiting, searching, repair).

chunks.t: Glossary › Value-work ratio
chunks.x: Value-work ratio: Value-work time ÷ total work time × 100%; the core indicator of theoretical-value improvement. Typically 10–30% today, with a target of 50–60% or more.

chunks.t: Glossary › Site theoretical value
chunks.x: Site theoretical value: The ideal state achievable with current equipment and methods: site theoretical value = value work + semi-value work (minimum). The first improvement goal.

chunks.t: Glossary › Technical theoretical value
chunks.x: Technical theoretical value: The ideal state in which new technology or methods also remove semi-value work: technical theoretical value = value work only. A guide for future technology development and investment.

chunks.t: Glossary › Required quality
chunks.x: Required quality: The quality the product is required to have. Higher is not always better: it is set after the planning, development and production functions have examined and verified it, and after mass-production feasibility has been confirmed.

chunks.t: Glossary › Over-quality
chunks.x: Over-quality: Quality beyond the required quality. Since quality and cost trade off, the excess only adds cost and adds no value.

chunks.t: Glossary › Required cost
chunks.x: Required cost: The cost frame set on the production side. The required quality must be secured within it. Holding quality down by adding inspection and repair breaks this frame.

chunks.t: Glossary › Good-part range
chunks.x: Good-part range: The range of conditions that yields good parts. In injection moulding, both too fast and too slow produce defects; only the range in between is the good-part range. Confirmed by physical trials and fixed as a range of process conditions, it becomes the GPC band.

chunks.t: Glossary › Management loss
chunks.x: Management loss: The gap between the current state and the site theoretical value, made of non-value work. It breaks down into five losses: motion, stop, speed, quality and flow (Loss structure chart). It can be tackled immediately by better management (3-tei, layout, ECRS).

chunks.t: Glossary › Technical loss
chunks.x: Technical loss: The gap between the site and technical theoretical values, made of semi-value work. It is resolved by method changes or equipment investment.

chunks.t: Glossary › Absolute-value thinking
chunks.x: Absolute-value thinking: Instead of the analytic approach of subtracting waste from the current state (current − waste = improved), define the theoretical value and add necessary semi-value work to design the ideal (theoretical value + semi-value = target state).

chunks.t: Glossary › Seven variation factors
chunks.x: Seven variation factors: The seven input (X) factors ZEVA controls: Man, Machine, Material, Method, Measurement, Management and Environment. Each is controlled by GPC-M or GPC-H.

chunks.t: Glossary › XY thinking
chunks.x: XY thinking: The mindset that OEE, time and quality are results (Y), not causes (X). To improve results, control the upstream causes (seven variation factors). Manipulating Y directly (stricter inspection, rushing workers, overtime) is not allowed.

chunks.t: Glossary › GPC (Good Process Conditions)
chunks.x: GPC (Good Process Conditions) (GPC): ZEVA's method-foundation control theory: define the range of process conditions verified by physical experiments to guarantee good products, and guarantee production within that range.

chunks.t: Glossary › GPC band
chunks.x: GPC band: The range of process conditions that guarantees good products, defined by GPC_min, GPC_max and the Target (theoretical value). It is not a statistical control limit but a range confirmed by physical experiments.

chunks.t: Glossary › GPC-M (Machine)
chunks.x: GPC-M (Machine) (GPC-M): The method specialised in range control of equipment parameters. Set the GPC band by physical experiment, monitor continuously by recording, and evaluate by band conformance rate, OEE, defect rate and X̄-R chart.

chunks.t: Glossary › GPC-H (Human)
chunks.x: GPC-H (Human) (GPC-H): The method specialised in eliminating variation in human work. Design work with ECRS and the principles of motion stability, define standard work with 4M standards, and evaluate by V.Score and CT achievement rate from CT measurement.

chunks.t: Glossary › Overall Labor Effectiveness
chunks.x: Overall Labor Effectiveness (OLE): The overall effectiveness of human work: OLE = Availability × Performance × Yield rate. It is the OEE idea applied to people and is a GPC-H metric, with a target of ≥ 85%. When it is low, break it down with V.Score (Variation Score) and CT achievement rate.

chunks.t: Glossary › V.Score (Variation Score)
chunks.x: V.Score (Variation Score) (V.Score): The coefficient of variation of work time, V.Score = σ ÷ μ; the core GPC-H metric. Target < 0.1. 0.1–0.3 stable, 0.3–0.5 slightly unstable, 0.5–1.0 unstable, ≥ 1.0 very unstable. Interpretation presupposes a stable process.

chunks.t: Glossary › CT achievement rate
chunks.x: CT achievement rate: The share of cycles completed within the standard CT. A GPC-H metric with a target of ≥ 95%.

chunks.t: Glossary › GPC band conformance rate
chunks.x: GPC band conformance rate: The share of measured values within the GPC band. A GPC-M metric with a target of ≥ 99%.

chunks.t: Glossary › Quality categories
chunks.x: Quality categories: The recording units for counting quality loss: Good, Rework, Repair, Scrap and Trial (pieces made to confirm conditions). Categories are counted in pieces; losses are counted in time.

chunks.t: Glossary › Defect rate
chunks.x: Defect rate: (Rework + Repair + Scrap) ÷ total production (excluding Trial). A GPC-M metric for the size of quality loss; the target is set per product and process from the required quality.

chunks.t: Glossary › Own-process completion
chunks.x: Own-process completion: The state in which only good products can be handed to the next process without added inspection, because the conditions (X) are inside the GPC band and standard work is followed. Do not accept, make or pass on defects. It is not a principle or a method but the state of a process where GPC-M / GPC-H holds, and the way responsibility is carried.

chunks.t: Glossary › Judgment criteria
chunks.x: Judgment criteria: The criteria an operator uses to judge good or bad on the spot (limit samples, gauges, numbers). They are written into standard work at each key point and set from the required quality.

chunks.t: Glossary › Outflow rate
chunks.x: Outflow rate: Outflow is a defect found in a process later than the one where it was made. Outflow rate = defects made in the process and found in a later process ÷ total production of that process (excluding Trial). It measures whether own-process completion holds.

chunks.t: Glossary › Principles of motion stability
chunks.x: Principles of motion stability: Three laws (distance/displacement, sequence accumulation, constraint and guide) for structurally eliminating work variation in GPC-H, based on the premise that every motion is a source of variation.

chunks.t: Glossary › Law of distance and displacement
chunks.x: Law of distance and displacement: First law of motion stability: shortening motion distance physically shrinks the room for variation. The shorter the distance, the less room to deviate.

chunks.t: Glossary › Law of sequence accumulation
chunks.x: Law of sequence accumulation: Second law of motion stability: reducing the number of motions removes opportunities for variation. Fewer motions means "rolling the dice" fewer times.

chunks.t: Glossary › Law of constraint and guide
chunks.x: Law of constraint and guide: Third law of motion stability: limiting degrees of freedom structurally blocks variation. Motions constrained by guides or stoppers approach zero variation.

chunks.t: Glossary › Hybrid triage
chunks.x: Hybrid triage: The mechanism that evaluates every improvement issue at the entrance (Phase 0) and routes it to Quick GPC or Deep GPC mode using four criteria: cause hypothesis, number of variables, risk and data. It is ZEVA's Layer 2.

chunks.t: Glossary › Quick GPC mode
chunks.x: Quick GPC mode: The fast improvement mode (1 day – 1 week) for issues with a cause hypothesis, low risk and few variables. A "think while running" approach using the H-T-C-A cycle; no statistical knowledge required.

chunks.t: Glossary › Deep GPC mode
chunks.x: Deep GPC mode: The deep analysis mode (1–3 months) for issues with unknown cause, high risk or many variables. A "stop and think deeply" approach using DMAIC to identify root causes statistically.

chunks.t: Glossary › H-T-C-A cycle
chunks.x: H-T-C-A cycle (H-T-C-A): The four-step improvement cycle of Quick GPC: Hypothesis → Trial (small quantity) → Check (immediate) → Action (standardize or retry).

chunks.t: Glossary › Temporary standard
chunks.x: Temporary standard: A provisional standard that applies a successful Quick GPC condition on the same day without waiting for formal revision. Valid for up to 30 days, within which formal approval is obtained; limited to a single line and always reversible.

chunks.t: Glossary › Knowledge base
chunks.x: Knowledge base: A shared database of Quick GPC trial results (both successes and failures), Deep GPC analyses, changed GPC bands and revised standard work. It prevents needless repeat experiments and improves triage accuracy.

chunks.t: Glossary › Escalation
chunks.x: Escalation: Switching from Quick GPC to Deep GPC. Triggers: no effect after three H-T-C-A cycles, no hypotheses left, recurrence of the problem, or a larger impact than expected.

chunks.t: Glossary › Work instruction
chunks.x: Work instruction (WI): A document used on the floor that shows work steps, key points and quality criteria. In ZEVA it is made so specific that it can be interpreted only one way by anyone, using photos and videos.

chunks.t: Glossary › PDCA-S (PDCA+S)
chunks.x: PDCA-S (PDCA+S) (PDCA-S): Plan, Do, Check, Act plus Standardize. It is the daily operation cycle that sustains the improved state, and as ZEVA principle ③ it feeds improvements back into standards and keeps updating the foundation.

chunks.t: Glossary › SOP (Standard Operating Procedure)
chunks.x: SOP (Standard Operating Procedure) (SOP): An official document defining the standard steps, conditions and responsibilities of a job or process. After Deep GPC the SOP is revised and embedded together with training.

chunks.t: Glossary › Four boxes
chunks.x: Four boxes: The logical thinking framework of theoretical-value improvement: ① current value, ② current way, ③ new way, ④ target value, each filled with a conclusion and grounds. Going back and forth between hypothesis and verification sharpens the improvement scenario.

chunks.t: Glossary › Loss structure chart
chunks.x: Loss structure chart: A chart that splits total actual time into value, semi-value and non-value work, breaks non-value work into five losses (motion, stop, speed, quality, flow) and shows their proportions. Quality-loss time (defects, repair, scrap) counts as non-value work whatever its cause. Used to decide which high-impact losses to tackle first.

chunks.t: Glossary › DMAIC
chunks.x: DMAIC (DMAIC): The five-step improvement cycle Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control. In ZEVA it is the Deep GPC cycle for statistically solving issues with unknown causes or high risk.

chunks.t: Glossary › Measurement System Analysis
chunks.x: Measurement System Analysis (MSA): A method for evaluating the error of the measurement system (gauge, appraiser, method). It checks repeatability and reproducibility (precision) and bias/calibration (accuracy) to guarantee data reliability.

chunks.t: Glossary › Design of Experiments
chunks.x: Design of Experiments (DOE): A method that changes several factor conditions in a planned way to find factor effects, interactions and optimal conditions with few trials. Variation intentionally introduced in DOE is not variation to eliminate but a source of learning.

chunks.t: Glossary › Gage R&R
chunks.x: Gage R&R (GRR): The typical MSA method quantifying repeatability (same appraiser and gauge) and reproducibility (between appraisers). Rule of thumb: %GRR 30% unacceptable.

chunks.t: Glossary › SIPOC
chunks.x: SIPOC (SIPOC): A one-page overview of a process in the flow Supplier – Input – Process – Output – Customer. Used in the Define phase to set scope.

chunks.t: Glossary › CTQ (Critical to Quality)
chunks.x: CTQ (Critical to Quality) (CTQ): A measurable product or process characteristic that is critical to meeting customer requirements. Clarified as the Y to improve in the Define phase.

chunks.t: Glossary › Regression analysis
chunks.x: Regression analysis: A statistical method that expresses the relationship between a result (Y) and one or more factors (X) as an equation and estimates the size of their effects.

chunks.t: Glossary › Analysis of variance
chunks.x: Analysis of variance (ANOVA): A statistical method that decomposes total variation into components by factor and tests whether differences in means between groups (e.g. lots, operators) are significant or due to chance.

chunks.t: Glossary › Hypothesis testing
chunks.x: Hypothesis testing: A statistical procedure that sets a null hypothesis ("no difference") and decides from data whether it can be rejected at a significance level (e.g. 5%). Examples: t-test, chi-square test.

chunks.t: Glossary › Control plan
chunks.x: Control plan: A document specifying what to measure, how often, by what method and how to react to abnormalities in the improved process. Created in the Control phase and handed over to PDCA-S.

chunks.t: Glossary › Pilot run
chunks.x: Pilot run: A trial of an improvement on a limited scope and quantity before full deployment, to verify effects and side effects. Performed in the Improve phase.

chunks.t: Glossary › DX (digital transformation)
chunks.x: DX (digital transformation) (DX): A term that reaches as far as changing the business model. ZEVA is about accelerating shop-floor improvement, which is narrower, so this material avoids the word DX and speaks of digitisation (Level 2) and digitalisation (Level 3) instead.

chunks.t: Glossary › Staged digitalisation model
chunks.x: Staged digitalisation model: A model that treats digitalisation as an accelerator, not a prerequisite, implemented in three levels: Level 1 (analog), Level 2 (digitisation), Level 3 (digitalisation). ZEVA works at every level, and the digital level is independent of improvement quality.

chunks.t: Formulas › Time
chunks.x:
Available time: Available time = Shift time − Planned non-production time (breaks, meetings) — The numerator of the takt-time formula.
Takt time: TT = Available time ÷ Required quantity — Set by demand. Example: 25,200 s ÷ 420 units = 60 s
Capacity: Capacity = Available time ÷ Neck CT — Demand can be met when CT ≤ TT.
Normal time: Normal time = Observed time × Rating — Rating is judged against normal pace = 100%.
Standard time: Standard time = Observed time × Rating × (1 + Allowance) — Example: 50 s × 1.10 × 1.12 ≈ 61.6 s

chunks.t: Formulas › Line balance
chunks.x:
Line balance efficiency (basic IE formula): Line balance efficiency = ΣCT ÷ (Neck CT × Number of processes) × 100% — Closer to 100% means a more even load. The basic IE formula uses the neck CT as its reference; ZEVA uses the takt time (next entry).
Line balance efficiency (takt-based): Line balance efficiency = Σ standard CT ÷ (reference time × number of processes) × 100% Reference time = the larger of takt time and neck time — The ZEVA method. The reference switches to the neck time only when the neck exceeds takt (spec v29, 16.5).
Line balance loss: Line balance loss = 100% − line balance efficiency — The share of waiting at non-neck processes.
Required workers (theoretical): Required workers = ΣCT ÷ TT — Round up, and aim to absorb the fraction through improvement.

chunks.t: Formulas › OEE
chunks.x:
Availability: Availability = (Loading time − Downtime) ÷ Loading time — Reduced by stops such as breakdowns and setup.
Performance: Performance = (Ideal CT × Total output) ÷ Operating time — Reduced by minor stops and reduced speed.
Yield rate: Yield rate = Good ÷ total production (excluding Trial) — Reduced by defects, repair and start-up losses.
OEE: OEE = Availability × Performance × Yield rate — In ZEVA a GPC-M metric, target ≥ 85%. It is a result (Y) indicator.

chunks.t: Formulas › Statistics
chunks.x:
Mean: x̄ = Σxi ÷ n — Centre of the distribution; says nothing about spread.
Range: R = Max − Min — A simple measure of spread.
Standard deviation (sample): s = √( Σ(xi − x̄)² ÷ (n − 1) ) — Divide by n when the data are the whole population (σ).
Coefficient of variation: CV = σ ÷ μ — Compares variation between data with different means.
Normal distribution coverage: μ ± 1σ ≈ 68.3% μ ± 2σ ≈ 95.4% μ ± 3σ ≈ 99.7% — Share of data expected within each range.
Work sampling: required observations: n = z² × p(1 − p) ÷ e² (95% confidence: z ≈ 2) — p: estimated ratio, e: allowed error (absolute). Example: p = 0.7, e = 0.05 → n ≈ 336

chunks.t: Formulas › Control charts & capability
chunks.x:
X̄ chart control limits: UCL / LCL = X̿ ± A2 × R̄ (n = 5: A2 = 0.577) — Monitors shifts in subgroup averages.
R chart control limits: UCL = D4 × R̄, LCL = D3 × R̄ (n = 5: D4 = 2.114, D3 = 0) — Monitors changes in within-subgroup variation.
Estimating σ from the chart: σ ≈ R̄ ÷ d2 (n = 5: d2 = 2.326) — Valid only when the process is in statistical control.
Cp: Cp = (USL − LSL) ÷ 6σ — Ignores off-centring.
Cpk: Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL) ÷ 3σ — Guideline ≥ 1.33 (sufficient), ≥ 1.67 (very good). Confirm stability first (Shewhart's principle).

chunks.t: Formulas › Theoretical value / ZEVA metrics
chunks.x:
V.Score: V.Score = σ ÷ μ (work time) — A GPC-H metric with a target of < 0.1. Bands: < 0.1 extremely stable / 0.1–0.3 stable / 0.3–0.5 slightly unstable / 0.5–1.0 unstable / ≥ 1.0 very unstable.
CT achievement rate: CT achievement = Cycles within standard CT ÷ All cycles × 100% — GPC-H metric, target ≥ 95%.
GPC band conformance rate: Conformance = Measurements within GPC_min–GPC_max ÷ All measurements × 100% — GPC-M metric, target ≥ 99%.
OLE (Overall Labor Effectiveness): OLE = Availability × Performance × Yield rate — The overall effectiveness of human work. A GPC-H metric, target ≥ 85%. When it is low, break it down with V.Score and the CT achievement rate.
Defect rate: Defect rate = (Rework + Repair + Scrap) ÷ Total production excluding Trial × 100% — GPC-M metric. The target is set per product and process from the required quality.
Outflow rate: Outflow rate = Defects made in the process and found in a later process ÷ Total production of that process excluding Trial × 100% — Measures whether own-process completion holds. Record both the process of origin and the process of detection for each defect.
Value-work ratio: Value-work ratio = Value-work time ÷ Total work time × 100% — Typically 10–30% today; target 50–60% or more.
Site theoretical value: Site theoretical value = Value work + Semi-value work (minimum) — The ideal achievable with current equipment and methods.
Technical theoretical value: Technical theoretical value = Value work only — The ideal when new technology also removes semi-value work.
Management loss: Management loss = Current − Site theoretical value (= non-value work) — Resolved by better management.
Technical loss: Technical loss = Site theoretical value − Technical theoretical value (= semi-value work) — Resolved by method change or equipment investment.
Design approach (absolute-value thinking): Theoretical value + Semi-value = Target state (vs. Current − Waste = Improved) — Work backward from the ideal instead of extending the present.
Sequence accumulation (intuition): Probability all motions succeed = (1 − p)n (p: error probability per motion, n: number of motions) — Example: p = 1%, n = 30 → about 74%. Fewer motions = more stable.
